A scholar of comparative religion, Frithjof Schuon, made the same point in 1970: the superhuman value of a revealed Book cannot be fully apparent from its earthly form or its conceptual content alone, because its divine and miraculous quality is of a different order from the most perfect dialectic or the most brilliant poetry. It shows first in a richness of meaning that cannot be imitated, and then in a kind of underlying divine "magic" that shines through the outward form and is proved by what it does in souls and in the world, across space and across time. Only that divine substance explains the spiritual power of the Qur'an's verses, the miraculously rapid spread of early Islam in the conditions in which it happened, the stability of Muslim institutions and the extraordinary fruitfulness of Islamic doctrine.

### A warning for the enemies and good news for the friends

Allah veiled the eyes of the outsiders, so His beloved ﷺ went unseen by them, and having lost the light of His care they wandered through the valleys of conjecture. Signs brought by the Messenger ﷺ and miracles shown to them only made their doubts and suspicions deeper. Such is the way of people who have turned from the Real: the clearer the proofs, the blinder they become to the truth, as Allah said, "neither signs nor warners are of any benefit to those who refuse to believe" (10:101). To force them to concede the proof, He told them that they were unable to compete with the miracle He had given them in the Qur'an, a miracle triumphant over mankind from first to last. He made them acknowledge that even if they joined forces, strengthened themselves with others like them, and spent every effort and stratagem, they could not bring a surah like any surah of the Qur'an. He said "if you are unable", then declared that they could not and would not, "and you will never be able". It is as if He said: look to yourselves, and beware the idolatry that leads to the punishment of the Fire fuelled by men and stones. When the believers' hearts were gripped with dread at the mention of the Fire, He steadied them by adding "prepared for the disbelievers", and in that is good news for the believers. This is the Real's way: when He frightens His enemies He gladdens His friends. The disbelievers' deceit vanishes before the prophets' miracles, and in the same way the pretensions of the confused melt away once the lights of the truthful shine out. The mark of the false claimant is that the driving cries return to his heart. The mark of the person of truthful intent is that the divine subjugation takes hold of his heart. Rare is the person who can tell these two apart.

Those whose hearts are attached to things other than Allah find the call of true religion repellent. They are so attached to their supposed deities that they cannot believe them unreal, and they cannot believe that the truth is what a mortal like themselves proclaims.

### In short

- "You will never be able to" is a prophecy made in the face of the Arabs' pride and hatred, and it has never been falsified. Its fulfilment is itself a miracle.
- The inimitability lies not only in style but in the Qur'an's truth, justice, freshness under repetition, and power to move and to transform.
- The Fire's fuel is the disbelievers and stones, sulphur or their own idols, and "prepared" shows that Hell exists already, as the hadiths of the falling stone and the Fire's two breaths confirm.
- The challenge covers the shortest surah, as Musaylimah's attempt showed, and every supposed answer to it, ancient or modern, has been a failure that the enemies of Islam themselves would have preserved had it been otherwise.
- The verse ends with a mercy: the Fire is "prepared for the disbelievers", which is a reassurance to those who believe.

25.text:
After the Fire, the Gardens. "Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,” for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺. They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever". Having described the punishment prepared for His enemies who deny Him and His messengers, Allah turns to the state of His happy, loyal friends who believe in Him and His messengers, hold to the faith and do good. This pairing is why the Qur'an is called mathānī, according to the sounder view of the scholars: it mentions faith and then disbelief, or disbelief and then faith, the wretched and then the happy, or the reverse. Mentioning like with like is a different thing, called tashābuh.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Give good news ˹O Prophet˺"** means: inform them of what will delight them. The warnings of the previous verses were for the disbelievers, and now the Messenger ﷺ is told to address the believers. The address to the Makkan idolaters that began at verse 21 ends here, with a verse revealed about the believers, so that their reward is mentioned right after the reward of the disbelievers.

**"to those who believe and do good"** means those who have faith in Allah, in Muhammad ﷺ and in the Qur'an, and who perform righteous deeds, the obligatory and the voluntary acts of worship, the acts of obedience that bind them to their Lord, or, more broadly, any righteous deed. The condition of good deeds is added on purpose. Faith alone does not earn these glad tidings. Faith does save a person from staying in the Fire forever, and every Muslim, however great a sinner, will in the end be brought out of Hell after a period of punishment. But no one escapes the Fire altogether without the good deeds the Sharīʿah defines.

**"that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow"** means gardens of trees and dwellings with rivers running beneath the trees and the palaces, rivers of water, milk, honey and wine. The Arabic nahr is the channel in which water flows, so named because the water carves its way through it, and calling the rivers "running" is a figure of speech. From the hadith it is known that the rivers of Paradise do not run in valleys, that the banks of al-Kawthar, the Prophet's ﷺ river in Paradise, are domes of hollow pearl, that the soil of Paradise is fragrant musk and its stones are pearls and jewels. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that these rivers have their source beneath hills, or mountains, of musk. Masrūq related the same from ʿAbdullāh: the rivers of Paradise come out from under mountains of musk. We ask Allah for Paradise, for He is the Most Beneficent, Most Gracious.

**"Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,”"** means that whenever they are fed from these gardens, with fruit of every kind, they will say that this is what they ate before. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr that the grass of Paradise is saffron and its hills are musk, and that the boys of everlasting youth will serve the believers fruit, then bring them more that looks the same, and the people of Paradise will remark that this is what was just brought, and the boys will tell them to eat, for the colour is the same but the taste is different.

**"for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺"** is explained in two ways. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, as reported through Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī from ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, said the fruits resemble one another while their tastes differ. On this view "before" means earlier in Paradise itself, and the resemblance between its own fruits is the proof. ʿIkrimah said they resemble the fruits of this world but taste better. Sufyān ath-Thawrī reported through al-Aʿmash and Abū Ẓabyān that Ibn ʿAbbās said nothing in Paradise resembles anything in this world except in name, and in another narration, that only the names are shared. Fruit that carries the same name and shape as earthly fruit lets the believers recognise it and desire it, while the taste is new. Whichever view is taken, the point is that the believers will have a joy in Paradise they never knew before, and that it renews itself at every moment. The fruits of Paradise may share a name with the fruits of the earth, but their nature is different.

A note of caution belongs here. Modernists have for some time liked to claim that when the Qur'an speaks about the fruits and the other joys of Paradise, its language is figurative, hinting at a spiritual bliss that cannot by nature be touched or tasted. Symbolic or analogical interpretation of the Qur'an is not ruled out. Many genuine scholars, the Sufis especially, have practised it with illuminating results. But no real Sufi ever claimed that such interpretation, iʿtibār, is the same thing as tafsīr, or that his reading was the only valid one. Its purpose has always been to aid spiritual realisation or to elaborate doctrine, never to deny or oppose the ordinary exegesis. What the modern exegetes overlook, in their zeal and their simplicity, is that using a thing as a metaphor or symbol does not mean it has no objective existence. Since the Qur'an speaks of the fruits of Paradise and the like, they must exist objectively, though not physically in the current sense of the word, and their nature and state, which we do not know, can safely be left to Allah. That way lies safety, and that is the Straight Path.

**"They will have pure spouses"** means spouses, ḥūrīs and others, purified from everything filthy and impure. Ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported Ibn ʿAbbās's words: purified from filth and impurity. Mujāhid said: from menstruation, from relieving themselves, from urine, spittle, semen and pregnancy. Qatādah said: purified from impurity and from sin, and in another narration, from menstruation and pregnancy. ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abū Ṣāliḥ, ʿAṭiyah and as-Suddī said the same. In short, they will be clean outwardly and pure inwardly, free of everything physically repellent, like excrement and menstruation, and of everything morally repellent, like bad temper or unfaithfulness. They will have none of the unpleasant traits people have on earth.

**"and they will be there forever"** means ultimate happiness. The believers will enjoy a delight that never ends, safe from death and from any break in their bliss. They will neither die nor be expelled from it. In this too the joys of Paradise differ from the joys of the earth: they are not short-lived, and no one will tremble at the thought of losing them. May Allah count us among these believers. He is the Most Generous, Most Kind and Most Merciful.

### A glimpse of the next world

The call of truth is unmistakably marked with a divine radiance. Its inimitable style and its unanswerable reasoning show it to be a message from Allah. Those who deny it in spite of this will find no refuge anywhere in Allah's universe. Those who find Allah in the word of Allah are already given a glimpse of the next world, and it is they who will be admitted to the gardens of Paradise.

### Fear and hope

This verse is a caress for the friends of Allah. It gives them hope of everlasting bounty and bliss and encourages the faithful to obey and to seek an increase of blessing. The previous verse warned the strangers against confusion in the heart and idolatry on the tongue and threatened them with the Fire and with the bitter severing from the Real. The person of faith is the one who, hearing the first verse and thinking of Hell, becomes frightened and loses his ease, and then, hearing the second, becomes glad, makes his heart firm and his hope strong, and brings ease back into his heart. The Lord of the Worlds praises both states. Of the frightened He says, "The ˹true˺ believers are only those whose hearts tremble at the remembrance of Allah" (8:2). Of those at ease He says, "those who believe and whose hearts find comfort in the remembrance of Allah. Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find comfort" (13:28). It is the custom of the Generous Lord that whenever He sends a verse of fear to frighten His servants, He follows it with a verse of hope and mercy to put their hearts at ease, so that they do not despair.

Good news, then, for all who serve today on the field of obedience. Tomorrow their place is the assembly of "serenity, fragrance, and a Garden of Bliss" (56:89). Not everyone who reaches the paradise of approval reaches the generous gift of serenity. The paradise of approval is the furthest limit of the worshipful servants' pleasure. Serenity is the qiblah of the lovers' spirits. The High Chambers and the Abode of Peace make up the paradise of approval, while serenity in the Presence is the gift kept for the spirit of the passionate. Whoever watches over his actions will reach the paradise of approval, and whoever watches over his breaths will reach serenity. Who can explain that serenity, and how can it be put into words? When a thing does not come to the tongue, how can it be described? A wind begins to blow from the world of the unseen, and it is called the wind of bounty.

### What comes next

When the Jews asked why Allah strikes a parable about flies, in the verse where the idols cannot recover what a fly snatches from them, and about a spider, in the verse that likens false protectors to a spider's house, and what He could want with such lowly creatures, Allah revealed the verse that follows.

### In short

- The Qur'an pairs its warning with its promise. After the Fire prepared for the disbelievers comes the Garden promised to those who believe and also do good, for faith without deeds saves from eternal Hell but not from Hell altogether.
- Rivers run beneath the trees and palaces of Paradise, rising from mountains of musk. Its fruits share names and looks with what the believers knew, in this world or earlier in Paradise, but each taste is new, a joy renewed at every moment.
- The fruits of Paradise are real, not mere metaphors, even though their nature is unlike anything physical here.
- Its spouses are pure in body and character, and the whole of it lasts forever, with no fear of loss.

26.text:
The previous verses dared the doubters to produce a single surah like the Qur'an and then promised Gardens to those who believe and do good. Now the Qur'an turns to a specific complaint that the deniers had been making about its style. Allah had compared the hypocrites to a man who lit a fire and to travellers caught in a storm, and elsewhere He had spoken of a fly and a spider. The objectors said that a Book from God would never stoop to such lowly images. This verse answers them. "Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller." The believers, hearing such a comparison, "know that it is the truth from their Lord," while the disbelievers "argue, 'What does Allah mean by such a parable?'" Then comes the deeper point: the same parable becomes a test through which "He leaves many to stray, and guides many," and the only people it leads astray are "the rebellious," whose marks are listed in the verse that follows.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito"** answers the sneer directly. In human speech, being "ashamed" of something means refusing to do it. When Allah says He is not ashamed of a thing, it means simply that He does not refrain from it. Allah is far above shyness and embarrassment, and the expression is used to meet the objectors on their own terms. How could He disdain to mention a creature which all created beings together could never produce? The mosquito is among the tiniest and least regarded of creatures, so it serves as the extreme case: if a mosquito is fit for a parable, nothing is unfit. Grammatically, "parable" (mathal) is the direct object of the verb "strike" or "set forth," and the little word mā that follows it is read either as "whatever that parable may be" or as an extra word that stresses how slight the thing is. Baʿūḍah, the word for mosquito, is the singular of baʿūḍ, the small flying insects.

**"or what is even smaller"** renders the Arabic fa-mā fawqahā, literally "or what is above it." Most scholars understand "above" here as "bigger than it," so that the verse covers everything from the tiniest insect upward and the size of the creature makes no difference to the point being made. Others read it as "beyond it in smallness," which is the sense the translation adopts. Both readings lead to the same conclusion. A hadith uses the very same phrase: ʿĀʾishah reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that no Muslim is pricked by a thorn, fa-mā fawqahā, or anything beyond that, without a good deed being written for him and a sin erased. Muslim recorded it. Some scholars take "what is above it" to mean a fly or a spider in particular, since those are the creatures the Qur'an had already used and the objectors had mocked. A gnat, a fly, a spider or an ant: whatever the lowly creature, the lesson is the same.

**"As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord"** describes the first response to the parable. Mujāhid explained that the believers accept these comparisons whether they concern great matters or small, because they recognise them as the truth from their Lord, and by them Allah increases their guidance. The parable about a mosquito is as much a sign to them as a parable about the heavens.

**"And as for the disbelievers, they argue, 'What does Allah mean by such a parable?'"** is the second response. The question is not a request for information. Mā here is an interrogative of rejection, and "by such a parable" specifies what is being rejected. In plain terms they are saying, "What use is there in this?" They treat the smallness of the image as proof that the words cannot be from God.

**"Through this test, He leaves many to stray, and guides many"** is Allah's reply. One parable, two opposite results. As-Suddī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions that "many" whom He leaves astray means the hypocrites. Allah guides the believers through the parables, while the hypocrites, who know in their hearts that the parables are true, reject them anyway, and so their straying grows. That is how Allah leads them astray: by their own refusal. As for the believers, their guidance is increased by more guidance and their faith by more faith, because they hold firmly to what they know to be true. This is a gift He grants them.

**"And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious"** names the only people whom the parable harms. The word is al-fāsiqīn, those who have stepped outside obedience to Allah. When a date bursts out of its skin the Arabs say it has "fasaqat," and the mouse earned the name fuwaysiqah from its habit of leaving its hole to do damage. ʿĀʾishah reported in the two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that five animals are fawāsiq, to be killed whether one is in iḥrām or not: the crow, the kite, the scorpion, the mouse and the biting dog. In every case the idea is a creature that breaks out of its proper bounds. Fāsiq can describe both a disbeliever and a disobedient Muslim, but the disbeliever's fisq is the graver, and it is this kind that the verse means, because the next verse describes these people as breakers of Allah's covenant and spreaders of corruption.

### Why the verse came down

Several accounts explain the occasion, and they fit together. As-Suddī reported in his Tafsīr from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and some of the Companions that when Allah set forth the two parables about the hypocrites, the man who kindled a fire and the people in the rainstorm, the hypocrites said that Allah is far too exalted to make examples like these, and Allah sent down these verses, from "Surely Allah does not shy away" to "the losers" at the end of verse 27. Saʿīd reported from Qatādah that Allah does not shrink from the truth when He uses something as a parable, whether it is great or small, and that when He mentioned the fly and the spider in His Book the people of misguidance asked why He would mention such things, so He revealed this verse. Another account attributes the objection to the Jews. All of these groups shared one assumption: that the Word of God would never employ contemptible creatures like a gnat or an ant, since such a thing would embarrass even a man with ordinary dignity.

The Qur'an's reply is that when a speaker wants to describe something detestable, whether a thing, a person or a situation, using a gnat or something smaller as the image breaks no rule of eloquence or logic and offends neither dignity nor modesty. A parable is judged by whether it fits, not by the size of what it mentions. The Qur'an adds that doubts of this kind arise only in minds that disbelief has drained of the power to see things in proportion, while believers are never troubled by them.

### What the mosquito teaches

Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī reported from ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas that this verse is an example Allah gave of worldly life. A mosquito lives as long as it is hungry, but when it has fed and grown fat, it dies. So it is with the people Allah describes in the Qur'an: when they have gathered the pleasures of this life, Allah takes them away. He then recited, "When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair" (6:44). The same observation is made by others: the gnat is strong and flies while hungry, and once satiated it splits open and dies, just as "one exceeds all bounds once they think they are self-sufficient" (96:6-7).

Those who read "what is above it" as the fly see a lesson there too. The fly is insolent. However often you drive it away, it comes back. Had that quality been placed in the lion, no human being would be safe, but when Allah created strength in the lion He also created in it an aversion to people, and when He created boldness in the fly He paired it with weakness. In this pairing of qualities the perfection of His wisdom and the reach of His power are on display.

There is a further reflection on why nothing is too small for Allah to mention. Set beside the existence of the Real, the whole of creation is less than a speck of dust in the air, the vanishing of one limited thing in another. For that reason the Throne and the gnat stand equal before His power. Creating the Throne is not hard for Him and creating the gnat is not trivial for Him, for He is too holy to be touched by difficulty or ease. Since that is so, He is no more ashamed to draw a parable from a gnat than from the Throne and everything beneath it.

### Other parables in the Qur'an

The Qur'an uses small and ordinary things for its lessons again and again. It says, "O humanity! A lesson is set forth, so listen to it carefully: those idols you invoke besides Allah can never create so much as a fly, even if they all were to come together for that. And if a fly were to snatch anything away from them, they cannot even retrieve it from the fly" (22:73). It says, "The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah is that of a spider spinning a shelter. And the flimsiest of all shelters is certainly that of a spider, if only they knew" (29:41). It compares a good word to a good tree whose root is firm and whose branches reach the sky, always giving fruit by its Lord's permission, and an evil word to an evil tree torn out of the earth with nothing to hold it, and then explains that "this is how Allah sets forth parables for the people, so perhaps they will be mindful" (14:24-27). It sets forth the parable of a slave who owns nothing beside a free man who gives generously from a good provision (16:75), and of a dumb man who is a burden on his master beside a man who commands justice on a straight path (16:76). And it draws an example from the listeners' own lives, asking whether any of them would let their slaves become equal partners in their wealth (30:28). None of these images is grand. All of them are exact.

### A test that divides people

The verse itself gives the purpose of such parables: they are a trial. For people willing to think and understand, they become a means of guidance. For people who refuse to understand, out of indifference or out of stubborn hostility, they become a cause of deeper confusion. There is wisdom in the choice of each image, and the believer trusts that wisdom while the disbeliever makes fun of it and asks why God speaks of gnats, flies and spiders. Many are misled by these examples because they will not consider them, and many are guided because they learn from them. Allah misleads no one who does not deserve it, and the ones who deserve it are those who refuse to obey Him.

The root of the difference is willingness to learn. A person who does not want to learn never thinks seriously about an argument. He glances at it, looks for a flaw, and seizes on anything that can be made to look irrational or trivial. A person who wants to learn gives the argument real thought and soon realises that he is facing the truth. It makes no difference to such a person that the truth has been illustrated with a gnat or some other insignificant creature. The deniers' tactics, then, are the same in every age: belittling God's message, hunting for flaws in it, and portraying it as concerned with trivialities. The call of truth asks for no more than an honest look.

### Who counts as a fāsiq

Because the verse ends by naming al-fāsiqīn, a word that recurs throughout the Qur'an, it is worth fixing its meaning. The root fasaqa means to go out or to pass beyond a limit. In the language of the Sharīʿah, fisq means going outside the circle of obedience to Allah and transgressing His commands. Transgression does not always stop at disobedient actions. It can lead on to outright denial, so the Qur'an frequently applies the word to a kāfir. A Muslim who sins habitually is also called a fāsiq, and this is how the jurists ordinarily use the term, placing the fāsiq on one side and the kāfir on the other. In their usage, someone guilty of a major sin who has not repented, or who keeps up minor sins until they become a habit, is a fāsiq, while a man who commits such sins openly and without any shame is counted a kāfir. In this verse the fāsiq meant is the one whose rebellion has reached denial.

### Lessons drawn from the verse

One practical rule follows from verse 26. If a speaker or writer wants to explain something useful for the spiritual guidance of his audience, there is nothing sinful or improper in referring to a thing commonly thought contemptible or dirty, and it does not lower his dignity. The Qur'an itself, the hadith, and the writings of the Sufis and other great Muslim scholars all contain images of this kind, and their authors set aside the usual notions of delicacy for the sake of the real goal.

A second lesson concerns how Allah's guidance works. The verse does not say that the parable creates the straying. It says that through the parable Allah leaves astray those who are already rebellious. Guidance and misguidance both pass through the same words. What differs is the heart that receives them, and the verse that follows describes that heart.

### A reading for the inner life

Those whose inner eyes have been opened do not look at created things, or at traces and effects, for their own sake. If they look at all, it is to take heed, or to sharpen the faculty of insight. For such a person a gnat is a lesson and a fly is a lesson, and nothing in creation is beneath notice, because everything in it points beyond itself to the One who made it.

### In short

- The verse answers those who mocked the Qur'an for using images like a mosquito, a fly and a spider: Allah does not refrain from any parable, however small its subject, because a parable is judged by its fitness, not its size.
- Believers recognise such parables as the truth from their Lord, while disbelievers ask what God could mean by them.
- One parable produces two outcomes. It increases the guidance of those who think and the straying of those who refuse, and the only people it harms are the fāsiqīn, those who have broken out of obedience to Allah.
- The mosquito itself carries a lesson: it feeds, grows fat and dies, like people who gather this world's pleasures and are then taken away (6:44).

27.text:
Verse 26 ended by saying that Allah leads none astray through His parables except the rebellious. This verse tells us who they are. They are "those who violate Allah's covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ties Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land." Three marks are given: a broken covenant, severed relationships and corruption. Then the verdict: "It is they who are the true losers." The verse is both a description of the deniers and a mirror held up to anyone who wants to know what rebellion against Allah looks like in practice.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who violate Allah's covenant after it has been affirmed"** opens the description. What covenant is meant? Scholars give several answers that complement each other. The broadest view is that it is Allah's covenant with all His creatures: to obey Him and to avoid what He has forbidden. This covenant has been repeated in His Books and on the tongues of His Messengers, so ignoring it is breaking it. Many connect it with the pledge taken from all humanity before anyone came to the earth, when Allah brought forth the descendants of Ādam (Adam) and asked, "Am I not your Lord?" and they replied, "Yes, You are! We testify" (7:172). Having affirmed Allah as their only Lord, people are bound never to disobey Him, and His Books and prophets come to remind them of this pledge, renew it and teach them how to live by it. Those who break it can hardly be expected to learn from those very prophets and Books.

A second view is that the verse speaks of the disbelievers and hypocrites among the People of the Book. Their covenant was the pledge recorded in the Tawrāh that they would follow Muḥammad ﷺ once he was sent, believing in him and in what he brought. They broke it when they rejected him after they knew the truth about him and concealed that truth from people, even though they had sworn to Allah to do otherwise. Allah tells elsewhere how they tossed that covenant behind their backs and sold it cheaply. On this reading "after it has been affirmed" means after it was confirmed and bound upon them in their own scriptures.

A third view, reported from Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and also held by az-Zamakhsharī, is that the verse covers every disbeliever, idol worshipper and hypocrite. Allah took from them all a pledge to believe in His Oneness by showing them the signs that testify to His Lordship, and He bound them to obey His commands and avoid His prohibitions, knowing that His Messengers would bring proofs and miracles beyond the power of any creature. They broke the covenant when they denied what had been proven to them and rejected His Prophets and Books while knowing they were true. This explanation has been called very good, and it includes the other two.

**"break whatever ties Allah has ordered to be maintained"** is the second mark. Qatādah said it refers to the bonds of kinship, and this is like Allah's words, "Now if you hypocrites turn away, perhaps you would then spread corruption throughout the land and sever your ties of kinship" (47:22). Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī preferred this explanation. Others take the phrase more widely: everything Allah has commanded people to keep joined and nurtured, which they then cut, falls under it. Some include faith in the Prophet ﷺ along with kinship and other matters, and some mention the oaths and family ties that bound the objectors to Muḥammad ﷺ himself. On the grammar, "that it be joined" stands in for the pronoun in "what Allah has commanded," so the sense is "what Allah has commanded to be joined."

Taking the wide reading, the ties Allah has ordered to be maintained include every kind of relationship: the servant's bond with Allah, a person's bonds with parents and relatives, with neighbours and friends, the bond of one Muslim with another, and the bond of one human being with another. Islam itself can be described as the fulfilment of one's obligations in all these relationships, and that is also what following the Sharīʿah means. Religion is the divinely ordained law that binds us to discharge the rights of Allah (ḥuqūq Allāh) and the rights of His servants (ḥuqūq al-ʿibād). Neglect of these obligations breeds every sort of disorder among people, so that transgressors end up destroying others and themselves.

**"and spread corruption in the land"** is the third mark. Corruption here is first of all the damage done by transgression and by obstructing faith: keeping people away from the religion of Muḥammad ﷺ and from the Qur'an. The message of truth seeks to bring people into harmony with their own nature, so whoever blocks others from receiving it, by inventing groundless objections against the call raised by one of God's servants, is guilty of spreading corruption on the earth. The verse thus traces disorder in human society to its root: the sundering of the relationships Allah commanded people to keep.

**"It is they who are the true losers"** is the sentence passed. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said the loss is in the Hereafter, as in the similar verse, "it is they who will be condemned and will have the worst abode" (13:25). Ibn Jarīr explained the word khāsirūn, losers, as the plural of khāsir, one who has reduced his own share of Allah's mercy by disobeying Him, just as a merchant loses in trade by eating into his capital. The hypocrite and the disbeliever forfeit their share of the mercy Allah has stored up for His servants on the Day of Resurrection, and that is the moment when they will need it most desperately. Others say the loss covers both this world and the next, and that these are the duped, who end in a Fire made everlasting for them. The mention of loss carries a hint that real loss is the loss of the next world, since whatever is lost in this one is too small to deserve serious attention. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk related a rule from Ibn ʿAbbās: whenever Allah applies a description such as "losers" to people outside Islam, it refers to disbelief, but when such terms are applied to Muslims, they refer to sin.

### The mirror image in Sūrat ar-Raʿd

The qualities listed here are exactly the opposite of the qualities of the believers, and the Qur'an sets the two portraits side by side in Sūrat ar-Raʿd. There it asks whether the one who knows that the revelation is the truth can be like one who is blind, and then describes the people of reason as "those who honour Allah's covenant, never breaking the pledge, and those who maintain whatever ties Allah has ordered to be maintained, stand in awe of their Lord, and fear strict judgment" (13:19-21). A few verses later it describes their opposites in almost the same words as our verse: "those who violate Allah's covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ties Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land" (13:25), and gives them the curse and the worst abode.

### Three duties

Read together, the three marks of the rebellious point to three duties. A human being's first duty toward God is faithfulness to the covenant struck between Creator and creatures at the very beginning, namely that he remain God's servant. The second concerns his conduct toward his fellow human beings: it should be such that all the ties God has commanded him to keep are strengthened, not cut. The third is that he must not turn people away from the divine call by manufacturing baseless arguments against it. The rebellious fail in all three.

### Lessons drawn from the verse

- The mention of violating a covenant with Allah signals that breaking a contract or agreement with one's fellow human beings is also a grave sin, one that can rob a person of the ability to do good deeds.
- It is obligatory to maintain the relationships the Sharīʿah commands us to keep intact, and forbidden to break them. According to this verse the basic cause of disorder in human society is the cutting of these bonds.
- Real loss is measured in the Hereafter. Those who act against divine commands are the true losers, however prosperous they appear.

### A reading for the inner life

On the level of allusion, the verse describes someone who once travelled the way of spiritual desire and then went back to the life of ordinary people. He claimed he was ready to abandon his lower self, but when things became serious he proved insincere, trading the allusions of reality for the concessions of the law. The return of one who travels the path with his outward self (nafs) is blameworthy so long as a single dirham remains in his bag, and in the same way the return of one who seeks with his heart (qalb) is displeasing so long as a single breath (nafas) remains in his spirit (rūḥ). Whoever has died to the religion of whims finds in the decree of death a sweet place to drink.

"Cut what Allah has commanded to be joined" is read in the same spirit. The cords that bind a person to the Real are tied by cutting the cords that bind him to creation. Joining what belongs to Him is never complete without cutting what belongs to you, and when the order is reversed, so is the result. Among the things a servant is commanded to join is the sacred bond between the people of this path. One works sincerely for that bond rather than merely handing out favours. The outward efforts of such servants are devoted to connecting the cords of the path and setting its conditions in order, while their hearts wait on the guardianship of Allah Most High over His people. Corruption of the path "in the land" happens when the elders of the path stop attending to the small details of the affairs of those behind them, too busy to guide an aspirant with their words or to sharpen the aim of a seeker with their care. This neglect displeases the Real.

Finally, the verse is turned inward on the seeker himself. Part of breaking the covenant is any moment in which your innermost self turns away from witnessing Him. Part of cutting what you were commanded to join is any breath in which a worldly concern appears and His right goes unmet. And every hour that passes without your seeing Him is your own share of corruption in the land. That is loss made plain, a grave trial and a vast calamity.

### In short

- The rebellious of verse 26 are identified by three marks: they break Allah's covenant after it is confirmed, they cut the ties He commanded to be kept, and they spread corruption.
- The covenant is understood as the pledge of obedience taken from all creation and affirmed at "Am I not your Lord?" (7:172), as the People of the Book's pledge to follow the Prophet ﷺ, and as the pledge of Oneness that Allah's signs impose on everyone.
- The ties include kinship above all, and more broadly every relationship Allah ordered kept, with Him and with people.
- They are the losers because they have thrown away their share of Allah's mercy, like a merchant who has lost his capital, and the real loss is in the Hereafter.

28.text:
The verses before this one established that the Qur'an is beyond doubt, answered the deniers' objections and set out the fate of those who break Allah's covenant. Now the tone changes from argument to appeal. The Qur'an points to the blessings Allah has poured on human beings and asks how anyone could repay them with denial. "How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will all be returned." In a single sentence the verse sweeps through the whole of a human life: nothing, then life, then death, then life again, then the return to Allah. Each stage is a gift, and together they are an argument that needs no learning to grasp.

### Phrase by phrase

**"How can you deny Allah?"** is a question of astonishment. The Arabic kayfa, "how," can express amazement at people who persist in denial despite clear evidence, or it can be a rebuke, and here it is both. The immediate address is to the people of Makkah. On the face of it, they had never denied Allah's existence. What they denied was the Prophet ﷺ. Yet the Qur'an treats their rejection of the Messenger as a denial of Allah Himself, because to deny the one He sent is to deny Him. Behind the question stands Allah's own testimony to His existence: He is the Creator and the Sustainer, with full authority over His servants. How can anyone deny His existence or worship others alongside Him when the evidence lies in his own being?

**"You were lifeless and He gave you life"** states the first blessing. Ibn Jarīr reported from ʿAṭāʾ that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it this way: you did not exist before, you were nothing until Allah created you, and after He has made you die He will restore you to life at the Resurrection. Ibn ʿAbbās added that this is like Allah's words, "Our Lord! You made us lifeless twice, and gave us life twice" (40:11). "Lifeless" (amwāt) is taken by some in a more concrete sense: you were sperm drops in the loins of your fathers, and He gave you life in the wombs of your mothers and in this world by breathing the spirit into you. Another way to picture it is that before a person existed he was, at most, countless lifeless particles scattered without purpose, and Allah gathered them, formed a human being from them and gave it life. The Qur'an presses the same point elsewhere: "Or were they created by nothing, or are they their own creators? Or did they create the heavens and the earth? In fact, they have no firm belief" (52:35-36), and, "Is there not a period of time when each human is nothing yet worth mentioning" (76:1). There are many other verses on this theme.

**"then He will cause you to die"** is the second stage, when the lifespan Allah allotted comes to its end. The verse counts death among the blessings, and this deserves a pause. Life is the chief blessing, since without it no other blessing can be enjoyed. But physical death is also a blessing, because it is the door to the everlasting life of the next world, after which there is no death at all.

**"and again bring you to life"** is the Resurrection, when Allah will gather the scattered particles of every human being and give them a new life. So the sequence is this: the first "death" was the state of lifelessness before a person received life from Allah, the second death comes when his term is complete, and the second life is given on the Day of Judgment. This matches the two deaths and two lives confessed in 40:11.

**"and then to Him you will all be returned"** closes the circle. After the Resurrection people will rise from their graves, be assembled to give account of their deeds, and be rewarded or punished according to what they did in the world. Allah will requite each person for his works.

### Why begin with life

The earlier verses had affirmed the existence and Oneness of Allah and the truth of prophethood with self-evident proofs, and had refuted the false notions of the doubters. This verse and the next speak instead of Allah's blessings, and the point is this: if people will not take the trouble to weigh the arguments already given, they should at least do what any person of sound nature does and be grateful to their benefactor, for gratitude alone would show them why they ought to obey Him. Verse 28 deals with the blessings that belong to a person's very being, namely that he had no life until Allah gave him existence. Verse 29 goes on to the general blessings that human beings share with other creatures: the earth and all it contains, on which life immediately depends, and the skies, with which life on earth is bound up.

The same appeal can be put as a chain of favours. God created human beings from nothing, and that favour alone is great enough to demand complete surrender to Him. But He did not create them and leave it at that: He gave them an earth made to suit their needs perfectly. And there is more, since immediately after death a person is brought before the Lord of the universe to be judged. A situation like this demands that a person devote himself entirely to God, remembering and obeying Him throughout life and remaining His humble servant to the end.

### A proof of the Resurrection

The verse also serves as a proof against those who denied that the dead would rise. The disbelievers' position is strange: how can they deny the Oneness of Allah when the signs of His power are visible in their own existence? They were nothing and He brought them to life. The One who gave life the first time can plainly give it a second time, and the One who will give it a second time will hold people to account. The verse states the Resurrection and, in the same breath, supplies its evidence from the listener's own body and history.

### A call to wake up

Read as an allusion, the verse is a summons shouted to someone who has lost the thread of his own life. You who have let the end of your own thread slip from your hand! You who have tumbled into the well of your own mortal nature! Is there a clearer road than this that you are waiting for? Then why not walk it? Is there a wider field than this? Then why not ride out? Is there a brighter candle than this? Then why are you falling off the path? So many years have passed over you and you have still caught no scent. You have sat at so many tables and are still hungry. You have worn a thousand garments and are still naked. O Muslim, the playing field is open, so where are the riders? The court is in session, so where are the plaintiffs? The physician is present, so where are the sick? The beauty is unveiled, so where are the lovers?

"You were lifeless and He gave you life" is then heard as Allah's own address: You were dead and I brought you to life, so why do you not look? You were ignorant and I made you knowers, so why do you not perceive? I showed you the road, so why do you not walk? What is needed is a person able to catch the scent, for otherwise the world is already full of the east wind's fragrance.

The Pīr of the Ṭarīqah turned the verse into a prayer: "O God, what can a servant do against the beginningless decree? When he owns nothing, what is left to him? What is his effort worth? Whatever You want is what gets done. How could a servant rescue himself by striving?" The movement from death to life, in other words, is Allah's doing from first to last.

It is also said that death is of three kinds and life of three kinds. One death comes by the curse, one by regret and one by generous gift: the first belongs to the disbelievers, the second to the disobedient and the third to the God-fearing. Life likewise begins as a life of fear, grows into a life of hope and ripens into a life of love. Fear shows itself in kindness, hope in service, and love in remembrance.

### In short

- The verse expresses amazement that anyone could deny Allah when his own existence proves the Creator: he was nothing, Allah gave him life, He will take it, give it again and bring him back for judgment.
- Ibn ʿAbbās explained the two deaths and two lives, and linked the verse to the confession of the people of Hell in 40:11.
- Life is the first and greatest blessing, and even death is a blessing, because it opens onto a life that never ends.
- The verse asks for gratitude from those unwilling to follow arguments, and it proves the Resurrection from the simple fact of the first creation.

29.text:
Verse 28 pointed to the blessing that each person carries in his own being: he was nothing and Allah gave him life. This verse widens the view from the individual to the whole world he lives in. "He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens. And He has perfect knowledge of all things." Having shown the proof of His power in the creation of human beings themselves, Allah now points to a second proof that everyone can see: the creation of the earth and the heavens. The verse is at once a reminder of generosity, an account of how creation was ordered, and an argument that the One who built all this can certainly raise the dead.

### Phrase by phrase

**"He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you"** is a short phrase that gathers up every benefit a person draws from the earth and what it yields. The animals, the plants and everything else were made subservient to people as a blessing from Him. The countless rivers and trees from which people benefit and take pleasure are included, and so is the earth itself, created so that people may profit from it and learn lessons from it. The little word "for" (the Arabic lām in khalaqa lakum) expresses purpose: all of this was made for your sake. Elsewhere the same favour is stated even more widely: "He also subjected for you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all by His grace. Surely in this are signs for people who reflect" (45:13).

**"Then He turned towards the heaven"** uses the Arabic verb istawā. Its first meaning is to stand upright or to climb, from which it comes to mean turning one's attention to something, and in a wider sense taking a straight and firm decision that nothing can hinder. Here it means that He turned to the creation of the heaven. The implication is that for the All-Knowing and All-Powerful there was no difficulty at all in creating the universe once He had decided to do so. The word "then" raises a question about the order of creation, and that question is taken up below.

**"forming it into seven heavens"** means that He made the heaven into seven heavens, one above the other, positioned vertically above the earth, just as the seven earths lie one below the other. A grammatical point lies behind the translation: the Arabic pronoun attached to the verb (fa-sawwāhunna) is plural, "them," although it refers back to "the heaven" in the singular, because the sentence already implies the heavens as a plurality. The same construction appears in "so He formed the heaven into seven heavens" (41:12). The number also settles a historical dispute. The ancient Greek astronomers, and some Muslim philosophers who followed them, used to speak of nine heavens. The verse shows that this was nothing more than a conjecture.

**"And He has perfect knowledge of all things"** closes the verse. His knowledge encompasses the whole of His creation, as He says in another place, "How could He not know His Own creation? For He alone is the Most Subtle, All-Aware" (67:14). It covers things in their totality and in their individual detail, including every detail of the creation of the heavens and the earth. The phrase also completes the argument begun in verse 28. Will you not think, then, that the One who had the power to create all of this at the start, which is a far greater thing than you are, can also bring you back after you die?

### Was the earth made before the sky?

The verse says that Allah created what is in the earth and "then" turned to the heaven. Taken at face value, this means that the earth was created first, and most scholars understand it that way. Mujāhid said that Allah created the earth before the heaven, and that when He created the earth, smoke burst out of it, which is why He says, "Then He turned towards the heaven when it was still like smoke, saying to it and to the earth, 'Submit, willingly or unwillingly.' They both responded, 'We submit willingly'" (41:11). The surah known as Ḥā Mīm as-Sajdah lays the whole sequence out: Allah created the earth in two Days, placed firm mountains on it, blessed it and measured out its means of sustenance in four Days in all, then turned to the heaven while it was smoke and formed it into seven heavens in two more Days, assigning to each its mandate, and adorned the lowest heaven with lamps for beauty and for protection (41:9-12). These verses indicate that creation began with the earth and that the heaven was afterwards made into seven heavens. This is the normal order of building, the lower storeys first and the upper ones after, as scholars of tafsīr have often observed.

There is, however, a verse that seems to say the opposite. In Sūrat an-Nāziʿāt Allah asks, "Which is harder to create: you or the sky?" and describes how He built it, raised it high, formed it flawlessly, darkened its night and brought out its daylight, and only then says, "As for the earth, He spread it out as well, bringing forth its water and pastures, and setting the mountains firmly upon it, all as a means of sustenance for you and your animals" (79:27-33). The word for "spread it out" is daḥā. Scholars resolve the apparent tension in two ways.

The first is to say that "then" in our verse relates to the order in which the information is told, not to the order in which the events happened. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported this explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second, and more widely held, is to distinguish between creating the earth and spreading it out. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī records that when Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about this matter, he answered that the earth was created before the heaven, and that it was spread out only after the heaven had been created. Many scholars of tafsīr, early and recent, have said the same. On this understanding, "He spread it out" (79:30-32) means that after the work of creating whatever would dwell on earth and in heaven was finished, the earth's treasures were brought up to its surface. When the earth was spread out in this way, water burst out onto its surface, plants of every type, colour, shape and kind grew, and the stars began their courses together with the planets that revolve with them. In short, although the earth already existed when the heavens came into being, its final shape was given to it afterwards. "He spread out the earth after this" (79:30) therefore does not mean the earth was created after the skies. And Allah knows best.

### Everything was created for you

Because the verse says that everything in the earth was created "for you," scholars have drawn out several consequences.

The first is that there is nothing in the universe from which a human being does not derive some benefit, directly or indirectly. Some things he uses physically, as food or medicine. Other things serve him without his being aware of it. Poisonous and dangerous things bring him some good as well, and things forbidden to him in one respect may prove quite beneficial in another. And almost everything can teach him a lesson or shed light on his path toward the Hereafter. The great Sufi Ibn ʿAṭāʾ remarked on this verse that Allah created the universe for you so that it should serve you while you serve Allah. A wise person therefore knows that what was created for him will certainly reach him, and does not, in worrying about it, forget the One for whom he himself was created. This is recorded in al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ.

The second concerns the law. Some scholars concluded from this verse that since everything in the world was created for human beings, the use of everything is in principle lawful (ḥalāl) and permitted (mubāḥ), except for what the Sharīʿah has forbidden. On this view a thing remains lawful to use so long as the Qur'an or the hadith does not prohibit it. Other scholars took the opposite position: the mere fact that a thing was created for human benefit does not make its use automatically lawful, so the use of everything is in principle unlawful unless an explicit text of the Qur'an or the hadith, or an argument based on them, establishes that it is permitted. A third group of reliable scholars declined to take sides. Abū Ḥayyān, in his commentary al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, pointed out that this verse cannot support either view, because the lām in khalaqa lakum expresses causation, "created for your sake," and nothing about the lawfulness or unlawfulness of using particular things can be deduced from that. The rulings on what may and may not be used are given elsewhere in the Qur'an and the hadith, and it is those rulings that must be followed.

### Two notes carried over from verse 28

Two further points are usually discussed together with this verse because they complete the thought of the verse before it.

First, verse 28 shows that a person who does not openly deny Allah but refuses to accept the Prophet ﷺ as His Messenger and the Qur'an as His Book is still counted among those who do not believe in Allah.

Second, verse 28 mentions only one life after physical death, the life that begins on the Day of Resurrection, and says nothing about life in the grave, even though the Qur'an and the hadith speak explicitly of people being questioned in their graves about their faith and receiving some reward or punishment there. This life in the grave is an intermediate state (barzakh) between the life of this world and the life of the next. It is something like the life a person has in dreams. One might call it a supplement to this life and a prelude to the life to come. Since it is not a distinct life in its own right, it did not need to be mentioned separately.

### The chain of favours

Put together, verses 28 and 29 make a simple case. God created human beings from nothing, and that alone is reason enough for complete surrender to Him. He did not stop there but gave them an earth fitted perfectly to their needs, and set the heavens above them. And immediately after death each of them will stand before the Lord of the universe to be judged. A situation like this calls for a person to give himself wholly to God, remembering Him and obeying Him throughout his life and remaining His humble servant.

### A reading for the inner life

Heard as an address from Allah to His servant, the verse says something like this: I created everything in the kingdom of the earth for you and placed it at your disposal. My bestowal is not small, and My generosity toward those who burn for Me is not trivial. There will never be any going back on My kindness to you. Nor did I confine Myself to the kingdom of the earth. I raised the heavens too, so that you could gaze on them, so that your eyes could delight in them, and so that your daily provision could be stored in them. My servant, when you step into the street of My covenant, you have no idea what good news reaches those who dwell in heaven and those who dwell on earth, or how they congratulate one another. But I know, for I know everything and reach everyone.

There is a subtle point in the wording. Allah did not say, "Who created you for all that is in the earth." He said, "Who created for you all that is in the earth." In other words: all that fills the kingdom of earth and heaven was created for your sake, while you were created for My sake. To Mūsā (Moses) in particular He said, "And I have selected you for My service" (20:41), and to His creatures in general He said, "I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me" (51:56). The one who understood the worth of this declaration best, and gave thanks for this blessing, was the Prophet ﷺ himself, al-Muṣṭafā, the Chosen One. On the night of nearness and generosity, when he was taken up to the heavens, all of creation and the kingdoms of both worlds were scattered at the feet of his truthfulness, and that paragon did not so much as glance at them from the corner of his eye. He said, in effect, "I was not created for this." As the Qur'an says of that night, "The Prophet's sight never wandered, nor did it overreach" (53:17). Abū Yazīd al-Basṭāmī, who walked the road of the Prophet's ﷺ Sunnah so beautifully and kept such fine courtesy before the Divine Presence, said that he kept crossing perils until he found the kingdoms laid before him, and the lesson of his words is the same: the kingdoms are for the servant, but the servant is for Allah.

### In short

- Everything on the earth was created for human benefit, and the heavens were then formed into seven, a second visible proof of Allah's power after the proof of our own creation in verse 28.
- "Then" has prompted discussion: Ibn ʿAbbās explained that the earth was created before the heaven but spread out and finished after it, which reconciles this verse with 79:27-33.
- The seven heavens rule out the nine of the Greek astronomers, and "He has perfect knowledge of all things" (compare 67:14) completes the argument for the Resurrection.
- Scholars differ on whether "for you" makes the use of things lawful by default, and Abū Ḥayyān held that the phrase decides neither view.
- Inwardly, the verse teaches that the world was made for you while you were made for Allah.

30.text:
The verses before this one listed Allah's blessings and asked human beings to recognise their Benefactor rather than deny Him. Now the surah opens a story that runs for ten verses, the story of Ādam (Adam), the father of mankind. It continues the same theme and also illustrates it. Blessings are of two kinds, tangible and intangible. Food, water, wealth, houses and land are tangible. Honour, happiness and knowledge are intangible. The earlier verses dealt with the first kind, and these verses deal with the second: how Allah gave Ādam the gift of knowledge, made the angels bow to him in respect, and gave human beings the honour of being his children. The story begins before Ādam existed. "Remember when your Lord said to the angels, 'I am going to place a successive human authority on earth.'" The angels replied with a question: "Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness?" And Allah answered, "I know what you do not know."

### Phrase by phrase

**"Remember when your Lord said to the angels"** is addressed first to the Prophet ﷺ: mention to your people what Allah said to the angels. In doing so Allah reminds the children of Ādam of a favour that came before any other, for He spoke of them in the highest assembly before He had created them. The angels addressed were, on one view, angels who were already on the earth.

**"I am going to place a successive human authority on earth"** translates the Arabic khalīfah. Literally it means a successor, someone who steps into another's place. Under hereditary rule the word was commonly applied to a monarch succeeding his predecessor, and so it came to denote a person invested with authority. The verse uses the word in several overlapping senses. It means people who reproduce generation after generation and century after century, each replacing the one before, as Allah says, "He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others, so He may test you with what He has given you" (6:165), and, "Who makes you successors in the earth? Is it another god besides Allah?" (27:62), and, "Had We willed, We could have easily replaced you all with angels, succeeding one another on earth" (43:60), and again, "Then they were succeeded by other generations who inherited the Scripture" (7:169). It also means a deputy, one who acts on behalf of Allah by implementing His rulings in the earth, and in this sense the vicegerent announced here was Ādam himself. Al-Qurṭubī noted a further shade of meaning: a khalīfah is one who judges the disputes that arise among people, restraining them from injustice and sin. Some scholars think that Allah was not referring to Ādam alone, since the angels' reply about corruption and bloodshed would not fit a single prophet, but to the human race of which he was the father. Others add that the word recalls those who lived on the earth before. The offspring of the jinn used to inhabit it, and when they became corrupt Allah sent the angels against them and they were driven away to the islands and into the mountains. Ādam's race would take their place.

**"They asked, 'Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood'"** raises the obvious question: how did the angels know what human beings would do? Several explanations are given, and they do not exclude one another. Most authoritative scholars hold, on the basis of reports from the Companions, that Allah Himself told the angels on this occasion how human beings would behave on earth. Qatādah said that when Allah informed them that He would create a creation on the earth, they already knew that it would commit corruption there. Others say they inferred it from human nature, since Allah had told them that He would create man from clay and such a creature is prone to the acts they mentioned. Others say they understood it from the word khalīfah itself, since a judge and restrainer is needed only where there is wrongdoing to restrain. Others point to the precedent of the jinn, who had corrupted the earth and shed blood before. Behind the question lay an assumption the angels had formed. Ibn Jarīr cited a report from Ibn ʿAbbās that before man appeared the angels had taken it for granted that Allah would never create a being superior to them or greater in knowledge, since they had been created before him and had seen what he had not seen.

It is important to be clear about what the angels were not doing. They were not disputing with Allah, and they were not envious of the children of Ādam, as some have mistakenly supposed. Allah describes the angels as those who never speak before He speaks and never act except by His command, so they do not ask Him anything without His permission. Their words were a question asked in order to learn the wisdom behind the decision, as if they had said: Our Lord, what is the wisdom in creating such beings when they will cause trouble on the earth and spill blood? If the purpose is that You be worshipped, we already praise and glorify You and never cause corruption, so why create other creatures? Angels are innocent of objection and of pride. Their words were a humble submission and an offer of their own services. They were being curious, not critical.

**"while we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness"** describes what the angels were already doing. To glorify with praise is to say continually, "Glory and praise be to You." To proclaim His holiness is to declare Him far above anything that does not befit Him, to pray as He commands, and to mention Him in a state of purity. On the grammar, the lām in laka ("for You") is an extra particle, and the clause "we sanctify You" is a circumstantial qualifier. The implied sense is: since we already do all this, we are surely more entitled to be Your vicegerents. The angels thought that their nature, wholly good, incapable of evil and perfectly obedient, made them better suited to manage the affairs of the world.

**"Allah responded, 'I know what you do not know'"** is the first answer, given in the mode of authority. The angels did not understand the nature and the requirements of vicegerency on the earth, and Allah alone knew them fully. Scholars have unfolded the content of this answer in several ways, and all of them are true.

First, Allah knew that the benefit of creating this kind of being far outweighs the harm the angels mentioned, and this the angels did not know. Among the children of Ādam He would raise prophets and send messengers, and He would create the truthful, the martyrs, the righteous, the worshippers, the modest, the pious, scholars who practise what they know, the humble, and lovers of Allah who follow His messengers. Among Ādam's progeny there would be the obedient as well as the transgressor, and justice would prevail between them. The Ṣaḥīḥ records that when the angels ascend to Allah with the records of His servants' deeds, Allah asks them, though He knows better than they, "How did you leave My servants?" and they answer, "We came to them while they were praying and we left them while they were praying." This is because the angels who watch over people work in shifts, changing over at the Fajr and ʿAṣr prayers, so that the angels who have just descended stay with us while those who have been with us ascend with our deeds. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the deeds of the night are raised to Allah before the morning and the deeds of the day before the night falls. The angels' report, "We came to them praying and left them praying," is a living commentary on "I know what you do not know."

Second, some understood the answer as: I have a specific wisdom in creating them that you have no knowledge of. Third, some read it as a reply to the angels' words "we glorify Your praises and proclaim Your holiness," meaning: I know that Iblīs is not as you are, even though he stands among you. Fourth, some read the angels' words as a request to be allowed to inhabit the earth themselves instead of the children of Ādam, and Allah's answer as: I know whether your living in the heavens is better or worse for you. Ar-Rāzī and others mentioned this reading. And Allah knows best.

### Why did Allah tell the angels at all?

A question naturally arises. Why did Allah announce His decision to the angels? Was it simply to inform them, to seek their advice, or to draw out their opinion?

It cannot have been to seek advice. One turns to wise and trustworthy people for advice when one cannot see every side of a problem and does not wish to rely on one's own understanding alone, or when others have rights equal to one's own and must be consulted, as happens in the councils of the world. Neither situation applies here. Allah created the universe and knows the smallest particle of dust in it. He sees and hears everything, open or hidden. How could He need anyone's advice? Nor does He govern the universe on a parliamentary model in which all have equal rights and everyone must be consulted. He is the Lord and Master, and all His creatures, angels and human beings alike, are His slaves. None of them has the right to question His actions or to ask Him why He did this and not that: "He cannot be questioned about what He does, but they will all be questioned" (21:23).

Two reasons for the form of the announcement are given. The first is that Allah, in His wisdom, gave a plain statement the form of a consultation in order to teach human beings the value of consulting one another. The Prophet ﷺ was Allah's Messenger and could have received through revelation everything he needed to manage the affairs of the world, yet the Qur'an instructs him to consult his Companions, so that the Muslim community would learn the lesson from him and the practice of mutual consultation would be established through him. The second reason is suggested by the verses themselves. The angels had assumed, as the report of Ibn ʿAbbās shows, that Allah would never create a being superior to them in knowledge. Allah knew that He would create a being superior to all other creatures and greater in knowledge, one who would receive the gift of vicegerency. So He raised the matter in the assembly of the angels so that they would voice what they had been thinking, and then He could show them, in a vivid demonstration, where they had gone wrong.

In the reading of the Sufis the point is sharper still. The announcement was not a consultation with the angels at all. It was the laying of the foundation of Ādam's honour. Allah needed no help. He was unrolling the carpet of Ādam's dignity before Ādam existed.

### What the angels would learn

The verses that follow describe how Allah answered the angels a second time, in the mode of wisdom, by teaching Ādam the names of all things and asking the angels to name them. That demonstration belongs to the next verses, but its lesson belongs to the understanding of this one. Ādam was preferred over the angels because of his superiority in the station of knowledge. A deputy on the earth must know the names, properties and characteristics of the things found there, and the angels had no aptitude for that kind of knowledge. An angel cannot truly experience the pain of hunger and thirst, the turmoil of the passions, the agony of a scorpion's sting or a snake's bite, or the elation an intoxicant produces. Such things could be learned only by a being with Ādam's capacity, and he was taught them. Nothing in the Qur'an indicates that he was taught in private, apart from the angels. The teaching may have been open to both, with his nature able to receive it and theirs not. Or the teaching may have taken no outward form at all, the Ādamic nature being made to carry this knowledge within itself without formal instruction, just as an infant does not need to be taught to suck its mother's milk or a duckling to swim. Should someone ask why Allah, being all-powerful, did not simply change the angels' nature so that they could learn these things, the answer is that the question amounts to asking why He did not turn the angels into human beings, for with a different nature they would no longer have been angels.

Through this demonstration the angels came to see that purity and innocence are not the criterion for choosing a vicegerent. The criterion is knowledge of the things found on the earth, of how to use them, and of the consequences that follow from using them. A general principle can be drawn from this: a ruler must thoroughly know the nature, temperament and peculiarities of the people he governs, or he cannot establish justice and order. If a man has never known the pain of hunger, how can he do justice to someone who has been wrongfully kept hungry? When the angels found that another being was, by his special kind of knowledge, better suited to the task, they acknowledged it as humbly as they had spoken, and withdrew their opinion, declaring that all purity belongs to Allah and that they had no knowledge except what He had taught them. In this context "To You belongs all purity" carries a further implication: Allah is free of any charge of having withheld from the angels the knowledge He gave to Ādam, because, being All-Knowing and All-Wise, He gives each creature the kind and degree of knowledge and understanding that He alone knows to suit that creature's nature.

### Why a creature capable of evil?

Besides demonstrating Ādam's superiority in knowledge, Allah dispelled the angels' concern about the evil tendencies in human beings with the short answer, "I know what you do not know." There is a subtle suggestion in it. The very peculiarity that made man look unfit for vicegerency in the angels' eyes is exactly what makes him fit for it. A deputy is needed on the earth precisely to prevent bloodshed and disorder. Where there is no possibility of disorder, what need is there for an administrator? Allah's will and wisdom decreed that, just as He had created beings as innocent as the angels, beings as wholly evil as Satan and his progeny, and beings like the jinn in whom evil outweighs good, He would also create beings in whom good and evil are mixed in equal measure, who would strive to conquer the evil in themselves and grow in goodness in order to win the pleasure of their Creator.

The same thought can be put in terms of freedom. When God created man to live on the earth, He decreed that man should have freedom of will. The angels feared that man would be corrupted by this grant of power and freedom and would spread evil and bloodshed in the world, and history has shown that their fear was well founded. God was fully aware of the possibility. But He had a particular purpose in giving man power and freedom. Even if many human beings were corrupted by their power, a substantial number would still, with all their power and freedom, acknowledge God's greatness and their own helplessness, and who would freely choose the path of submission and obedience. Such people would be few by comparison, but they would be prized above all others. They are like the grain at harvest time, far outweighed in bulk by the chaff and straw, yet the only part of the crop that is really valued. If the chaff and straw are allowed to grow at all, it is only for the sake of the grain.

### Man as Allah's vicegerent: the principles of governance

Since these verses tell of a vicegerent appointed to keep order on the earth and to establish divine law, they yield the basic principles of human governance.

The ultimate sovereignty in the universe belongs to Allah alone. The Qur'an states this explicitly in many places: "It is only Allah Who decides" (6:57), "Indeed, to Allah alone belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth" (9:116), and, "The creation and the command belong to Him alone" (7:54).

In His wisdom, however, He chose to send His vicegerents to the earth to maintain spiritual and temporal order. Their function is to announce and establish His commandments, to teach people how to live by them, and sometimes to wield temporal power together with spiritual authority, under divine guidance. Allah makes the appointment Himself. It is in no sense a reward for a person's good deeds or spiritual striving. All authentic scholars of the Muslim Ummah agree that prophethood cannot be attained through personal effort or earned by merit. Allah, in His supreme knowledge and wisdom, chooses certain individuals as His messengers, prophets and vicegerents. The Qur'an declares this plainly: "Allah selects messengers from both angels and people" (22:75), and, "Allah knows best where to place His message" (6:124). These vicegerents receive His commandments directly and establish them in the world. The chain began with Ādam and continued unbroken to the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ.

### The Prophet ﷺ as the last vicegerent

The Prophet ﷺ came as the last vicegerent (khalīfah), the last Messenger (rasūl) and the last Prophet (nabī) of Allah, with special qualities that no other prophet shares. Some of them are these.

First, each earlier prophet was sent to guide a particular country or people, and his authority was limited to them. Mūsā (Moses) and ʿĪsā (Jesus) were sent to Banī Isrāʾīl, the Israelites. The Prophet ﷺ was sent to guide all human beings and all jinn, and his authority extends to every member of both species. The Qur'an declares the universality of his mission: "Say, O Prophet, 'O humanity! I am Allah's Messenger to you all'" (7:158). A hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim reports him saying that he was given superiority over the other prophets in six things, and the first of them is the universality of his prophethood.

Second, just as the earlier prophets' vicegerency was limited to particular peoples and lands, it was also limited to particular periods. When one prophet's age ended, another came as the new vicegerent. The Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ was sent as the last of all prophets, and his prophethood is not confined to a period but lasts until the end of time.

Third, the teachings and the Sharīʿah of each earlier prophet remained intact for a while, after which people gradually drifted from them and distorted them beyond recognition, and Allah would then send a new prophet with a new law. The Sharīʿah of the Prophet ﷺ is to remain alive in its complete form until the end of the universe. Allah has taken upon Himself to protect the words and the meanings of the Qur'an: "It is certainly We Who have revealed the Reminder, and it is certainly We Who will preserve it" (15:9). He has likewise made special provision for preserving the hadith, which contain the Prophet's ﷺ teachings. Through every upheaval of history there will remain, until the Day of Judgment, a group of people who preserve these teachings and transmit them accurately, aided and protected by Allah.
