O Ādam, keep Our compact in mind, and choose no one over Me. The tongue of Ādam's state replied: my heart travels with You and keeps You company, so where else could its love attach? When You are a heart's spirit and its very awareness, how could that heart forget to remember You?

### In short

- Allah Himself gave Ādam the words with which to repent, identified by many early scholars as the prayer of 7:23, "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves."
- Ibn ʿAbbās related a dialogue in which Ādam appealed to Allah's mercy preceding His anger and was promised a return to Paradise if he repented.
- Allah accepted his repentance because He is the ever-relenting and merciful, as 9:104, 4:110 and 25:71 confirm for every servant who turns back.

38.text:
Ādam (Adam) had been forgiven, yet the command to go down to the earth was not withdrawn. "We said, 'Descend all of you! Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.'" What changed after the pardon was not the destination but its meaning. The first command to descend, in the previous verse, was given in the mode of authority and came as a punishment, which is why it mentioned enmity. This second command is given in the mode of wisdom, and the descent is now an honour, the honour of vicegerency, which is why it speaks of the guidance that vicegerency requires. Allah told Ādam, Ḥawwāʾ (Eve) and their descendants that He would send them His guidance, the rulings of the Sharīʿah, through revelation, and that those who followed it faithfully would be free of both fear and grief.

### Phrase by phrase

**"We said, 'Descend all of you!'"** repeats the command of verse 36 in order to attach to it what follows about guidance. The address includes Ādam, Ḥawwāʾ and, on some accounts, the serpent, the peacock and Satan, and through Ādam it reaches his whole progeny. Allah had already announced that He would send down Books and raise prophets and messengers for his descendants.

**"Then when guidance comes to you from Me"** promises that guidance will come whenever and as often as Allah sends it. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said that al-hudā, the guidance, means the prophets, the messengers, the clear signs and the plain explanation. In short, it is a Book and a prophet.

**"whoever follows it"** means whoever accepts what is in Allah's Books and what His messengers bring, believing in Him and acting in obedience to Him.

**"there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"** is explained in complementary ways. They will have no fear about the Hereafter and no grief about what they left behind in this world. Or they will have no fear of any torment to come and no grief over what has passed. Some say the negation is perpetual: no fear will ever touch them once death itself is slain, and they will never grieve once Hell is shut. The parallel passage in Sūrat Ṭā Hā says, "Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray in this life nor suffer in the next" (20:123), which Ibn ʿAbbās explained as: he will not be misguided in this world nor miserable in the Hereafter. Those who follow the guidance will be admitted to Paradise.

### Two rewards that cover everything

The verse promises two things to those who follow divine guidance: no fear and no grief. Fear is the anxiety felt in anticipating some future trouble or pain. Grief is the sorrow felt at losing something valuable or failing to obtain something desired. Between them these two rewards cover every possible form of comfort and peace, since all distress is either dread of what may come or sorrow over what has gone.

The Arabic makes a subtle distinction between the two. For fear it uses a noun in a general statement, literally "no fear upon them." For grief it uses a verb with a pronoun as its subject, literally "they will not grieve." The implication is that complete freedom from every sense of loss is possible only for the friends of Allah, the awliyāʾ, who follow divine guidance in all its details. For everyone else, emperor or billionaire, grief at the loss of something valued or the frustration of a desire is unavoidable, being part of the very scheme of things. The friends of Allah need not grieve because they have annihilated their own desires and their very will in total submission to the will of Allah. The Qur'an tells us that the people of Paradise will thank Allah for taking away all regret and sorrow: "Praise be to Allah, Who has kept away from us all causes of sorrow" (35:34). Some measure of sorrow is therefore inevitable for every human being except those who have perfected and secured their relationship with Allah. The word "saints" is only a weak approximation of awliyāʾ Allāh, "the friends of Allah," a concept that bears only a faint resemblance to the Christian idea of a saint, which is why "friends of Allah" or "men of Allah" is the better rendering.

It should be made clear that the grief denied to the friends of Allah is grief over worldly losses and frustrated worldly desires. In anxiety about the next world, in fear of Allah and in deep awe before His glory, they are far ahead of everyone else. The Prophet ﷺ himself often appeared worried and deep in thought, not from fear of any worldly loss or trouble, but out of concern for his Ummah and awe before the divine majesty. Nor does the verse mean that prophets and the friends of Allah do not feel the instinctive human fear that frightening things arouse. The Qur'an itself relates that when the staff of Mūsā (Moses) became a serpent, "Moses concealed fear within himself" (20:67). That was an instinctive, physical fear, and the incident belongs to the earliest days of his prophethood, for when Allah said "Do not be afraid," the fear vanished altogether. It can also be explained differently: his fear did not come, as it does with ordinary people, from expecting harm from the serpent, but from the possibility that so extraordinary an event might lead the Israelites into misguidance. On that reading the fear was not worldly at all but concerned the next world.

### A reading for the inner life

Bad manners on the carpet get a guest shown the door. When Ādam misbehaved at the fountain of nearness, Allah said, "Descend, some of you enemies to others, and in the earth is a dwelling for you," after Ādam had enjoyed a place of nearness as his dwelling and his enjoyment for a time. They had lived in ease, and in the end they returned to want, and when they became poor they clung to poverty, hoping for reward, and even when things were easy again they hurried back to that state. Yet at the very moment Allah expelled Ādam from the Garden and sent him down to the earth, He gave him the good news that He would restore him to his former condition if his heart inclined to return. That good news is this verse: "when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve."

### In short

- After the pardon the descent was repeated, no longer as punishment but as the honoured mission of vicegerency accompanied by the promise of guidance, meaning Books and prophets.
- Whoever follows that guidance is promised freedom from fear about the future and grief over the past, the two forms that all distress takes, as 20:123 confirms.
- Total freedom from grief belongs only to the friends of Allah, who have surrendered their own will. Their fear and awe of Allah, and even instinctive human fear like that of Mūsā (20:67), are not what the verse denies.

39.text:
The promise of the previous verse has a counterpart. "But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever." The guidance that was promised to the children of Ādam (Adam) divides them into two groups. Those who follow it have neither fear nor grief, and those who reject it have the Fire without end. With this verse the first address to humanity, delivered at the moment of its descent to the earth, is complete.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs"** means those who reject the guidance when it comes, refusing to believe in Allah's Books and calling His scriptures and His messengers liars. The "signs" are His revelations and proofs, the Book and the prophet sent with it. Allah does not show Himself plainly in this world. He reveals Himself through His signs, and in this way He tests His creatures. Only those who are able to read His signs will find Him, and those who deny the signs have failed the test for which they were sent to the earth. The one who brings the message of truth stands before people as Ādam stood before the angels, and whoever is too proud to acknowledge him is following in Satan's footsteps.

**"will be the residents of the Fire"** describes them as the rightful owners of Hell, its proper inhabitants, the people to whom it belongs as a home belongs to those who live in it.

**"They will be there forever"** means that they will remain in Hell perpetually, never dying and never being released, and will find no way out of it. The parallel verse in Sūrat Ṭā Hā puts the same warning in terms of this life as well as the next: "But whoever turns away from My Reminder will certainly have a miserable life, then We will raise them up blind on the Day of Judgment" (20:124), and that misery stands opposite the security promised to those who follow the guidance (20:123). The pairing in these two verses, fear and grief removed for the believer and the Fire made permanent for the denier, is the pattern that the rest of the Qur'an will fill in.

### Favours without gratitude

Those who receive Allah's favours without gratitude, and who pay no attention to affirming the truth (taṣdīq) and realising it in themselves (taḥqīq), will have a painful punishment deferred until the end, and a separation from Allah that is already upon them in the here and now. The disbeliever's loss, in other words, does not wait for the Hereafter. The Fire is the final form of a distance that began the moment the signs were denied.

### In short

- Those who disbelieve and deny Allah's signs, His Books and His messengers, are the people of the Fire and will remain there forever, neither dying nor leaving.
- Allah tests people through His signs rather than by appearing openly. To reject the signs is to fail the test, as 20:124 confirms with its promise of a miserable life and a blind resurrection.
- Ingratitude for favours brings punishment later and separation from Allah now.

40.text:
With this verse the surah turns to a new audience. "O children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you. Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine, and stand in awe of Me alone." Up to this point Sūrat al-Baqarah has spoken about the Qur'an itself, warned the open deniers and the hypocrites, called everyone to worship Allah alone, presented the Qur'an as an inimitable miracle, and told the story of Ādam (Adam) to show Allah's power and wisdom. Now it addresses the People of the Book directly, and it continues to do so, with the Jews especially in view, all the way to verse 123. The tone at the start is friendly and persuasive: a reminder of noble ancestry, a list of blessings, a call to honour an old agreement, and a warning to fear no one but Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O children of Israel!"** means the descendants of Yaʿqūb (Jacob), for Israel is his second name. Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī recorded that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās said that a group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ, and he asked them, "Do you know that Israel is Yaʿqūb?" They said, "Yes, by Allah," and he said, "O Allah, bear witness." Aṭ-Ṭabarī recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that the word Israel means "the servant of Allah." It is a Hebrew word. Some scholars have observed that among the prophets only the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ has several names, apart from Yaʿqūb, who has two, Yaʿqūb and Isrāʾīl. The Qur'an addresses the Jews here not as the children of Yaʿqūb but as the children of Israel, so that the very title reminds them that they are the children of "the servant of Allah" and should follow their father in worshipping and obeying Allah alone. The address is a way of saying: O children of a pious, righteous servant of Allah who obeyed Him, be like your father and follow the truth, much as one might say, "Son of a generous man, be generous," or, "Son of a scholar, seek knowledge." The Qur'an uses the same device when it says, "O descendants of those We carried with Noah in the Ark! He was indeed a grateful servant" (17:3). The address "O children of Israel" is repeated at the beginning and near the end of the long passage that follows, a familiar rhetorical means of making an appeal persuasive. The passage opens briefly, with four verses inviting them to Islam and three urging good deeds, before the long and detailed address begins.

**"Remember My favours upon you"** calls them to gratitude. Mujāhid said that Allah's favour to the Jews was that He made water gush from the rock, sent down manna and quails, and saved them from slavery under Pharaoh. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said the favour is that prophets and messengers were raised among them and Books were revealed to them. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as Allah's support for them and their forefathers in rescuing them from Pharaoh and his people. Others list the Scripture and the messenger, the escape from Pharaoh and from drowning, the parting of the sea, the clouds sent to shade them, and the honey and quails. The verse resembles what Mūsā (Moses) said to his people: "O my people! Remember Allah's favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you, made you sovereign, and gave you what He had never given anyone in the world" (5:20), meaning anyone of their own time. The favours were bestowed on their forefathers, but the descendants inherited them, and the right response is gratitude expressed through obedience.

**"Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine"** speaks of an agreement with two sides. The covenant that Allah took from them concerned the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ: that when he was sent they would believe in him and follow him, and that in return Allah would grant them what He had promised and lift from their necks the chains and burdens laid on them because of their errors. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah and Mujāhid identified the covenant with the one described in Sūrat al-Māʾidah, which the Tawrāh also records: "Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel and appointed twelve leaders from among them and then said, 'I am truly with you. If you establish prayer, pay alms-tax, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend to Allah a good loan, I will certainly forgive your sins and admit you into Gardens under which rivers flow'" (5:12). That covenant mentions prayer and alms, but its most important clause is faith in all of Allah's messengers, which includes the Prophet ﷺ, and so, according to Ibn ʿAbbās as cited by Ibn Jarīr, the covenant here means believing in the Prophet ﷺ and obeying him. Other scholars identify the covenant with a pledge recorded in the Tawrāh itself: Allah would send a great prophet from the descendants of Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) whom all peoples would obey, and that whoever obeyed him would have his sins forgiven, enter Paradise and receive a double reward. Ar-Rāzī gathered several of the announcements made by earlier prophets about the coming of Muḥammad ﷺ. Abū al-ʿĀliyah put it more generally: Allah's covenant with His servants is that they embrace Islam and hold to it. As for Allah's side, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said "I will fulfil Mine" means "I will be pleased with you and admit you to Paradise," and as-Suddī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said the same. The verse quoted from Sūrat al-Māʾidah makes this clear: Allah forgives the sins of those who keep the covenant and admits them to Paradise. It also includes His promises of a good life in this world and a beautiful reward on the Day of Judgment.

**"and stand in awe of Me alone"** means fear Me and no one else. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means: fear the punishment I may send upon you as I sent it upon your forefathers, such as the transformation into apes. The verse thus begins with encouragement and ends with warning, in the hope that they would come back to the truth, follow the Messenger ﷺ, obey what the Qur'an commands and forbids, and believe in it. The warning had a particular point. The scholars of the Israelites were afraid that if they spoke the truth about the Prophet ﷺ they would go against popular feeling and lose both their followers and their income, so these verses urge them to speak the truth without fear, since Allah alone deserves to be feared.

### Who the People of the Book were

In the time of the Prophet ﷺ the disbelievers and hypocrites fell into two kinds. On one side were the idolaters, who had no religious learning, were mostly unlettered, and followed the customs of their forefathers, such as the people of Makkah in general, whom the Qur'an calls the ummiyyūn. On the other side were those who believed in the earlier prophets, knew the earlier revealed Books such as the Tawrāh and the Injīl, and were regarded as educated. Some of them followed Mūsā but did not accept ʿĪsā (Jesus) as a prophet, and these were the Jews. Others followed ʿĪsā but did not believe that Mūsā, as a prophet, was protected from sin, and these were the Christians. Because they believed in the Tawrāh (Torah) or the Injīl or both, these two groups are called in the Qur'an Ahl al-Kitāb, the People of the Book. Being educated, they were respected and trusted by those around them and their opinion carried great weight. If they came to the straight path, others could be expected to follow. The Jews were the dominant group in Madīnah and its surroundings, and since Sūrat al-Baqarah is a Madīnan surah, after dealing with the idolaters it addresses the People of the Book in a special way.

The greatest favour God grants a people is to send them His prophet and so open the road to eternal salvation, and before the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, the last of the prophets, this favour had been the privilege of the Children of Israel. In time, however, their religion ceased to be a matter of conscious conviction and deteriorated into a set of lifeless rituals handed down from one generation to the next. The coming of the Prophet ﷺ brought the reality to light. Those whose feeling for the truth was still alive recognised his prophethood and followed him, while those whose religion had become merely inherited found his message strange and rejected it. Given the clear prophecies in the Tawrāh of an Arab prophet to come, recognising him should not have been difficult, but believing in him was against their worldly interests. Over centuries a religious establishment had grown up in which they held pride of place, honoured as the heirs of prophets and holy men, looked to for spiritual leadership, and supported by tributes and offerings all year round. It seemed to them that accepting the Arab Prophet would end their privileged position and demolish the whole structure of their livelihood.

### Rulings and lessons

Al-Qurṭubī observed that when Allah asks the Israelites to worship and obey Him, He reminds them of the blessings He has showered on them, whereas He asks the followers of the Prophet ﷺ to do so without mentioning His blessings at all: "remember Me; I will remember you" (2:152). This is a subtle sign of the superiority of this Ummah. The Muslim community has a direct relationship with Allah. It begins by recognising the Benefactor, and through knowing Him comes to recognise His bounties. Other peoples begin with the bounties and only through them reach a knowledge of the Benefactor.

The verse also shows that keeping an agreement one has entered into is obligatory and breaking a promise is forbidden, as another verse states outright: "O believers! Honour your obligations" (5:1). A hadith reported by Muslim adds that promise-breakers, before their final punishment in the next world, will be humiliated before all humanity when it is gathered on the Day of Judgment, for a flag will be planted as a mark of shame beside each one who committed this sin, and the greater the betrayal, the higher the flag.

### A reading for the inner life

The verse alludes to the Real's gentleness, generosity and loving kindness toward His servants. He reminds them of His favour as if to say: I am the generous Lord, the grateful, the forgiver of servants. I have come forward with kindness in the face of every disloyalty, I invite My servants to praise Me in spite of all their offences, and I ask them to be grateful for My blessings. So He says to the Children of Israel: remember My blessings, be grateful for them and recognise your duty toward Me, so that you may deserve increase and enjoy a good name and good fortune.

The Children of Israel and this community were addressed very differently. To them He said, "Remember My blessings." To this community He said, "Remember Me" (2:152). To them He gave blessings, and to this community He gave companionship. The one group He kept at a distance from Himself through the witnessing of blessings, and the other He kept close to Himself by stipulating love. As a lover might say: I travelled to You seeking the highest things, while others travelled seeking a comfortable life. The Pīr of the Ṭarīqah prayed: O God, the one who really works is the one whose work is with You, and the one who really has a friend is the one whose friend is like You. How could anyone who has You in both worlds set You aside? The wonder is that the one who has You weeps more than anyone. The one who has not found weeps at not finding, so why does the one who finds weep too? And yet, when someone has a friend like You, any complaint from him is a disgrace.

"Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine" belongs to a family of verses in which Allah answers the servant's step with His own. "Call upon Me, I will respond to you" (40:60). "Remember Me; I will remember you" (2:152). It is as if He said: My servant, you open one door and I will open another. Open the door of turning back and I will open the door of good news, for those who turn to Allah "will have good news" (39:17). Open the door of spending and I will open the door of replacement, for "whatever you spend in charity, He will compensate you for it" (34:39). Open the door of striving and I will open the door of guidance, for "those who struggle in Our cause, We will surely guide them along Our Way" (29:69). Open the door of seeking forgiveness and I will open the door of forgiving, for whoever "seeks Allah's forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (4:110). Open the door of gratitude and I will open the door of increase, for "if you are grateful, I will certainly give you more" (14:7). My servant, come back to My covenant and I will come back to yours.

God's covenants with His servant are said to be many, and whenever the servant is loyal in one of them, the Lord of the Worlds answers with a loyalty of His own. The first is that the servant pronounces the words of the shahādah, and its counterpart from the Lord of the Worlds is the protection of his life and property, as in His words that whoever says "there is no god but God" has placed his wealth and his property under My protection. The last is that if the servant keeps his gaze pure and guards his thoughts, its counterpart is what He has prepared for His righteous servants: things no eye ever saw, no ear ever heard, and no mortal heart ever imagined. Between that beginning and this end lie many intermediate covenants. In each of them the servant contributes deeds and words, and God contributes a reward beyond reckoning. One of the people of this path put some of them this way: keep My covenant by presence at the gate, and I will keep yours with great reward. Keep My covenant by guarding the secrets, and I will keep yours with My beautiful kindnesses. Keep My covenant by preferring no other to Me, and I will keep yours by never holding back My gentleness and good. Keep My covenant with beautiful striving, and I will keep yours with constant contemplation.

### In short

- The surah now addresses the Jews of Madīnah as "children of Israel," the children of Yaʿqūb, whose name means "servant of Allah," reminding them of their ancestry so that they might follow their father in obedience.
- The favours are the rescue from Pharaoh, the parted sea, the shading clouds, manna and quails, water from the rock, and above all prophets and Books (compare 5:20).
- The covenant is the pledge of 5:12 to believe in and support Allah's messengers, which binds them to believe in the Prophet ﷺ, in return for forgiveness and Paradise. Keeping agreements is obligatory (5:1).
- Allah addresses this Ummah with "remember Me" (2:152) rather than "remember My favours," a sign of its direct relationship with Him, and every step the servant takes toward Allah is answered by a step from Him.

41.text:
Having reminded the Children of Israel of their covenant, the verse now spells out what it requires of them in the present. "Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures. Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain. And be mindful of Me." Four commands follow one another: believe in the Qur'an, do not lead the way in rejecting it, do not sell the truth for worldly profit, and keep your duty to Allah. Each of them answers a temptation that the Jewish scholars of Madīnah actually faced.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures"** refers to the Qur'an, which Allah sent down to Muḥammad ﷺ, the unlettered Arab prophet, through Jibrīl (Gabriel), as a bringer of good news, a warner and a light. It contains the truth from Allah and confirms what was revealed before it in the Tawrāh and the Injīl: the Oneness of Allah, prophethood, the description and traits of Muḥammad ﷺ, and some of the prescribed laws. Abū al-ʿĀliyah explained it as: O People of the Book, believe in what I have sent down that agrees with what you have, for they found the description of Muḥammad ﷺ written in the Tawrāh and the Injīl. Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Qatādah said the same. Since the Qur'an was sent to confirm the essential teachings of the Tawrāh, the covenant itself obliged the Israelites to believe in it. What the Qur'an confirms about the Tawrāh and the Injīl is that they are Books of Allah as originally revealed. The distortions introduced into them over time are no part of the original texts, so no question arises of the Qur'an confirming those additions.

**"Do not be the first to deny them"** is explained by Ibn ʿAbbās as: do not be the first to disbelieve in the Qur'an and in Muḥammad ﷺ when you know more about him than anyone else. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: do not be the first of the People of the Book to disbelieve in Muḥammad ﷺ after hearing that he has been sent, and al-Ḥasan, as-Suddī and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said likewise. Ibn Jarīr held that "them" refers to the Qur'an mentioned at the start of the verse. Both views are correct, because the two are bound together: whoever disbelieves in the Qur'an has disbelieved in Muḥammad ﷺ, and whoever disbelieves in Muḥammad ﷺ has disbelieved in the Qur'an. "The first" means the first among the Children of Israel, for there were people of Quraysh and of the Arabs generally who rejected the Prophet ﷺ before the People of the Book did. The verse speaks of the Children of Israel in particular because the Jews of Madīnah were the first of them to be addressed by the Qur'an, so their rejection would make them the first of the People of the Book to reject it.

Disbelief is the gravest sin whether one is the first to commit it or the last, so why single out being first? Because the first to deny bears not only the sin of his own denial but the additional burden of misleading everyone who follows his example, and so earns a multiplied punishment. Those who come after will lean on those who went before and the leaders will carry the followers' sins. Do not, in other words, establish disbelief as a continuing practice, for the responsibility of the one who starts a practice is greater than that of the one who merely imitates it. From this a general rule follows: whoever is in any way responsible for others falling into sin shares the burden of their sin, and whoever helps others toward a good deed shares in its reward. Many verses of the Qur'an and many hadiths repeat this point.

**"or trade them for a fleeting gain"** means: do not exchange faith in My signs and belief in My Prophet for the life of this world and its pleasures, which are small and bound to end. The signs in question are especially the passages describing Muḥammad ﷺ in their Book. Do not suppress them for fear of losing what you hope to earn from the lowly people among you, whether income, position or leadership. Do not prefer your cheap worldly share to the grandeur of Allah's truth. The Arabic word āyāt means both "signs" and "verses," and in context the prohibition is plain: no one may take people's money for twisting or hiding the verses of Allah's Book to please them or to serve their worldly interests. On this there is complete consensus in the Ummah.

**"And be mindful of Me"** means have taqwā of Me, fear Me and no one else in this matter. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported that Ṭalq ibn Ḥabīb defined taqwā as acting in obedience to Allah, by a light from Allah, hoping for Allah's mercy, and avoiding disobedience to Allah, by a light from Allah, fearing Allah's punishment. Here the command warns the People of the Book against deliberately hiding the truth, spreading its opposite, and opposing the Messenger ﷺ.

### Wages for teaching the Qur'an

The verse does not deal with the question of accepting a wage for teaching the Qur'an or reporting its verses correctly, but the question is important in its own right and the jurists differ on it. Imām Mālik, Imām al-Shāfiʿī and Imām Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal consider such wages permissible. Imām Abū Ḥanīfah and some other jurists held them impermissible, because the Prophet ﷺ forbade using the Qur'an as a means of livelihood. Circumstances later changed radically. In earlier times those who taught the Qur'an received a living allowance from the Bayt al-Māl, the public treasury of the Islamic state. When Islamic society fell into disorder, through Western imperialism among other factors, they lost that support. Teaching the Qur'an to children is a full-time occupation, and the teachers could not take up other demanding work without breaking the essential chain by which the Word of Allah is passed from one generation to the next. For this reason the Ḥanafī jurists ruled that accepting wages for teaching the Qur'an is permissible, and according to the Hidāyah, the well-known manual of Ḥanafī law, this is the ruling to be given in these times. Later jurists extended the permission to related duties such as leading the prayer, calling the adhān, and teaching hadith and fiqh, since these are connected with teaching the Qur'an and the survival of Islam depends on them equally. This is set out in ad-Durr al-Mukhtār and in ash-Shāmī's commentary on it.

Ash-Shāmī, the famous Ḥanafī scholar, explained at length in that commentary and in his own book Shifāʾ al-ʿAlīl that the later jurists allowed wages for teaching the Qur'an only because of an essential religious need, without which the whole Islamic order would be disturbed, and that the permission is therefore limited to such needs. It follows that paying or receiving wages for reciting the Qur'an in order to pass on the reward to the dead, or for some worldly purpose, remains forbidden, since it meets no essential religious need. Both the reciter who takes such wages and the person who pays them commit a sin, and since the recitation earns no merit, there is nothing to transfer to the dead. Ash-Shāmī refers to many authoritative works, including Tāj ash-Sharīʿah, al-ʿAynī's commentary on the Hidāyah, and the marginal notes of Khayr al-Dīn al-Ramalī on al-Baḥr ar-Rāʾiq, and cites al-Ramalī in particular to the effect that paying for the recitation of the Qur'an beside a grave or elsewhere in order to transmit its reward to the dead was never reported from the Companions, their successors or the great scholars of the early centuries, and is therefore an innovation (bidʿah) in religion.

### A reading for the inner life

The belief that this verse calls for is of more than one kind. The generality of believers believe on the basis of reasoned proof, inferring the truth by argument. The elite believe through clear evidence, having been drawn near, for the Real has drawn close to them and so they believe in Him. And the final stage of belief is direct witnessing, which belongs to the elect of the elect. As for the closing words, those who fear Allah's punishment are many, but those who stand in awe of Him through knowing and seeing Him are rare.

### In short

- The Children of Israel are commanded to believe in the Qur'an, which confirms the Tawrāh and the Injīl as originally revealed, including their descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ.
- They must not be the first of the People of the Book to reject it, because whoever leads others into sin carries their sins as well as his own, just as whoever leads others to good shares their reward.
- Concealing or twisting Allah's verses for money, position or popularity is forbidden by consensus, and the verse warns them to fear Allah rather than their followers.
- The separate question of wages for teaching the Qur'an divides the jurists, with the Ḥanafīs permitting it out of necessity while forbidding paid recitation for the dead as an innovation.

42.text:
The address to the Children of Israel continues with a prohibition aimed especially at their scholars. "Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly." Two things are forbidden here, and two things are commanded by implication. They are forbidden to blend truth with falsehood and to conceal the truth, and they are therefore required to make the truth known and to explain it plainly. The verse speaks to people who possessed real knowledge, who had the description of the Prophet ﷺ in their own Books, and who were tempted by fear and greed to blur it or bury it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do not mix truth with falsehood"** forbids them to confuse the truth that Allah revealed with falsehood of their own making. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it simply: do not mix truth with falsehood and facts with lies. Qatādah said it means do not mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, when you know that Islam is Allah's religion and that Judaism and Christianity as now practised are innovations with no origin in Him, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have said the same. Another explanation is that the Jewish scholars would mix the description of the false messiah with the description of Muḥammad ﷺ, so that people could no longer tell which was which. The verse makes clear that it is not permissible to combine truth and falsehood in such a way that the listener is left confused about what the truth is.

**"or hide the truth knowingly"** forbids the second offence. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as: do not hide the knowledge you have of My Messenger and of what he was sent with, for his description, which you know well, is written in the Books in your possession. They knew it to be the truth and were convinced of it, and yet they concealed it. "Knowingly" may also mean: while you know the immense harm this evil will do to people, who will be misled and brought to the Fire by following the falsehood you have blended into the truth. Concealing the truth out of fear or greed is forbidden, and it is this particular temptation, the fear of losing followers and income, that the verse confronts.

### The scholar and the caliph

Al-Qurṭubī related in his commentary a story that illustrates the duty this verse imposes. It comes through a chain of reliable reporters and is taken from the Musnad of ad-Dārimī.

During a visit to Madīnah, the Umayyad caliph Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik asked whether anyone was still alive who had kept company with a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ. He was told that only Abū Ḥāzim remained, and he sent for him. The caliph opened by accusing him of discourtesy and disloyalty, since every person of standing in Madīnah had come to pay respects except him. Abū Ḥāzim answered: may Allah protect the leader of the Muslims from saying what is not true. You did not know my name before today and I had never set eyes on you, so how could I have come to meet you, and how is that disloyalty? The caliph looked around for support, and Imām az-Zuhrī spoke up to say that Abū Ḥāzim was right and the caliph wrong.

The caliph changed the subject. Why, he asked, do I dislike the thought of dying? Because, said Abū Ḥāzim, you have made your world flourish and let your dwelling in the next world fall into ruin, and no one likes leaving a thriving city for a wasteland. The caliph admitted it and asked what it would be like to stand before Allah tomorrow. Abū Ḥāzim said that the one who has done good will come to Allah like a traveller returning to the people he loves, while the one who has done evil will come like a runaway slave dragged back to his master. The caliph wept and sighed that he wished he knew how Allah would deal with him. Weigh your deeds against the Book of Allah, said Abū Ḥāzim, and you will know. Which verse, asked the caliph? Abū Ḥāzim recited: "Indeed, the virtuous will be in bliss, and the wicked will be in Hell" (82:13-14). The caliph observed that Allah's mercy is vast and may reach even wrongdoers, and Abū Ḥāzim answered with another verse: "Indeed, Allah's mercy is always close to the good-doers" (7:56).

The questions went on. Who is the most honourable of Allah's servants? Those who are considerate of their fellow human beings and have the understanding to recognise the truth. Which is the best of deeds? Carrying out what Allah has made obligatory and keeping away from what He has forbidden. Which prayer is most likely to be answered? The prayer of a person for someone who has done him good. Which is the best charity? Giving a person in distress as much as you can despite your own need, without making him feel indebted and without hurting him by putting him off. Which is the best speech? Telling the truth plainly and without reservation to someone who can harm you or from whom you hope for a favour. Who is the wisest of the Muslims? The one whose actions are governed by obedience to Allah and who calls others to it. And who is the most foolish? The one who helps another person commit an injustice, for he has sold his religion to serve that person's worldly interests.

Then the caliph asked pointedly what Abū Ḥāzim thought of him. Abū Ḥāzim tried to be excused, but the caliph insisted on a word of counsel, so he said: leader of the Muslims, your forefathers seized power over people by the sword and against their will, after killing hundreds of men, and then they left this world. I wish you could know what they are saying now, after their death, and what people are saying about them. One of the courtiers, afraid of the caliph's displeasure, rebuked Abū Ḥāzim for speaking so rudely. He replied that he had said nothing rude, only what Allah commands, for Allah has bound the scholars to speak the truth before people and not to hide it, and he recited the verse about those who were given the Scripture, that they must "make it known to people and not hide it" (3:187).

How can we put ourselves right now, asked the caliph? Give up your pride, Abū Ḥāzim said, acquire fellow feeling for people, and give them justly what is due to them. Would he come and live at court? May Allah protect me from it, he said, for I fear that if I lived with you I would come to love your wealth and splendour and suffer a grievous punishment for it in the next world. Was there anything he needed? Yes, he said: help me escape the Fire and enter Paradise. That is not in my power, said the caliph. Then there is nothing you can do for me, he replied. Asked to pray for him, Abū Ḥāzim prayed: O Allah, if Sulaymān is pleasing to You, make the good of this world and the next easy for him, and if he is Your enemy, drag him by the hair toward the deeds You approve of. Asked for one piece of special advice, he said: keep it short. Fear your Lord and revere Him to the point that He never finds you where He has forbidden you to be and never misses you from where He has commanded you to be.

Later the caliph sent him a hundred gold dinars. Abū Ḥāzim returned them with a letter: if these dinars are payment for my words, then blood and pork are cleaner in my eyes than this money. If you consider it my due from the public treasury, then Islam has hundreds of scholars and servants. Send the same to each of them and I can accept it. Otherwise I have no need of it. His refusal shows that no wage may be taken for worship or for an act of obedience to Allah.

### Why they did it

As the recognised representatives of revealed religion in Arabia, the Israelites were the people others asked about the Arab Prophet. Feigning innocence, they would raise points designed to turn people away from him and his mission. They urged others to follow the truth and live by it, yet when their own turn came they failed to accept it. When answering the call of God means giving up positions of honour and prestige, those who owe their religious rank to worldly elevation find it extremely hard. For the truly devout these considerations are no obstacle. Where others find their satisfaction in worldly pleasures, the true believer finds it in remembering God, spending for His cause, obeying His commands and walking steadfastly on His path. He knows that what deserves fear is God's punishment, not worldly loss.

### A reading for the inner life

Take care not to mix truth and falsehood, truthfulness with lying, the approved with the unapproved. This does not mean refusing to recognise falsehood. You must recognise falsehood in order to avoid it, and recognise truth in order to pursue it. The Prophet ﷺ, al-Muṣṭafā, prayed: O God, show us truth as truth and grant us to choose it, and show us falsehood as falsehood and grant us to avoid it. The masters of the realities read the verse as a warning not to mix the share of the lower self with the food of the heart, for the two cannot coexist. The owner of a heart rejoices in the rightful claim of truth, while the servant of the self is tied to the self's portion, and these two cannot meet. This world is trifling and the next world precious, and these cannot agree. Friendship with the Creator is felicity without beginning or end, while friendship with created things is a ready affliction. "Allah does not place two hearts in any person's chest" (33:4). Worship of God and worship of self are opposites, and they cannot be housed in one nature. Love for the self and love for the loving Friend will not both reach you. Choose one or the other, for you will not have both.

### In short

- The Jewish scholars are forbidden to blend truth with falsehood, for instance by confusing the description of the Prophet ﷺ with that of the false messiah, and forbidden to conceal the truth they know, above all his description in their Books.
- By implication the verse commands scholars to declare the truth plainly, as Abū Ḥāzim did before the caliph Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, citing 3:187, and to refuse payment for doing so.
- Concealing truth from fear or greed is the besetting temptation of those whose religious rank depends on worldly standing.
- Inwardly, truth and falsehood cannot share one heart (33:4): a person must choose between the self's portion and the heart's food.

43.text:
After three verses about faith and doctrine, the address to the Children of Israel turns to deeds, naming only the most important of them. "Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down." These are commands to people who have accepted the truth, telling them what the law now requires. They are also, read closely, an invitation to join the Muslim community in its worship, since the bowing of the Islamic prayer is something the Israelites' own rituals did not include.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Establish prayer"** means perform the five prescribed prayers fully, with their obligatory and recommended parts. Muqātil said that this command to the People of the Book means praying behind the Prophet ﷺ. Whenever the Qur'an insists on prayer it uses, with one or two exceptions, the word iqāmah, "establishing." Literally the word means making something straight or keeping it firmly in place, and since what stands straight and firm usually lasts, it also means establishing a thing and making it permanent. Joined to the word ṣalāh in the Qur'an and the hadith, it signifies not merely saying prayers but performing the five prayers steadfastly, in the prescribed form, at the prescribed hours, and with all their necessary conditions. The great rewards and blessings promised for prayer are all tied to iqāmah in this sense. The Qur'an says, for example, that "genuine prayer should deter one from indecency and wickedness" (29:45). Prayer bears this fruit only when it is performed in the full sense of iqāmah. If one meets people who are regular in their prayers yet indulge in indecent or evil conduct, one should not doubt the verse. Such people have been praying, but they have not been observing the conditions of iqāmah.

**"pay alms-tax"** commands zakāh from one's wealth. Muqātil said that for the People of the Book this meant paying it to the Prophet ﷺ. The Arabic word zakāh has two root meanings, to purify and to grow. Zakāh is not a tax imposed by the state or by society. In the language of the Sharīʿah it is the portion of one's possessions that is set apart and spent in full accordance with the injunctions of the Sharīʿah, out of wealth that Allah placed in one's hands. The verse by itself does not show that prayer and alms were obligatory on the Israelites before Islam, but another verse does: "Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel and appointed twelve leaders from among them and then said, 'I am truly with you. If you establish prayer, pay alms-tax…'" (5:12). The two duties bound them too, even if their outward forms were different.

**"and bow down with those who bow down"** means pray with those who pray, that is, with the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, and be humble before Allah together with the humble of his community. Muqātil said that Allah here commands the People of the Book to be with the Ummah of Muḥammad ﷺ and among them, and the phrase also means: be among the believers in doing the best of what they do, and foremost among their deeds is prayer. This passage was revealed concerning the Jewish scholars who used to tell their relatives among the Muslims to stay firm on the religion of Muḥammad ﷺ because it was the truth.

Lexically, rukūʿ means bowing, and could even cover prostration, which is bowing in its fullest form, but in the terminology of the Sharīʿah it means the particular bowing prescribed in prayer. Why is this one gesture singled out from all the movements of prayer? One answer is that it is a figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole, just as "the recitation of the Qur'an at dawn" stands for the dawn prayer in another verse, and just as the word sajdah in some hadiths stands for a whole unit of prayer or even the whole prayer. On this reading the verse simply means: pray along with those who pray. A fuller answer is that the ritual prayer of the Israelites and others included prostration but not bowing. This particular bowing, rukūʿ, is peculiar to the Islamic prayer, so "those who bow down" can only be the Muslim community, and the verse in effect asks the Israelites to accept Islam and pray alongside the Muslims.

### Patience and prayer as a cure

It was usually love of money and love of power that made it hard for the Jews, and especially their scholars, to accept Islam. These verses prescribe the remedy for both diseases: fortify yourself with ṣabr and ṣalāh, patience and prayer. "Patience" is a weak translation of ṣabr, which has three senses: bearing pain and misfortune patiently, restraining oneself from sin, and remaining steadfast in obedience to Allah. In this wide sense patience is the perfect cure for love of money, because money is never an end in itself but only a means of satisfying appetites, and once a person has firmly resolved not to follow his appetites like a slave, he no longer needs much money, and love of it no longer blinds him. Prayer is the cure for ambition and love of power, because inwardly and outwardly it is an exercise in humility, and the more carefully it is performed, the more it purifies a person of love of money and power, of ambition and pride. These being the real substance of every spiritual disorder, once they are brought under control it becomes easy to accept Islam and to stay firm in faith.

There is a difference between the two remedies. Patience requires only the restraint or abandonment of excessive appetites and needless desires. Prayer requires, in addition, the performance of prescribed actions and the temporary renunciation of perfectly lawful desires and needs that the Sharīʿah otherwise permits, such as eating, drinking, speaking and walking, and it requires this five times a day and night at fixed hours. Once a person decides to give up needless desires, the urge weakens within days, so patience is not so difficult after all. But prayer, with its conditions, its fixed hours and its suspension of basic human activities, is demanding for human nature. One might object, then, that the Qur'an prescribes a remedy that is itself hard to take. The Qur'an admits that regular, steadfast prayer is exacting, and the verses that follow show the way through: prayer is not a burden to the humble in heart. The human heart loves to roam freely through the vast spaces of thought and fancy, and since every organ of the body serves the heart, it wants them free as well. Prayer demands the surrender of that freedom, and this annoys the heart and pains the organs it governs. The disease is restless motion, and its cure is the opposite, restfulness. This is what khushūʿ, usually rendered "humility," really signifies: the restfulness of the heart. A person cannot empty the heart of thoughts by trying. The only way is to absorb the mind in one thought so completely that all others fall away on their own. The verses that follow supply that thought, and once the heart is at rest, prayer becomes easy, regular prayer gradually cures pride and ambition, and the way to perfect faith becomes smooth. Such is the well-ordered art of spiritual medicine the Qur'an teaches, as against the fashionable systems of thought-concentration and meditation, dressed in a pseudo-mystical or Eastern style but born of the anxieties of the modern West, which only further disorder an already disordered mind.

### Prayer in congregation

"Establish prayer" shows that prayer is obligatory. "Bow down with those who bow down" shows that it is to be performed in the company of other Muslims, in congregation (jamāʿah). Many scholars cite this verse as proof that congregational prayer is obligatory for men. The crucial question is the degree of the obligation, and the jurists differ.

A large body of Companions, their successors and jurists of the Ummah hold that praying in congregation is necessary (wājib) and that abandoning it is a sin. Some Companions went so far as to hold that praying alone without a valid excuse is not permissible at all. The literal wording of the verse supports this view, and so do several hadiths. Abū Dāwūd reported a hadith to the effect that a man who lives near a mosque has no valid prayer except in the mosque. Muslim reported from Abū Hurayrah that a blind Companion asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to pray at home, as he had no one to lead him to the mosque and back. The Prophet ﷺ gave permission, but as the man was leaving asked whether he could hear the call to prayer from his house. He said he could, and the Prophet ﷺ told him that in that case he must come. In Abū Dāwūd's version of the same hadith the Prophet ﷺ said, "Then I see no room for a concession in your case." Al-Qurṭubī cites a hadith from Ibn ʿAbbās in which the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever hears the call and does not go to the congregation has not prayed at all, unless he has a valid excuse. On the strength of such reports, Companions like ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī ruled that a man within earshot of the mosque's call who still misses the congregation without excuse has no accepted prayer at home. Hearing the call here means the call of a man with an ordinary voice, not one with an extraordinarily loud voice or one amplified by a loudspeaker.

The majority of the Companions, their successors and the later jurists hold instead that congregational prayer is an emphasised sunnah (sunnah muʾakkadah), the most emphasised of its kind, like the sunnah prayer before Fajr, so that it comes very close to being obligatory. On the basis of other verses and hadiths they read the imperative "bow down with those who bow down" as emphasis, and they understand the hadiths that seem to deny the validity of praying at home as meaning that this is not the complete way to pray.

The most comprehensive statement on the matter comes from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, as reported by Muslim. He said that whoever wishes to meet Allah tomorrow as a true Muslim should keep the five prayers steadfastly in the place where the call is regularly given, for Allah laid down for your Prophet ﷺ the ways of good guidance (sunan al-hudā), and praying the five prayers in congregation is one of them. If you pray at home as that man does, he said, pointing to someone, keeping away from the congregation, you will have abandoned your Prophet's ﷺ Sunnah, and abandoning his Sunnah leads to going astray. Whoever performs wuḍūʾ properly and walks to a mosque has a sin forgiven, a good deed recorded and a rank raised for every step. And he recalled that in their time no one stayed away from the congregation except a known hypocrite, so that even a sick man who could not walk would be brought to the mosque supported between two men and stood in the row.

This statement brings out the great importance of the congregation while fixing its precise status among the "ways of good guidance," which the jurists call as-sunan al-muʾakkadah. Hence if a man prays at home without a proper excuse such as illness, his prayer is valid, but he has earned Allah's displeasure by neglecting an emphasised sunnah. If neglecting the congregation becomes his habit, he commits a grave sin. And if all the people around a mosque desert it and pray at home, they become liable to punishment under the Sharīʿah. Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said that if persuasion fails to correct such people, they are to be confronted with force.

### A reading for the inner life

Keep the good manners of the Presence, for preserving good manners is the most perfect form of service. The alms spoken of here allude also to the alms of aspirations: just as you pay the alms of wealth, pay the alms of your aspirations. As the poet said on their behalf, everything has an alms to be paid, and the alms of beauty is a mercy like Mine. Through the abundant increase of aspirations and the subtleties of vision that He creates in those who pursue and seek Him, they are raised high, until their states turn into states of bewilderment. And "bow down with those who bow down" means follow the practice of the pious forefathers, the salaf, in what they used to do, and avoid isolation, for being in a dense congregation is sounder than being separated from people.

### In short

- Having called the Israelites to faith, the verse calls them to the chief deeds: steadfast, properly performed prayer (iqāmah), zakāh as the purifying portion of wealth, and bowing with those who bow.
- Since the Israelites' prayer had prostration but no rukūʿ, "those who bow down" are the Muslims, and the verse invites the Jews to pray behind the Prophet ﷺ with his community.
- Patience and prayer are prescribed as the cure for love of money and love of power, and prayer becomes light only through khushūʿ, the restfulness of the heart.
- The verse is a chief proof for congregational prayer: some hold it obligatory, the majority an emphasised sunnah so stressed that habitual neglect is a grave sin, as Ibn Masʿūd's statement in Muslim shows.

44.text:
The address to the Children of Israel now exposes a contradiction in the conduct of their religious scholars. "Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture? Do you not understand?" They told others to do what they themselves refused to do, and they did so while reading a Book that condemned exactly that. The question is asked in a tone of disavowal and astonishment, and although it was addressed to the Jewish scholars of Madīnah, it reaches everyone who preaches goodness to others and neglects it in his own life.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you preach righteousness"** uses the word al-birr, which embraces every kind of righteousness and every act of obedience to Allah. Here it includes the Oneness of Allah and following Muḥammad ﷺ, which the Jewish leaders would urge upon people of humble standing. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the narration of al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ, said the verse came down concerning the Jews of Madīnah, one of whom would say to his brother-in-law, his relatives, or Muslims related to him by nursing: hold fast to your religion and to what this man, meaning Muḥammad ﷺ, commands you, for what he has brought is the truth. They urged people to follow Islam while holding back from it themselves. Qatādah, as reported by ʿAbdur-Razzāq from Maʿmar, said that the Israelites would order people to obey Allah, to fear Him and to do good, and then contradict their own orders, and as-Suddī said the same. Ibn Jurayj said the verse concerns the People of the Book and the hypocrites, who commanded people to pray and fast but did not practise what they commanded. Whoever commands others to do good, he said, should be among the first to do it.

**"and fail to practice it yourselves"** means, as Ibn ʿAbbās explained through Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, that you forget to practise it yourselves. You forbid people to reject the prophethood and the covenant recorded in your Tawrāh, while you yourselves have forgotten the covenant that you would accept My Messenger. You have broken that covenant and rejected what you know is in My Book. Their advice to their relatives shows that they knew Islam to be the true faith, but being enslaved to their desires they were not prepared to accept it themselves.

**"although you read the Scripture"** means that you recite the Tawrāh, which contains the threat of punishment for those whose deeds contradict their words, and which denounces in the strongest terms the scholar who does not act on his knowledge. They could not plead ignorance.

**"Do you not understand?"** asks whether they have no sense of what they are doing to themselves, so that they might wake from their slumber and recover from their blindness, see the evil of their actions and repent. Have you not even the ordinary common sense of human beings? The question is one of rebuke, and the clause about forgetting themselves is its real target.

### Preaching without practice

Allah does not blame the People of the Book for commanding righteousness. Enjoining good is itself part of righteousness and an obligation for scholars. What He condemns is that the one who calls others to goodness should himself ignore the call. The scholar is required to heed what he invites others to. The Prophet Shuʿayb put it this way: "I do not want to do what I am forbidding you from. I only intend reform to the best of my ability" (11:88). Commanding good and doing good are both required, and according to the soundest view of the scholars of the early generations and those who came after, neither duty is cancelled by neglecting the other.

The hadith describes the punishment of those who fail in this. Imām Aḥmad reported that Abū Wāʾil said that he was riding behind Usāmah when Usāmah was asked why he did not advise ʿUthmān. He answered that he did advise him, in private, and would not open a door he would hate to be the first to open, nor flatter a man as the best of men even if he were his leader, because of something he had heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said he heard him describe a man who, on the Day of Resurrection, will be brought and thrown into the Fire, his intestines will spill out, and he will go round and round dragging them like a donkey circling a millstone. The people of the Fire will gather round him and ask what happened to him, since he used to command them to do good and forbid them evil. He will say: yes, I commanded good and did not do it, and I forbade evil and did it myself. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim also recorded this hadith. Anas reported that on the night of the Ascension the Prophet ﷺ passed by people whose lips and tongues were being cut with scissors of fire, and when he asked who they were, Jibrīl (Gabriel) told him that they were preachers of his Ummah who urged people to good deeds and neglected themselves. According to a hadith reported by Ibn ʿAsākir, some people in Paradise will see acquaintances of theirs in Hell and ask how they came to be there, when they themselves reached Paradise through the very good deeds they had learned from them, and those in Hell will answer that they used to say it all with their tongues and never acted on it. Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī said that three verses made him hesitate to preach to people: this verse, and "O believers! Why do you say what you do not do? How despicable it is in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do" (61:2-3), and the words of Shuʿayb quoted above.

### Must a sinner stay silent?

None of this means that a person who is himself slack in good deeds, or a transgressor in some respect, may not give good counsel to others, or that someone who has fallen into a particular sin may not try to dissuade others from it. Doing a good deed is one virtue, and urging others to do it is a distinct virtue. Abandoning one does not oblige a person to abandon the other. A man who does not pray is not thereby required to give up fasting, and a man who does not pray is not thereby forbidden to tell others to pray. Likewise, doing something the Sharīʿah forbids is one sin, and failing to dissuade those one can influence from it is another, and committing the first does not entail committing the second.

Imām Mālik cited Saʿīd ibn Jubayr as saying that if everyone decided to stop enjoining good and forbidding evil on the grounds that he was himself a sinner with no right to preach until he was free of all sin, no one would be left to counsel anyone, for who is entirely free of sin? Al-Ḥasan of Baṣrah said that this is exactly what Satan wants: that people, obsessed with a false notion of purity, should neglect their duty to teach and advise others. Mawlānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī used to say that when he noticed a bad habit in himself, he would deliberately denounce that very tendency in his sermons, so that the blessing of the sermon might help him rid himself of it.

In short, the verse does not say that a person indifferent to good deeds in his own life may not preach. It says that the preacher must not neglect good deeds in his own life. Why, then, does it single out the preacher, when neglect of good deeds is impermissible for preacher and non-preacher alike? Because the preacher's offence is graver and more blameworthy. He sins knowing that it is a sin and cannot plead ignorance, whereas the non-preacher, especially if he is unlettered, may be guilty of failing to seek knowledge but can to some degree plead ignorance of the law. Moreover, when a scholar or a preacher sins, he is in effect mocking the Sharīʿah. Anas reported from the Prophet ﷺ that on the Day of Judgment Allah will forgive the unlettered and the ignorant far more readily than He will forgive the scholars.

### A reading for the inner life

Will you urge others to be foremost while you are content to lag behind? Will you call people to Us while you yourselves hang back from Us? Will you give drink to the arriving caravans while you keep away from the water? Will you argue with others over fine points while content with your own bankruptcy in everything but externals? Do you weigh a speck or a grain in other people while tolerating heaps of sand and mountains in yourselves? As the poet said, do you look at the mote in my eye and not see the beam in your own? Do you hand round the choicest drink and never drink yourselves? "Although you read the Scripture," you persist in secret pretensions, denying the shameful thoughts and the plain urges toward blameworthy things that your hearts conceal. Do you not understand how blameworthy such qualities are and how ugly such deeds?

### In short

- The Jewish scholars of Madīnah urged their relatives to hold to Islam as the truth while refusing it themselves, and the verse rebukes this contradiction in people who read the Tawrāh and knew its warnings.
- Enjoining good is not what is condemned. Enjoining good while neglecting it is, and the hadith describes the punishment of such preachers: dragged intestines in the Fire, lips cut with scissors of fire.
- A sinner may and should still counsel others, for otherwise no one would preach. Doing good and urging good are separate duties, and neglecting one does not excuse neglecting the other.
- The preacher is singled out because he sins knowingly and mocks the law he teaches, and the unlettered will be forgiven more readily than the learned.

45.text:
After a string of commands to the Children of Israel, verse 45 tells them where the strength to obey will come from. "And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble", it says, and the next verse goes on to describe who those humble people are. On the surface the address is still to the Israelites who were being called to accept the Prophet ﷺ, but the instruction is worded for everyone who finds Allah's commands heavy, which is to say for all of us.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And seek help"** means ask for assistance in your affairs. Scholars read it in two complementary ways. Some take it as help in carrying out the duties Allah has prescribed and keeping away from what He has forbidden. Others widen it to help in sacred and worldly affairs alike, since patience and prayer bring a person close to Allah, and when a person is close to Allah, He helps him, protects him and lifts his difficulties from him. Allah commanded His servants to use these two means to win the good of this life and the next.

**"through patience"**, in Arabic ṣabr, is restraining the self in the face of what it dislikes. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said the verse means: make use of patience and the obligatory prayer in your search for the Hereafter, and added that patience here is fasting. Similar reports come from Mujāhid. Al-Qurṭubī and other scholars noted that this is why Ramaḍān is called the month of patience, an expression found in the hadith literature. Another view is that patience here means holding back from evil, which explains why it is paired with the acts of worship and above all with prayer. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, in a report preserved by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, distinguished two kinds of patience: a good patience when calamity strikes, and a better one in staying away from what Allah has forbidden. Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported to have said much the same.

**"and prayer"**, aṣ-ṣalāt, is named separately to stress how much weight it carries. The prayer is among the best supports for holding firmly to Allah's commands. A hadith says that whenever something troubled the Prophet ﷺ he turned at once to prayer. The Qur'an itself says that genuine prayer should deter a person from indecency (al-faḥshāʾ) and wickedness, and that the remembrance of Allah is a greater deterrent still (29:45).

**"Indeed, it is a burden"** uses a pronoun, "it", that has been read in two ways. Mujāhid took it to refer to the prayer, and this was the preferred reading of Ibn Jarīr. It is also possible that it refers to the whole counsel just given, patience and prayer together. The Qur'an speaks in the same way elsewhere. When the people of knowledge rebuked those who envied Qārūn (Korah), they said that Allah's reward is better for those who believe and do good, and that none attain it except the steadfast (28:80). And when it commands that evil be answered with what is better, it adds that only the patient and the truly fortunate manage it (41:34-35). Whichever reading is taken, the point is that prayer is heavy, grievous and hard to keep up.

**"except for the humble"**, al-khāshiʿīn. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported Ibn ʿAbbās explaining them as those who believe in what Allah has sent down. Others describe them as people who are at peace in their obedience, or simply those who are humble before their Lord. For such people the burden lightens.

### Why were the Israelites told this?

One explanation is that the address is aimed at the Jews of Madīnah at the moment when greed and the love of leadership were standing between them and faith. They were therefore directed to forbearance, which was understood as fasting, and to prayer. The reasoning is neat: greed grows out of appetite, and fasting weakens appetite, while prayer breeds humility and kills pride. Seen in the light of the previous verses, the people who had found it so hard to give up their positions of honour were being handed the two tools that make such sacrifice possible. For the truly devout, worldly considerations of this kind are no hindrance at all, because they find in remembrance, spending and obedience the satisfaction that others seek in worldly gain.

### What is humbleness of heart?

The humility the verse praises is khushūʿ, and the Qur'an and hadith mean by it a settledness and lowliness of the heart that grows out of sensing Allah's greatness and one's own smallness beside it. Once a person has it, obedience and submission stop being a strain and become easy, even pleasant. It can also show on the outside: such a person carries himself with discipline and courtesy, is modest, and looks as if his heart has been broken, in the sense that vanity and self-admiration have gone out of him. The order matters, though. A person who does not carry real humility and fear of Allah inside has no khushūʿ, however modest his manner and however lowered his gaze. It is not even proper to put on the signs of it on purpose. When ʿUmar saw a young man sitting with his head hanging down, he told him to lift his head, because humbleness of heart lives in the heart. Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī said it is not a matter of rough clothing, coarse food and a bowed head. Rather, it is treating the high and the low alike wherever truth is at stake, and keeping the heart free for Allah and for the duties He has laid down. Ḥasan al-Baṣrī described ʿUmar as a man who spoke loudly enough to be heard, walked quickly and struck hard when he struck, yet no one doubted that his heart was truly humble. Al-Qurṭubī summed it up: deliberately wearing the look of a humble man is a form of self-deception and a trick of Satan, and is blameworthy, but if the signs appear in someone without his knowing it, he is excused.

A related word, khuḍūʿ, often appears alongside khushūʿ and the two are almost synonyms. The difference lies in the roots. Khushūʿ properly refers to the lowering of the voice and the glance when this comes from genuine modesty and fear, as in the verse describing the Day when all voices will be hushed before the Most Compassionate (20:108). Khuḍūʿ refers to the bodily posture of humility, as in the verse about necks bent in submission before a compelling sign (26:4).

### Is prayer valid without it?

Scholars had to decide what place khushūʿ holds in the law of prayer. The Qur'an and the Sunnah press its importance again and again. Allah commands prayer "for My remembrance" (20:14), and since heedlessness is the opposite of remembrance, a person who drifts into forgetfulness of Allah during prayer is not fulfilling the duty of remembering Him. Another verse warns, "do not be one of the heedless" (7:205). The Prophet ﷺ said that prayer is nothing but lowliness and humility, and another hadith says that a man whose prayer does not hold him back from indecency and evil only moves further from Allah. A heedless prayer plainly does not restrain anyone from wrongdoing, so such a person moves further away.

Drawing on these texts in his Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm ad-Dīn, al-Ghazālī argued that khushūʿ must be a necessary condition of prayer, on which its acceptance depends. He cited the Companion Muʿādh ibn Jabal and jurists of the rank of Sufyān ath-Thawrī and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as holding that prayer without khushūʿ is not valid.

The four Imāms of jurisprudence and the great majority of jurists took a different position. They regard khushūʿ as the very essence of prayer, yet they do not make it a condition for the whole of it. The one thing they require is that at the opening takbīr the worshipper should turn to Allah with his whole heart and form the intention (niyyah) of praying for His sake alone. If he fails to keep khushūʿ for the rest of the prayer, he earns no reward for that part, but from the standpoint of fiqh he is not counted as someone who abandoned prayer, and he is not liable to the punishment for giving up the prescribed prayers without excuse.

Al-Ghazālī himself explained why the two camps differ. The jurists do not deal with inner states of the heart (aḥwāl). Their task is to set out the outward rules of the Sharīʿah on the basis of what the limbs visibly do, and deciding who will be rewarded in the next world is not within the remit of fiqh. Since khushūʿ is an inner state, they did not make it a condition for the full duration of prayer but tied validity to its lowest degree, the turning of the heart to Allah at the start together with the intention to worship Him alone. A second explanation rests on a principle the Qur'an states clearly in other places: nothing is imposed on people beyond their capacity. Apart from a few gifted individuals, people simply cannot hold khushūʿ from the first takbīr to the final greeting, so the jurists, rather than bind people to something they cannot do, made it a condition only at the beginning.

Al-Ghazālī closed his discussion by saying that, for all the importance of khushūʿ, one may rely on Allah's boundless mercy and hope that the inattentive worshipper will not be classed with those who leave prayer altogether. After all, he tried to discharge the duty, turned away from everything else for at least a few moments, and had Allah alone in mind while forming his intention. A half-hearted prayer at least keeps a person's name off the roll of those who habitually disobey Allah and desert the prayer entirely. The matter therefore holds both fear and hope: fear of having earned punishment, and hope of eventual forgiveness. The right response is to fight one's own laziness and indifference as hard as one can, knowing that only Allah's mercy brings success in that fight.

### The homily on patience

The devotional reading of the verse hears in it a command to the Prophet ﷺ: tell your community to be patient in their affairs so that they may reach what they long for, since patience is the key to relief. Then comes a warning to anyone who would enter the path without that patience. Whoever lacks the patience of the Men should stay off their playing field. Whoever does not have the legs of men should not dress in men's clothes, and whoever lacks the wealth of having nothing should not boast of selflessness. The Prophet ﷺ himself, the paragon of the world, was not left an hour without sorrow once he stepped onto this field. If he sat cross-legged for a while, he was told to sit like a servant. If he put a ring on his finger, a verse of rebuke came down (23:115). If he set his foot boldly on the ground, the command came not to walk on the earth exultantly (17:37). When trial pressed on him from every side he sighed that no prophet had been tormented as he had been, and the answer from the Exalted Presence asked whether someone whose heart and spirit witness Him could complain about the weight of trial. Every drop of grief's venom that the treasuries of the Unseen contained was then poured into a single cup and set in his hand, and a curtain was lifted from his innermost core so that he could drink it while gazing on Allah's beauty, in keeping with the words "be patient with your Lord's decree, for you are truly under Our Eyes" (52:48). The tongue of his state answered that poison poured by the Beloved's hand is sweet, that even if that hand were fire it would be a bed of roses, and that whatever comes from Him is sweet whether it heals or hurts.

On the closing phrase, the same reading says humbleness is a stipulation of the prayer and the mark of the servant's neediness. Those who are humble in prayer are praised by the Real and chosen from among His creatures, as in the opening of Sūrat al-Muʾminūn, where success is promised to the believers who humble themselves in their prayers (23:1-2). This humbleness, it adds, has both an outward side and an inward side.

### In short

- Patience (ṣabr, the quality of aṣ-ṣābirūn) and prayer (aṣ-ṣalāt) are the two means Allah gives for carrying out His commands, and "patience" has been read as fasting, as holding back from sin, and as steadfastness under hardship.
- "It is a burden" refers to prayer, or to the whole counsel, and it is heavy for everyone except the humble, al-khāshiʿīn.
- Khushūʿ is a state of the heart, not a posture. ʿUmar, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī all warned against faking its signs.
- Al-Ghazālī, with Muʿādh, ath-Thawrī and al-Baṣrī, held khushūʿ necessary for a valid prayer. The four Imāms and most jurists require it only at the opening takbīr, while agreeing that the heedless part of a prayer earns no reward.
- The right attitude to one's own distracted prayers is a mixture of fear and hope, together with hard effort against laziness.

46.text:
Verse 46 finishes the sentence begun in verse 45. Prayer is a burden for everyone except the humble, and the humble are "those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return". The verse therefore answers a practical question: what makes prayer light for some people and crushing for others? The answer is certainty about the meeting with Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"those who are certain"** translates yaẓunnūna, a verb from ẓann, a word that in everyday Arabic usually means to think or suppose. Here it means certainty (yaqīn). Ibn Jarīr pointed out that the Arabs use ẓann for certainty as well as for doubt, and the Qur'an does the same elsewhere: when the wicked see the Fire and "realize" that they are bound to fall into it (18:53), the verb is the same, and there is no doubt left in that moment. Scholars agree that certainty is the plain and most obvious sense, and that what is intended is a settled reckoning (ḥusbān), not a hopeful guess.
