Most jurists and hadith scholars hold a middle position. It is better to report a hadith in the exact words one heard, and never to alter them deliberately, but if the exact words cannot be recalled it is permissible to convey the meaning in one's own words. The hadith about conveying "just as he heard it" can mean conveying the meaning exactly and without alteration, which a change of wording does not necessarily violate. Al-Qurṭubī pointed out that this very hadith has reached us in different wordings in its different versions, which is itself proof that changing the words is allowed when necessary. As for the nabiyy and rasūl incident, two explanations are offered. The word nabiyy carries a loftier sense than rasūl, since rasūl can be used of any messenger at all, whereas nabiyy is reserved for those Allah has chosen to address directly through revelation (waḥy), who stand above all other men. The other explanation is that in prayers the words appointed by Allah or by His Prophet ﷺ carry a power that no other words have. This is why those who compose protective formulas, taʿwīdh or ʿawdhah, and those who recommend words of supplication, are so careful to keep to the authentically reported wording without the slightest change. Prayers considered especially effective therefore belong to the first category of speech, in which both the words and the meanings are intended and both must be guarded.

### Remorse too late

The devotional reading paints the aftermath. The Israelites could not ward off the opening of heaven above them by any stratagem, nor loosen the cords of affliction beneath them by relying on their usual ways. When the fangs of pain bit into them they gnashed the teeth of remorse, and what good was that once the situation was past help?

### In short

- Told to enter bowing and to say ḥiṭṭah, "absolve us", the Israelites crawled in on their backsides and said "a seed in a hair" or "wheat", mocking the command in deed and word.
- The rijz sent on them was the plague, which killed about seventy thousand. Hadiths in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere call the plague a rijz with which earlier nations were punished.
- Jurists agree that altering the words of the Qur'an, hadith or a divine command so as to distort the meaning is forbidden. Where the words themselves are intended, as in the adhān, the recitations of the prayer and the Qur'an, they may not be changed even if the meaning survives.
- Reporting a hadith by its meaning is permitted by most scholars for a reporter who knows Arabic perfectly, though some early scholars allowed no change at all.

60.text:
Verse 60 returns to the wilderness and to another favour, water from stone. "And remember when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, 'Strike the rock with your staff.' Then twelve springs gushed out", and each tribe knew which spring was its own. The verse ends with the same combination as before, a gift and a warning: "Eat and drink of Allah's provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land".

### Phrase by phrase

**"when Moses prayed for water for his people"**. This too belongs to the years of wandering. Parched with thirst in the wilderness, the Israelites asked Mūsā (Moses) to pray to Allah for water, and he did. The favour Allah asks them to remember is that He answered the supplication of their prophet when he asked Him to provide them with water.

**"We said, 'Strike the rock with your staff'"**. Allah told him to strike a particular rock with the staff he carried. The reports describe it as a rock Allah had given him, and one commentary identifies it as the rock that had once run off with his robe, a light, cube-shaped stone of marble about the size of a man's head. Ibn ʿAbbās described it as a square stone that Mūsā was commanded to strike. Another report pictures it with twelve protrusions resembling nipples, each of which released a spring when struck.

**"Then twelve springs gushed out, and each tribe knew its drinking place"**. Twelve springs burst from the stone, three on each side according to Ibn ʿAbbās, and each of the twelve tribes was assigned its own. The tribes were twelve because Yaʿqūb (Jacob) had twelve sons, each of whom had a large family that came to be reckoned a tribe with its own organisation and its own head. Each tribe knew which spring was its drinking place and did not share it with the others, so that there would be no quarrelling over water. Ibn ʿAbbās added that wherever they moved, they found the same bounty in the same manner as in the place they had left, so they never needed to travel in search of water. This report is part of the long hadith about the trials that an-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded.

**"Eat and drink of Allah's provisions"**. The food is the manna and the quails, and the water is what came out of the rock. You eat and drink what I provided, Allah is saying, without any toil or hardship on your part, so worship the One who did this for you.

**"and do not go about spreading corruption in the land"** means do not repay the favour with acts of disobedience that cause favours to be taken away. Corruption here means disobeying Allah and overstepping His commands, or acting against what Mūsā told them. Grammatically, mufsidīn, "spreading corruption", is a circumstantial phrase that reinforces the verb lā taʿthaw, which comes from ʿathiya, to act corruptly.

### The same story in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf

The story appears again in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, which was revealed in Makkah, while this sūrah was revealed in al-Madīnah, and scholars note two differences in the telling. In al-Aʿrāf, Allah speaks about the Children of Israel in the third person, telling the Prophet ﷺ what He did for them, whereas here, in a sūrah addressed to the Jews of al-Madīnah, He speaks to them directly. And in al-Aʿrāf the verb says that the water trickled forth (7:160), describing the first moment when it began to flow, while here it says that it gushed out, describing what came next, when the water burst out in full force. Allah knows best.

### On denying miracles

Al-Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī observed that denying miracles is a serious error, and even an error of logic. Allah has given one kind of stone the unusual property of drawing iron to itself. There is nothing logically or rationally impossible, then, in His giving another stone the property of absorbing water from the earth and releasing it again. That explanation is offered for people who look at things superficially. In truth there is nothing impossible in Allah producing the water inside the stone itself, and those who call it impossible do not understand what the word "impossible" technically means. The devotional reading adds a different observation. The One who can draw water out of solid rock can also quench thirst without any water. Yet He chose to make the effect of the miracle appear through Mūsā and to tie him to the place where help was sought, so that Mūsā would exert his own self (nafs) in going to the stone and bear the responsibility of striking it with his staff. In that way a measure of human effort was woven into the carrying out of the decree when he asked for water for his people.

### Praying for rain

The verse answers a practical question: in time of drought, must formal prayers be offered to ask Allah for rain? Mūsā simply prayed, and Allah provided miraculously, so the essential thing in asking for rain is the supplication itself. In the Sharīʿah of Mūsā a plain prayer sufficed, and Imām Abū Ḥanīfah held that this principle holds in the Islamic Sharīʿah as well. The Prophet ﷺ acted differently on different occasions. An authentic hadith reports that he once went out of the city to the open ground used for the ʿĪd prayers, offered formal prayers, delivered a khuṭbah and then prayed for rain. According to a hadith recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim from the Companion Anas, on another occasion he prayed for rain while delivering the Friday khuṭbah, and Allah sent rain. Whatever form the prayer takes, scholars agree that it will not be effective unless it is joined to repentance for one's sins, an admission of one's helplessness, sincere humility and an affirmation of one's servitude to Allah. Someone who persists in sin and transgression has no right to expect his prayer to be answered. If Allah in His mercy grants it anyway, that is His will, and He is able to do all things.

### Twelve drinking places

The devotional reading finds a further lesson in the arrangement of the springs. The Real wanted each people to follow its own way (sunnah), to keep within its own boundary (ḥadd) and not to dispute with its neighbours, so He gave each tribe a marker by which it knew its own drinking place and did not trespass on the others'. Once He had met their needs, He asked them to be grateful, to keep His command and to stop choosing sin, and so He said, "do not go about spreading corruption in the land". The drinking places differ, and each comes to its own. One is sweet and fresh, another salty and bitter, one clear and pure, another dried up to a few drops. Every people has a water carrier who leads it and a scout who drives it on. So it is that the lower selves arrive at the wells of craving and desire, the hearts at the wells of piety and obedient works, the spirits at the wells where unveiling and witnessing are found, and the innermost selves at the wells of the realities. These last are snatched away from created being and its outward markings, then from sensory awareness and human attributes, and finally pass away into the reality of finding and of the Essence.

### In short

- In answer to Mūsā's prayer, Allah had him strike a rock and twelve springs flowed, one for each of the tribes descended from Yaʿqūb's twelve sons, so that no tribe quarrelled with another over water.
- The report of Ibn ʿAbbās in the hadith of the trials describes a square stone with three springs on each side that travelled with them.
- Al-Aʿrāf tells the same story in the third person and in Makkah, and its verb describes the first trickle, while this verse describes the full flow (7:160).
- Al-Bayḍāwī argued that denying such miracles is irrational, since the One who made the magnet can make a rock give water.
- Asking for rain requires, above all, supplication joined to repentance and humility. Abū Ḥanīfah held a plain prayer sufficient, while the Prophet ﷺ sometimes prayed formally with a khuṭbah and once prayed from the Friday pulpit.

61.text:
Verse 61 closes the list of favours with the Israelites' complaint about the food, and then widens out into a verdict on the whole people. They said, "O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal", and asked for herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils and onions instead. Mūsā (Moses) answered, "Do you exchange what is better for what is worse?", and told them that any village would have what they wanted. Then the verse states the outcome: "They were stricken with disgrace and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah", because they rejected His signs and killed His prophets, and all of this was "for their disobedience and violations". Allah is saying, in effect: remember My favour in sending you manna and quails, a good, pure, wholesome food that cost you no effort, and remember your ingratitude in asking Mūsā to swap it for something inferior.

### Phrase by phrase

**"when you said, 'O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal'"**. The "same meal" was the manna and quails, which they ate day after day. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that they grew bored and impatient with the food they were given and began to remember the life they had lived before, when their diet was lentils, onions, garlic and herbs. This happened in the wilderness of Tīh, and one view links it to the city of verse 58. The divine provision had been given so that, freed from the struggle for a living, they could devote themselves wholly to carrying out God's commands, but they began demanding spicy cooked dishes instead. Discontented with the plain necessities, they hankered after worldly luxury.

**"So call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces"** means ask your Lord for us. The Arabic "of" here is explanatory: the things named are what the earth grows.

**"of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions"**. Herbs, cucumbers, lentils and onions are well known. The word rendered "garlic", fūm, was discussed at length. Ibn Masʿūd read it as thūm, which is plainly garlic, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Ḥasan that Ibn ʿAbbās explained fūm as garlic. Al-Ḥasan also mentioned that in the old languages the expression fūmū lanā meant "bake for us", and Ibn Jarīr commented that if this is right, fūm is one of those words whose pronunciation shifted, the letter fāʾ replacing thāʾ because the two sound alike. Others said fūm is wheat, the grain used for bread, and al-Bukhārī noted the view that it covers every grain or seed that is eaten, which is why some translations render it as "corn" or "grain". Allah knows best.

**"Moses scolded them, 'Do you exchange what is better for what is worse?'"**. The question in Arabic opens with a particle of rebuke. Mūsā was criticising them for asking for inferior food while they lived in ease, eating what was tasty, wholesome and pure, and what came to them with no labour or effort. They were not content with what Allah had chosen for them, and had no patience with the way He managed their food and clothing. In their confusion they slid back into their old habits of coarser eating and settled for a lower state.

**"You can go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for"**. The word miṣr means any city, as Ibn ʿAbbās said, though Ibn Jarīr reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas that it refers to Miṣr, the Egypt of Firʿawn (Pharaoh), and one early commentary glosses it as "the place you came from". The correct view is that it means any town at all, as Ibn ʿAbbās and other scholars held. Mūsā's point was that what they were asking for is cheap and plentiful in any city they might enter, so he would not trouble Allah with a request for it, least of all when it was the inferior choice. One account adds that they refused to change their minds, that Mūsā then prayed, and that Allah's reply was: go down to a city, whichever it may be, and there in its fields and markets you will find what you demanded. Because the request sprang from boredom and arrogance and there was no need to grant it, it was turned down. On the view that connects this episode with verse 58, Allah directed them through Mūsā to a certain town in the wilderness, where they could till the land and grow what they liked.

**"They were stricken with disgrace and misery"**. The two words are dhillah and maskanah, and the verb pictures them as stamped or cast upon the people. The verse indicates that the Children of Israel were struck with humiliation and that it would not cease: they would go on suffering humiliation at the hands of everyone who dealt with them, along with the disgrace they felt within. Al-Ḥasan said that Allah humiliated them and left them with no protector, placing them under the feet of the Muslims, who arose at a time when the Magians were already collecting the jizyah from the Jews. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and as-Suddī said that "misery" means poverty, and ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī said it means paying the tax. Other commentators take "disgrace" as the poll tax and "misery" as the garb of poverty, and one adds that the marks of poverty and lowliness accompany them even when they are rich, the way a coin never loses the stamp of its mint. All of this came from following their whims and repeatedly turning away from what Allah had chosen for them. Scholars describe the disgrace in two directions: they lost respect in the eyes of others and lost largeness of spirit in themselves.

**"and they invited the displeasure of Allah"**. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said that they deserved Allah's anger. Ibn Jarīr explained the verb, bāʾū, as "they went back carrying" the wrath, comparing the verse of Sūrat al-Māʾidah in which Hābīl tells his brother that he wants him to bear his sin along with his other sins (5:29), where the same root is used of carrying a burden away with oneself. So the sense is that they returned laden with Allah's anger, that His wrath settled on them and that they had earned it. One commentary paraphrases: they deserved to be forsaken by Allah.

**"for rejecting Allah's signs and unjustly killing the prophets"**. This is what the Children of Israel were repaid with, humiliation and misery, and the wrath was part of the humiliation they had earned by defying the truth, disbelieving in Allah's signs and belittling those who carried His law, the prophets and their followers. They rejected the Messengers and even killed them, among them, as one commentary notes, Zakariyyā and Yaḥyā, slain without any right and for no crime. There is no worse disbelief than disbelieving in Allah's signs and murdering His prophets. One early commentary applies the first charge to the Jews of the Prophet's ﷺ own time, reading the signs rejected as Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. Two hadiths illuminate the charge. In a hadith of the Two Ṣaḥīḥs the Messenger of Allah ﷺ defined kibr, arrogance, as refusing the truth and looking down on people, and both halves of that definition fit the conduct described here. And Imām Aḥmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the people in the worst torment on the Day of Resurrection will be a man killed by a prophet or who killed a prophet, an unjust ruler, and one who mutilates the dead.

**"This is a fair reward for their disobedience and violations"** gives a further reason for the punishment. Disobedience is doing what is forbidden. Violation, or transgression, is overstepping the limits between what is allowed and what is forbidden. One early commentary points to their disobedience over the Sabbath and to their killing of prophets and declaring forbidden things lawful. The repetition of "this was because" is for emphasis. Allah knows best.

### A disgrace that lasts

Scholars treat the disgrace of this verse as permanent. One form it takes is that temporal power has been taken from the Jews for good. The only exception scholars allow is the forty days, close to the Day of Judgement, in which the Dajjāl (Antichrist), who will be of Jewish stock, will hold an irregular sway like a robber's, which cannot be called sovereign power in any proper sense. Allah had made clear to them through Mūsā that if they persisted in disobedience they would always live under the domination of other nations, as the Qur'an says: your Lord declared that He would send against them, until the Day of Judgement, people who would make them suffer terribly (7:167). The classical summary of how the Companions, their successors and the great commentators understood the verse runs: however rich they become, they will be despised by other people, and whoever gets power over them will humiliate them and fasten on them the marks of servitude.

The fullest parallel is the verse of Sūrat Āl ʿImrān: they are stricken with disgrace wherever they are found, except by a rope from Allah or a rope from men, and they have drawn Allah's anger and been branded with misery for the same reasons given here (3:112), an explanation of which aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim transmitted. The rope from Allah refers to those whom Allah Himself, by His own command, has exempted from this disgrace, such as children, women and those wholly devoted to prayer and worship who never take up arms against Muslims. The rope from men is a peace treaty made with the Muslims, or leave to reside in a Muslim land as jizyah-paying subjects, the jizyah being the tax on non-Muslims under Muslim rule that frees them from military service and similar duties. And since the Qur'an says "from men" rather than "from Muslims", a third case is possible: the Jews may make political arrangements with non-Muslims and live in peace under their backing and protection.

Scholars also examine the kind of exception the verse makes. An exception can be of two sorts. In the first, the thing excepted is or was part of the whole from which it is excepted, as in "the tribe came except Zayd", where Zayd is a member of the tribe but excluded from the act of coming. In the second, the thing excepted never belonged to the whole, as in "the tribe came except the donkey". If the exception in the verse is of the first kind, the meaning is that all Jews live in disgrace always and everywhere, apart from the two situations named, protection of women, children and the like by Allah's own command, or protection under a treaty with Muslims or with some non-Muslim nation. If it is of the second kind, the meaning is that the Jews as a group remain essentially and permanently in disgrace, with the exception of some individuals who find protection under Allah's command, and of others who receive the support of other nations and so disguise their own disgrace.

### The modern doubt

Reading 3:112 alongside this verse, a twentieth-century commentator addresses a doubt that arises in some Muslim minds at the sight of the state of Israel established in Palestine. The Qur'an seems to say that the Jews will never have a sovereign state, yet they have taken Palestine and set one up. His answer is that, behind the appearances, this is not an independent sovereign state but a stronghold established by the Western powers in the midst of Muslim countries to protect their own interests. In his judgement it could not survive a month without their backing, and those powers regard it as their instrument. It therefore lives, in the Qur'an's words, "through a rope from men". He adds that the part of Palestine in question amounts to a mere dot on the world map when set against the vast territories ruled by Christian states, by Muslim states, and even by states whose people do not believe in Allah at all, and he asks whether so small a holding, kept under an American and British umbrella, can cancel the disgrace that Allah has decreed. On this reading there is no real ground for misgiving about what the Qur'an says.

### Masters of separation

The devotional commentary gathers the verse into a single moral. The Israelites were neither satisfied with the good that God chose for them nor patient under His management of their basic food and clothing. In their confusion they fell back on their habitual eating of impure things and found contentment at a lower level, so He returned them to the suffering of ignominy and bound them to perpetual disappointment. They went so far as to shed the blood of prophets, shamelessly violating the sanctity of God's command. Since they would not repent, He punished them for their ugly deeds and left them to the contemptible states their own souls had chosen. Sincere counsel (naṣīḥah) had failed, and so retribution and public disgrace (faḍīḥah) overtook them. The Israelites, it is said, were a people divided in their aspirations and scattered in their aims. They would not be content with one food, and they would not be satisfied with one object of worship either, so that when they saw a people devoted to idols they said to Mūsā, "Make for us a god like their gods" (7:138). This is the mark of the masters of separation (arbāb at-tafriqah). Patience with the One is hard, as God says of those who, when their Lord alone is mentioned in the Qur'an, turn their backs in aversion (17:46). A people who cannot bear one dish will struggle to bear one Lord.

### In short

- Bored with manna and quails, the Israelites asked for the herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils and onions of their old life, and Mūsā rebuked them for trading the better for the worse. Fūm was read as garlic, as "bake for us", as wheat, or as grain in general.
- "Any village" means any town, and the request, born of boredom and arrogance, was refused.
- Disgrace and misery were stamped on them: humiliation under others, poverty, and the tax, marks that follow them even in wealth.
- The cause was rejecting Allah's signs and killing His prophets, the worst of disbelief, together with disobedience and transgression. A hadith defines arrogance as rejecting truth and despising people.
- Sūrat Āl ʿImrān (3:112) adds the two exceptions, a rope from Allah and a rope from men, which scholars use to explain any apparent respite, including the modern state.
- The deeper fault was a divided heart, unable to be content with one food or one God.

62.text:
After a long account of the Israelites' defiance and its punishment, verse 62 states the rule that governs everyone. "Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians", it says, naming four communities, and then lays down one condition for all of them: whoever "believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve". Having described the fate of those who defy His commands, fall into what He forbade and overstep His limits, Allah now makes clear that the righteous and obedient among the earlier nations received the reward of their good deeds, and that this remains true until the Day of Judgement for everyone who meets the condition.

### Why the verse comes here

The previous verse told how the Israelites drew Allah's wrath on themselves through habitual insolence and disobedience. A listener, or a Jew hearing it, might conclude that after such transgression no repentance of theirs could be accepted. This verse removes that misgiving by stating a general principle. Whatever a person's past conduct, once he submits himself fully to Allah's commands in both belief and deed he is acceptable to Allah and will receive his reward. Since the Qur'an is Allah's final message, full obedience after its revelation can only mean accepting Islam and following the Last Prophet, Muḥammad ﷺ. The verse therefore assures everyone that on accepting Islam all his former transgressions, whether of belief or of action, are forgiven and he becomes worthy of the rewards of the next world. Whoever follows the unlettered Prophet and Messenger ﷺ gains lasting happiness, with no fear of what is to come and no sorrow over what is gone.

### The occasion of revelation

The reports connect the verse with Salmān al-Fārisī and the monks he had lived among before reaching the Prophet ﷺ. Mujāhid related that when Salmān told the Prophet ﷺ the story of those monks, the Prophet ﷺ said that they would be in the Fire. Salmān said that the whole earth turned dark for him, until this verse was revealed, from "Indeed, the believers" to "nor will they grieve", and it was as though a mountain had been lifted off him. As-Suddī gave the fuller form. The verse came down about the monks whose company Salmān al-Fārisī had kept. When he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ he described their worship and their striving: they prayed and fasted, he said, they believed in you, and they testified that you would be sent as a prophet. When he had finished praising them the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Salmān, they are among the people of the Fire", and then Allah revealed this verse. A report traced through Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd, and from other Companions, says that the verse was revealed about Salmān al-Fārisī, a notable of Jundishapur, and that what follows it was revealed about the Jews.

### Phrase by phrase

**"the believers"**. On one reading these are those who believed in the prophets before the coming of Muḥammad ﷺ, that is, those among the earlier peoples who believed in Mūsā (Moses) and all the other prophets. On another, they are those who believe in what was revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ. When Allah sent him as the last Prophet and Messenger to all the children of Ādam (Adam), mankind became obliged to believe in him, obey him and refrain from what he forbade, and those who do so are the true believers. His Ummah was given the name muʾminūn, believers, because of the depth of its faith and certainty and because it believes in all the previous prophets and in the matters of the unseen.

**"Jews"**. The Jews are the followers of Mūsā who took the Torah as their reference for judgement. Scholars offer several accounts of the name Yahūd. It can be derived from a word meaning to turn back in repentance, as in Mūsā's prayer, "we have turned (hudnā) to You", so that they were called Yahūd because they repented, or because they were kind to one another. It was also said that the name comes from Yahūdhā (Judah), the eldest son of Yaʿqūb (Jacob). Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said they were so called because they swayed when they read the Torah. One early commentary describes those meant here as the people who deviated from the religion of Mūsā.

**"Christians"**. Once ʿĪsā (Jesus) had been sent, the Israelites were bound to follow him and obey him, and his followers and companions are called an-Naṣārā because they gave help and support to one another. They are also called Anṣār, helpers, from the words of the disciples, al-Ḥawāriyyūn, when ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, asked who would stand up with him for Allah and they answered that they would (61:14). It was also said that they took the name from a land called an-Nāṣirah (Nazareth), a view reported from Qatādah, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn ʿAbbās. Allah knows best. Naṣārā is the plural of Naṣrān.

**"and Sabians"**. Who the Ṣābiʾūn were is disputed. Sufyān ath-Thawrī related from Layth ibn Abī Sulaym that Mujāhid said the Sabians stand between the Magians, the Jews and the Christians and have no specific religion, and the like is reported from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, ʿAṭāʾ and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. Others said they were a sect of the People of the Book who read the Zabūr (the Psalms), and others that they were a people who worshipped the angels or the stars. One early commentary calls them a Christian sect whose members shaved the middle of their heads, read the Gospel, venerated the angels and said, "our hearts have turned (ṣabaʾat) to Allah". Another calls them a Christian or Jewish sect, and another a group said to have followed prophets on the faith of Ibrāhīm (Abraham). A modern writer identifies them with followers of Yaḥyā (John the Baptist) who lived in ancient Iraq, counted as People of the Book, prayed facing the Kaʿbah in Makkah, and are now extinct. Other scholars admit that nothing is definitely known about their beliefs and practices, and think it most probable that they worshipped the stars. The view that seems nearest the truth, and Allah knows best, is Mujāhid's, shared by Wahb ibn Munabbih: the Sabians were neither Jews, Christians, Magians nor polytheists. They had no particular religion that they followed and enforced, but went on living according to their natural disposition (fiṭrah). This is why the idolaters of Makkah used to call anyone who embraced Islam a Ṣābiʾ, meaning one who had left every religion on earth. Some scholars added that the Sabians are those whom no prophet's message ever reached.

**"whoever truly believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good"** means whoever from among these groups comes to believe in the Prophet's ﷺ own time and does righteous deeds in keeping with the Law that was given to him, or, as another gloss puts it, does right in what lies between him and his Lord. The grammar is noted: the verbs "believes" and "does" are singular because "whoever" is singular, while the pronouns that follow are plural because the meaning is plural. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah related that Ibn ʿAbbās, commenting on this clause, said that Allah afterwards revealed, "Whoever seeks a way other than Islam, it will never be accepted from them" (3:85). His statement means that, now that Muḥammad ﷺ has been sent, no work of any person is accepted by Allah unless it conforms to his law. Before his coming, everyone who followed the guidance of his own prophet was on the right path, rightly guided and saved. So the verse describes the position before Muḥammad ﷺ was sent, and since then Islam, devotion and dedication to Allah alone, is the only way of life Allah accepts.

**"will have their reward with their Lord"** means the reward of their deeds awaits them with Him, in Paradise.

**"And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve"**. They will have no fear of the torment to come and no grief over anything they left behind. The same promise is made to the close servants of Allah, who will have no fear nor grieve (10:62), and the angels announce it to the dying believer who said "Our Lord is Allah" and stood firm: do not fear, do not grieve, rejoice in the Paradise you were promised (41:30). One commentary adds a further sense: they will have no fear on the day when death itself is slain and Hell is closed, and their security is everlasting.

### Only two articles of faith?

The verse names only faith in Allah and faith in the Last Day, and some have taken this to mean that these two suffice for salvation. Scholars reject that reading. The Qur'an says again and again that a person who denies the prophets, the angels or Allah's Books is no Muslim. Faith in Allah is the first article of the Islamic creed and faith in the Day of Judgement the last, and by naming the first and the last the verse says compactly that the whole creed, from beginning to end, is required. There is a further reason. A person can know anything about the essence and attributes of Allah, or about what will happen on the Day of Judgement, only through the prophets and the Books of Allah, and those Books reach the prophets through an angel. Faith in Allah and the Last Day is therefore impossible without faith in the angels, the Books and the prophets.

### Why mention the Muslims in an invitation to Islam?

If the verse invites people to Islam, why does it name those who have already accepted it? Scholars answer with an analogy. A king in a similar position might declare that his laws apply impartially to all his subjects, and that whoever obeys them will be rewarded regardless of whether he was formerly a friend or a foe. The friend has always been loyal, so the warning and the promise are really aimed at the foe, but the form of words carries a message of its own: the king's favour does not flow from personal attachment to his friends but depends on the quality of obedience and loyalty, so the foe too can earn it by acquiring that quality. That is why the Muslims are named alongside the non-Muslims, and it should never be taken to imply that salvation can be reached without accepting Islam.

A modern commentator draws out the same point from the other side. The Muslims are not set apart here but grouped with the other communities associated with prophets, which shows that no community is inherently superior to another in God's sight and that only true belief and righteous action are rewarded with salvation. Belonging to a particular community confers no status with God. The people who gather round a prophet in his lifetime live by true belief and righteous action. They hear his call and their spirits are stirred. An intellectual revolution takes place inside them, and their whole pattern of life changes from the rule of personal desire to the rule of God's teaching. These are the people to whom the prophets gave glad tidings of eternal blessing. As generations pass, religion turns into a kind of national inheritance. Tidings that were given on the basis of faith and deeds come to be treated as the fruit of ethnic affiliation. People begin to assume a special relationship with God that others do not share, so that anyone born into the community is assured of salvation whatever his faith and deeds amount to. Paradise is for us, hell is for them. God has no such relationship with any community. He looks only at a person's thoughts and deeds, and in the Hereafter people will be judged by their deeds and character, not by the group they belong to.

### The misreading to avoid

The verse has been pressed into service by some modern writers, pleased with their own liberalism and tolerance, to claim that it opens salvation to every "person of good will" whatever creed he follows. Read in its context and alongside the other relevant verses of the Qur'an, it does no such thing. It promises salvation in the next world to those who accept Islam, and it is an invitation extended to the Jews, the Christians, the Sabians, and in fact to the followers of every religion and to unbelievers too. The specific names serve only as examples.

### The devotional reading

The mystical commentary reads the verse as a statement about the breadth of divine acceptance. The diversity of paths, given the unity of their source, does not stand in the way of a gracious acceptance. For anyone who affirms the Real through His signs and believes what He has said about His truth and His attributes, the differences between laws and the variety of names under which religion appears do not decide who merits His good pleasure. That is why the verse joins "the believers" with "the Jews" and the rest, and then says "whoever believes", meaning that if they fear God, each along his own way of knowing Him, every one of them has a beautiful homecoming and an ample reward. The believer, muʾmin, is anyone who is under the protection (amān) of the Real, and for someone under His protection it is only fitting that no fear should touch him and no grief. Scholars read this, like the rest of the verse, in the light of Ibn ʿAbbās's statement and the verse of Āl ʿImrān (3:85): the acceptance is real, and the way into it, since the coming of Muḥammad ﷺ, is his religion.

### In short

- The verse states the rule for every community: faith in Allah and the Last Day together with good deeds earns reward and security, whatever a person's past.
- It was revealed when Salmān al-Fārisī grieved over the fate of the monks he had known.
- Ibn ʿAbbās explained that it was followed by 3:85, so that since the sending of Muḥammad ﷺ only Islam is accepted, while before him each people was saved by following its own prophet.
- The Sabians are variously described, most plausibly as a people with no fixed religion living by their fiṭrah, which is why the Makkans called converts to Islam "Sabians".
- Naming the first and last articles of faith stands for the whole creed, and naming the Muslims shows that reward depends on obedience, not on belonging.

63.text:
Verse 63 recalls the solemn moment at which the Israelites bound themselves to the Torah, and the extraordinary scene that accompanied it. "And remember when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you", Allah says, and then gives the terms: hold firmly to that "which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful". The verse that follows tells how quickly the pledge was broken.

### Phrase by phrase

**"when We took a covenant from you"**. Allah reminds the Children of Israel of the pledges, covenants and promises He took from them: to believe in Him alone without partner, to follow His Messengers, and to act according to what is in the Torah. In the words of one commentary, He took their consent. The covenant concerned the teachings they had received from God, the Ten Commandments and the Book that contained them.

**"and raised the mountain above you"**. The story behind this clause is told in the reports. Having received the Torah, Mūsā (Moses) came back from Mount Ṭūr (Sinai) and recited it to the Israelites. Its injunctions were strict, but their conduct and cast of mind called for strict discipline. They first said they would not obey until Allah Himself told them that this was His Book, and the seventy men whose story was told under verse 55 went to the Mount and heard Allah attest it. On their return they testified that the Torah was Allah's Book, but added something of their own: they told the people that Allah had permitted them to act on its injunctions only as far as they were able, and had promised to forgive whatever they could not manage. A people already inclined to rebellion, faced with stern commands, now had a fresh excuse for negligence, and they flatly refused to obey, insisting that such demanding rules were beyond their endurance. In answer to this insolence, Allah commanded the angels to lift Mount Ṭūr and hold it in the air over their heads, as a threat that it would fall and crush them if they did not keep their covenant. Left with no choice, the Israelites submitted. The parallel verse describes the mountain hanging over them "as if it were a cloud", while they were sure it would fall on them (7:171). In the hadith about the trials, Ibn ʿAbbās said that their refusal to obey was what made Allah lift the mountain over their heads, so that they would listen. One commentary puts it that the mountain was uprooted from the earth and set above them when they refused to accept the Torah, and another that it was raised to inspire awe and to warn them against breaking the contract. A Jewish tradition preserved in the Talmud tells the same story, of God holding a mountain upside down over them and telling them to accept the Torah's teachings or be destroyed on the spot.

The mountain is aṭ-Ṭūr, the same mountain named in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, according to ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās and others, and this is the more obvious view. Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās explains that ṭūr is the name for a mountain on which vegetation grows, and that a bare mountain is not called ṭūr.

**"Hold firmly to that which We have given you"** means the Torah, as al-Ḥasan said. Mujāhid read it as a command to adhere to it strictly. Other glosses bring out the force of the Arabic: take it forcefully, that is, seriously and with effort, comply with it in earnestness and diligence, and do not treat it casually or lazily.

**"and observe its teachings"**, literally "remember what is in it". Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ said this means read the Torah and put it into practice. One commentary spells out what is to be remembered: its promises of reward and its threats of punishment, and what it declares lawful and unlawful. Another adds: reflect on it.

**"so perhaps you will become mindful"**. The aim of the whole command is taqwā. Holding to the Book and acting on it is how a person wards off Allah's wrath and punishment, obeys Him, and guards himself against the Fire and against acts of disobedience, taking care about what he earns with his Lord.

### Was this compulsion in religion?

A doubt naturally arises. The Qur'an says elsewhere that no one is to be forced into religion, yet here a mountain is held over people's heads. The answer is that no one was being forced to change his religion. The Israelites had already accepted Mūsā as Allah's prophet and had willingly covenanted with Allah that they would act on His Book if one were given to them. They now stood as rebels against a law they themselves acknowledged to be divine, and they were being threatened with punishment for persisting in rebellion. Even a secular state treats rebels quite differently from foreigners or enemies, leaving a rebel only two choices, to submit or to forfeit his life. This is the same reason why, in the Islamic Sharīʿah, it is the apostate (murtadd) who is liable to capital punishment and not the outright disbeliever. The Israelites were threatened as offenders against a law they recognised but refused to obey.

### Every believer's covenant

What happened to Mūsā's people happens, in its own way, to everyone who embraces true faith. To believe is to contract with God to live and to die according to His will, and the pledge is a weighty one: on one side a tiny, helpless speck in God's world, on the other the God whose might upholds the universe. Whoever keeps his word is granted God's eternal blessings. Whoever turns away from his commitment stands in grave danger of being cast into the Fire, never to come out. Everyone who binds himself by the contract of faith should therefore live in fear of breaking his religious vows and bringing catastrophe on his own head.

### Sight without insight

The devotional reading widens the covenant to all responsible beings. Some responded willingly, because God made Himself known to them and they declared His oneness. Others responded unwillingly, because He veiled them and they did not wish to recognise Him. No proof could be more powerful than seeing with one's own eyes the mountain, Ṭūr, lifted up overhead, but the Israelites lacked the light of inner sight (baṣīrah), and so the witnessing of physical sight (baṣar) did them no good.

### In short

- The covenant was the Israelites' pledge to believe in Allah alone, follow His Messengers and live by the Torah.
- When they refused the Torah's demands, Mount Ṭūr was lifted over their heads until they submitted, as 7:171 also records.
- "Hold firmly" means take the Book seriously and act on it, remembering its commands, prohibitions, promises and threats, so as to attain taqwā.
- This was not compulsion in religion but the treatment of rebels who had already accepted the law, which is why the Sharīʿah punishes the apostate and not the mere disbeliever.
- Faith is itself a covenant, and seeing miracles is useless without inner sight.

64.text:
Verse 64 records the sequel to the covenant: "Yet you turned away afterwards". It then reminds the Israelites why they still exist to be addressed: had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy, "you would have certainly been of the losers".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Yet you turned away afterwards"** means that after giving so firm a pledge, under a mountain, you still deviated and broke it. You turned your back on the covenant and rebelled. The devotional reading stresses the "afterwards": they went back to disobedience after witnessing the signs with their own eyes.

**"Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy upon you"**. The breach of the covenant was so grave that one might have expected utter destruction to come down on them as punishment. Allah in His mercy spared their physical existence, though they will answer for their treason in the next world. Scholars explain the grace and mercy in several complementary ways: Allah forgave them, He went on sending them prophets and messengers, He deferred His punishment, He bore with them, and He accepted their repentance when they asked forgiveness. Scholars distinguish two kinds of divine mercy. The general mercy extends to believers and disbelievers alike and shows itself in worldly well-being and prosperity. The special mercy belongs to believers only and will show itself above all in the next world, in salvation and nearness to Allah.

**"you would have certainly been of the losers"** means losers in this life and in the Hereafter because of breaking the covenant, among those duped and left exposed to Allah's punishment. Had it not been for His decree of respite and His forbearance through acts of grace, says the devotional reading, He would have punished them without delay and brought a great calamity down on them, and their deeds would have been a total loss.

### Who is being addressed

The last phrase of the verse appears to be addressed to the Jews who were the Prophet's ﷺ contemporaries. Faith in him is itself part of the covenant, so these Jews too are included among those guilty of breaking it. Allah asks them to recognise that it is His mercy alone that has kept Him from sending down on them, despite their treason, the kind of catastrophic punishment in this world that used to fall on earlier unbelievers and traitors. A number of authentic hadiths state that it is through the barakah of the Prophet ﷺ that such sweeping punishments no longer descend on any people, and for that reason some commentators identify the grace and mercy of this verse with the sending of Muḥammad ﷺ as Prophet and Messenger. One early commentary reads the verse exactly so: His grace in deferring your punishment, and His mercy in sending Muḥammad ﷺ to you.

To drive the point home, the next verse turns to another group of earlier transgressors and the dreadful punishment that overtook them all at once.

### In short

- After the pledge under the mountain the Israelites still broke their covenant.
- They were spared the destruction they deserved by Allah's grace and mercy: His forgiveness, His patience, His continued sending of prophets, and, on one reading, His sending of Muḥammad ﷺ, through whose barakah sweeping punishments ceased.
- Allah's general mercy reaches everyone in this world. His special mercy, in the next, is for believers alone.
- Without that mercy they would have been losers in both worlds.

65.text:
Verse 65 turns from the broken covenant to one group of covenant-breakers whose punishment the Jews of Madīnah knew well. "You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath", it says, and then records the sentence passed on them: "Be disgraced apes!" The story is told at length in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, and here it is used as a warning.

### Phrase by phrase

**"You are already aware"**. The Arabic opens with a particle of oath: you certainly know, and you have heard, what happened to the people among you who transgressed. The story was part of their own history, told of their own ancestors. Allah is saying: remember, O Jews, that Allah sent His torment on the town that disobeyed Him and broke its pledge and covenant to keep the Sabbath holy.

**"those of you who broke the Sabbath"**. The episode belongs to the time of Dāwūd (David). Allah had appointed Saturday, the Sabt, as the sacred day of the Israelites, set apart for prayer and worship, and fishing was forbidden on it. The town in question lay by the sea, and one commentary identifies it as Aylah (Eilat). Its people were very fond of fish, and the test was sharpened by the fact that on the Sabbath the fish came in abundance, plainly visible, while on other days they stayed away (7:163). The people devised ways round the prohibition. Before the Sabbath they set out nets and ropes and dug pools, so that when the fish came in on Saturday they were trapped, and after the Sabbath ended at nightfall they went and gathered them. Another description has them fastening a cord to a fish's tail on Saturday, tying the far end to something on the shore and leaving the fish in the water, then hauling it out to eat on Sunday. Al-Qurṭubī says that at first they invented all kinds of clever pretexts of this sort for catching fish on Saturday, and gradually began doing it openly. The town divided over the matter. The transgressors stood on one side, and on the other stood a number of scholars and pious men who tried to dissuade them. When their warnings were ignored, they broke off from the sinners altogether and moved to a separate quarter of the town.

**"We said to them, 'Be disgraced apes!'"**. One day the pious party noticed that no sound was coming from the other quarter. Curious, they went to look and found that all the transgressors had been turned into apes. Allah changed them from human beings into monkeys, the animal whose form is closest to the human, and the punishment matched the crime: their deceitful devices looked lawful on the surface while being wicked underneath, just as an ape resembles a man without being one. Al-ʿAwfī reported Ibn ʿAbbās saying that their bodies were changed into those of apes and swine, the young becoming apes and the old swine, and Qatādah said the same of the two groups. Shaybān an-Naḥwī reported Qatādah describing them as howling apes with tails, who had been men and women. The apes could recognise their relatives and friends, and would come up to them weeping in remorse, looking for sympathy and help. After three days they all died. One commentary glosses the sentence as "become humiliated and base apes", and another notes that they were rejected and cast out because of their trickery.

### Are today's apes their descendants?

No. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded Ibn ʿAbbās saying that those who violated the Sabbath were turned into apes and then perished, leaving no offspring. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās saying that Allah turned them into apes because of their sins, that they lived only three days, since no transformed person ever lives longer than that, and that they neither ate, drank nor bred. Allah changes the shape of whomever He wills, doing what He wills with whom He wills, but the apes, the swine and the rest of creation were created in the six days that He mentions in His Book. The rule, then, is that people whom Allah transforms into beasts as a punishment cease to breed and leave no progeny. A hadith recorded by Imām Muslim from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd settles the point: some people asked the Prophet ﷺ whether apes and swine were descended from the transformed Jews, and he reminded them that apes and swine existed in the world before that, and said that when Allah sends this kind of punishment on a people, their line ends with it and there is no further breeding.

### Was the change only moral?

Some modern Muslims have tried to explain the metamorphosis away, suggesting that these Jews did not physically become beasts but only acquired the evil characteristics of apes and swine. Scholars reject this. It denies an explicit statement of the Qur'an, which no Muslim can do and remain a Muslim, and in denying the possibility of physical change it sets limits to Allah's power. Even as exegesis it is flimsy, because these people had been showing beastly traits, a swine's greed and an ape's cunning, before the punishment ever fell. If nothing more than that was meant, where was the change that the Qur'an presents as a punishment for the offenders and a warning to everyone else? The same writers, it is observed, readily accept Darwin's speculation that apes evolved into man, for which no verifiable data has been gathered, while looking askance at the Qur'an's statement that men were changed into apes, though the one change is rationally and logically as possible as the other.

### The metamorphosis of hearts

Alongside the bodily event, the devotional reading points to an inner one: the metamorphosis (maskh) of this community took place in their hearts. When the Israelites abandoned God's command and disdained the laws laid on them, the punishments came quickly, in their disgrace, in their transformation, and in the other things the Qur'anic text includes. For violating the covenant and rejecting the limit God had set, the community was punished with the transformation of their hearts and the alteration of their states, as Allah says elsewhere that He turns away the hearts and eyes of those who refused to believe at first (6:110). A punishment that falls on the heart is far worse than one that falls on the body. On this theme a poet is quoted: you who ask me how I have fared since he left, I suffered what tormented me while it made him glad. I strutted about in our days of togetherness, feeling safe from the tricks of time, but his turning away from me went on until nothing of what I had known remained.

A modern commentator draws the moral plainly. The Israelites were commanded to keep the Sabbath holy and refrain from worldly pursuits on it. They violated it, working on the Sabbath as on any other day, and then went further and dressed up what they were doing as conformity to God's will. That audacity brought God's displeasure, and they became apes. Whoever turns against the law of God puts himself on a level with animals, who follow no code of ethics, and those who play games with divine law should fear losing their human dignity and being brought down to the level of beasts.

### In short

- In the days of Dāwūd the people of a seaside town evaded the Sabbath ban on fishing by trapping fish on Saturday and collecting them afterwards, while their pious neighbours warned them in vain (7:163).
- Allah turned the transgressors into apes, the young into apes and the old into swine according to Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah, and they died within three days without offspring.
- A hadith in Muslim confirms that today's apes and swine are not their descendants.
- The transformation was physical, and reading it as merely moral contradicts the Qur'an, though scholars also speak of an inner transformation of hearts that is worse than any change of body.

66.text:
Verse 66 states the purpose of the punishment just described. "So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing", it says. A punishment that is remembered keeps on working long after the people who suffered it are gone.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We made their fate an example"**. The Arabic word is nakāl, an exemplary punishment designed to deter others from doing what these people did. Allah made the people of this town, who violated the Sabbath, an example through the manner in which He punished them, just as He says of Pharaoh that He overtook him and made him an example in this life and the next (79:25). One commentary adds that the punishment was also a chastisement for the sins they had committed before.

**"to present and future generations"**, literally "to what was before it and what was after it". Ibn ʿAbbās explained: We made this town an example to the towns around it by the way We punished its people, which matches the verse in which Allah says He destroyed the societies around the Makkans after varying the signs for them so that they might return (46:27). Others take the phrase of time rather than place: an example to the people of that age and to those who came after them, so that they would not do the same and earn the same fate. Allah, whose oneness they had pledged to uphold, made them a warning to their contemporaries and a reminder to later generations by preserving their story.

**"and a lesson to the God-fearing"**. The word is mawʿiẓah, an admonition and reminder. The torment that overtook this town came from indulging in what Allah had forbidden and from deceit, so those who have taqwā, al-muttaqīn, should take care to keep clear of such conduct lest what befell that town befall them. The God-fearing are singled out because they, unlike others, are the ones who actually benefit from the lesson, being mindful of the consequences of their actions in the life to come and of Allah's repayment of those who transgress His limits. One early commentary identifies the God-fearing here with Muḥammad ﷺ and his Companions. Scholars also note that those who saw the event, or heard about it, fell into two groups. For the disobedient it was a deterrent and a warning that moved them to repent, and for the obedient it was a lesson and a reminder to stay firm in obedience. It serves both purposes still.

The Prophet ﷺ drew the practical lesson himself. Imām Abū ʿAbdullāh ibn Baṭṭah recorded from Abū Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: do not do what the Jews did, making lawful what Allah has forbidden by means of the flimsiest tricks. This hadith has a good (jayyid) chain.

### Tricks and legal devices

The Jews who were turned into apes had used certain ruses to justify their sin in their own eyes, and this raises a delicate question of fiqh. Some modern writers have accused the master jurists of Islam of inventing elaborate stratagems (ḥiyal, plural of ḥīlah) to help the rich and powerful get round the Sharīʿah. The charge is a petty slander, but it has had some success with the uninformed because it plays on the Arabic word ḥīlah. A word's dictionary meaning is one thing and its technical meaning within a science is another. Literally, ḥīlah does mean a trick or stratagem. As a technical term of fiqh it means a device for giving legitimacy to an action in a situation of need, by making the modifications to it that the Sharīʿah requires. It is not a way of bypassing the Sharīʿah but a way of helping people conform to it in circumstances where necessity or human weakness would otherwise push them to break it.

This verse helps to make the distinction clear. The transgression of the Jews was not an open and explicit breach of the divine law. It was the use of tricks that necessarily amounted to negating the command, such as the cord tied to the fish on Saturday and pulled in on Sunday. A ruse of that kind not only cancels an injunction of the Sharīʿah but mocks it, and that is why those who practised such tricks were judged disobedient and rebellious and were punished so terribly. It does not follow that the ḥiyal of the jurists are impermissible. Those devices serve the opposite purpose. Not only are they an integral part of fiqh, some were suggested by the Prophet ﷺ himself. Exchanging one measure of good dates for two measures of poor dates is, under the Sharīʿah, a form of usury. The Prophet ﷺ indicated a device for avoiding the breach when such a transaction is needed: rather than barter one commodity for another, use money as the medium, first selling the two measures of poor dates for cash and then buying one measure of good dates with the cash. The intention here is to conform to the Sharīʿah, not to evade it, and no negation of it is intended or takes place. The same principle governs all the devices the jurists have proposed to keep people from doing what the Sharīʿah prohibits, and to compare them with the tricks by which the Jews negated and mocked the law is a travesty of the truth.

### A lesson in loss

The devotional reading sees the people of this verse as a picture of all who are tried by abandonment and branded with disappointment. Their condition became a lesson, and the mere sight of what became of them is enough to make one choke on grief. Whoever falls into misery after enjoying status becomes a target of scorn for every ignoble person. This is what remains for those brought low after the wrath of kings and the cold shoulder of chieftains, as the poet lamented: the youths surrounded me and ganged up on me, and from behind they set the dogs on me.

### In short

- The Sabbath-breakers were made a nakāl, an exemplary punishment, for the towns around them and for all later generations, as Pharaoh was (79:25, 46:27).
- The lesson is addressed to the God-fearing because they are the ones who take it to heart, deterring the sinner and steadying the obedient.
- The Prophet ﷺ warned against imitating the Jews by making forbidden things lawful through flimsy tricks.
- The legal devices (ḥiyal) of the jurists are the opposite of such tricks: they help people obey the Sharīʿah in hard cases, as in the Prophet's ﷺ own advice on exchanging dates through a cash sale.

67.text:
Verse 67 opens the story that gives this sūrah its name, al-Baqarah, the Cow. Mūsā (Moses) told his people, "Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow". They answered, "Are you mocking us?", and he replied, "I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!" The favour that the Israelites are being asked to remember here is the miracle at the end of the story, when a murdered man was brought back to life by means of the cow and named his killer.

### The murder behind the command

The reports fill in what the verse assumes. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded ʿUbaydah as-Salmānī's account. There was a wealthy man among the Children of Israel who had no children, and whose only heir was his nephew. The nephew killed him for the inheritance, carried the body by night and left it at the door of another man. In the morning he raised the cry for vengeance, and the people took up their weapons and came close to fighting one another. The wiser among them asked why they should kill each other while the Messenger of Allah was in their midst, so they went to Mūsā and laid the matter before him, and he told them that Allah commanded them to sacrifice a cow. Ibn Jarīr reported something similar. Other accounts give a different motive. According to the Mirqāt, a commentary on the Mishkāt, a man wanted to marry a girl, her father refused, and the suitor was so enraged that he killed the father and disappeared. The Maʿālim at-Tanzīl cites al-Kalbī for the statement that no ruling about killing had yet been sent down by Allah, which, if correct, would place the incident before the revelation of the Torah. In any case, the killer was unknown, and the Israelites asked Mūsā to pray to Allah to reveal him, or, as another account has it, simply asked him how the culprit could be traced. Under Allah's command, he told them to sacrifice a cow.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow"**. The command, as first given, meant any cow at all. Had they simply obeyed, as Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUbaydah said, slaughtering any cow would have been enough.

**"Are you mocking us?"**. Instead of hurrying to obey, they answered stubbornly, asking whether he was making fun of them by answering a question about a murder with an order about a cow.

**"I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!"** means I take refuge with Allah from being one of the ignorant (al-jāhilīn), those who indulge in mockery. God forbid, Mūsā is saying, that he should ever mock the believers, or be counted among the ignorant who lie about Allah and ridicule people. A prophet does not joke about Allah's commands.

### How the story ended

Since the following verses dwell on the Israelites' questions, it helps to know where the story goes. Had they not quibbled, any cow would have served, but because they quibbled the matter was made harder for them, until they were sent looking for one particular cow. They found it with a man who swore he would sell it for nothing less than its hide filled with gold, and they paid that price. They slaughtered the cow and struck the dead man with a piece of it. He stood up, and when they asked him who had killed him he said, "that man", pointing to his nephew, and then died again. The nephew was denied his inheritance, and from then on anyone who murdered in order to inherit was barred from inheriting. The Israelites' habit of raising doubts and objections is on full display in the exchanges that follow, and the hadith notes that had they obeyed without so many questions, no strict conditions would have been laid on them.

### The cow as a mirror

The devotional reading treats the story of the cow and the listing of its qualities as one of the subtle wisdoms and precious pearls of the Qur'an, which is an all-encompassing ocean with kingly pearls and night-brightening gems in its depths. The reader is invited to take all that the Exalted Lord says here about the Israelites' cow as an allusion to attributes of his own. Whoever does so becomes worthy to dive into that ocean and is given access to its hidden wonders and unseen pearls. Three attributes are set out in the verses: first, the cow is neither old nor young, second, it is golden and bright in colour, and third, it is not broken in to plough the earth. The first describes the seeker whose feet go straight on the circle of the Ṭarīqah once the intoxication and greed of youth no longer veil him and the weakness of old age does not yet hamper him. Revelation reached al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ when he was neither a raw youth nor had reached the most feeble stage of life that the Qur'an describes (16:70), and had there been a more complete state, revelation would have come at that time. When longing for God is joined to the intoxication of youth, there is fear of highwaymen on the road, and it is rare for a young man in his first ardour to pass them safely. That is why al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ said that your Lord marvels at a young man who has no youthful recklessness. The second attribute describes the seeker who steps onto the field of the Ṭarīqah in the fullness of his nature and stands straight on it: Unity dyes him in the colour of love, and the colour of love is colourlessness, washing out every mixture, as the Qur'an promises that Allah will strip away whatever rancour is in the breasts of the people of Paradise (7:43). The third attribute is taken up under verse 71.

### In short

- An Israelite was murdered, by his nephew for the inheritance according to the main report, and the people asked Mūsā to find the killer.
- Allah's answer was to sacrifice a cow, and any cow would have done had they obeyed at once.
- They accused Mūsā of mocking them, and he took refuge in Allah from the foolishness of joking about His command.
- Their endless questions made the task hard, until they paid a cow's hide full of gold for the one cow that fitted, and the dead man rose to name his killer.
- The cow's three attributes are read inwardly as the marks of a true seeker.

68.text:
Verse 68 begins the Israelites' interrogation. They said, "Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type" of cow it should be, and Mūsā (Moses) relayed the answer: "The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!"

### Phrase by phrase

**"Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type of cow it should be"**. Once they realised that Mūsā was in earnest, they asked him to pray to his Lord to explain the nature of the cow, whether, as one commentary puts it, it should be large or small. Allah mentions here the obstinacy of the Children of Israel and the many needless questions they put to their messengers, and because they were obstinate He made the ruling harder on them. Had they slaughtered any cow it would have sufficed, as Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUbaydah said, but they made the matter difficult, and so Allah made it more difficult for them.

**"The cow should neither be old nor young but in between"**. The Arabic says neither fāriḍ, an aged cow, nor bikr, a young one that has not yet calved, but ʿawān, in between. This is the explanation of Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Wahb ibn Munabbih, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, as-Suddī and Abū al-ʿĀliyah. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās adding that she was at the age when a cow is at its strongest and fittest, neither old nor young.

**"So do as you are commanded!"** means carry out the sacrifice, and ask no further questions.

### The seeker's age

In the devotional reading, the Israelites were bound to carry out the command directly, but they frittered away their time on outward details, imagining that they could afford to linger in digressions from the duty their covenant imposed. Their misery was doubled as a result, and the disgrace they had been warned of overtook them. The description "neither old nor young, but in between" is read as an allusion to the person suited to the spiritual path, the Ṭarīqah: someone neither swept along by the impetuosity and drunkenness of youth nor paralysed by the weakness and frailty of age, but alert, sobered from his intoxication while still keeping some of the vigour of youth.

### In short

- Taking Mūsā seriously at last, the Israelites began asking for specifications instead of obeying.
- The first answer: a cow in the prime of life, neither aged nor too young to have calved.
- Each needless question narrowed the field and made the duty harder, which is the pattern of the whole passage.
- Inwardly, the "in between" cow pictures the seeker who has outgrown youthful recklessness without yet losing his strength.

69.text:
Verse 69 records the second question. They said, "Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour", and the answer came: "It should be a bright yellow cow", pleasing to those who look at it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour"**. Still debating and still stubborn, they asked what colour the cow should be.

**"It should be a bright yellow cow, pleasant to see"**. The Arabic describes a yellow cow whose colour is fāqiʿ, intense. One commentary calls it golden, a very deep yellow. Al-ʿAwfī reported Ibn ʿAbbās describing the colour as a deep yellow with a whitish cast. As-Suddī explained "pleasant to see" as pleasing to anyone who looks at it, which is also the view of Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. Wahb ibn Munabbih said that if you looked at the cow's hide you would think the rays of the sun shone out through it. One early commentary gives a different picture, a cow with yellow hooves and horns and a black body, and a light colour overall. The modern text of the Torah says the cow was red, but scholars regard this as an error, unless the cow was so deeply yellow that it looked blackish or reddish. Allah knows best.

### Those who remind others of God

The devotional reading connects the cow's striking colour, which no eye could miss, with certain people in the story of the spiritual path whose very presence overwhelms the hearts of others, because they have been clothed in the robe of divine invincibility (jabarūt) and raised up from witnessing the unseen. Such a person is seen to be heedless of ordinary human states and overtaken by the remembrance of the Real. Hence the tradition describing God's friends as people whose very sight brings God to mind.

### In short

- The second specification: a cow of intense, radiant yellow that delights the eye, so bright, in Wahb's words, that the sun seemed to shine through its hide.
- The later Torah's "red heifer" is judged a mistake, or a description of a yellow so deep it looked red.
- The cow's unmissable colour is read as a figure for God's friends, whose sight reminds people of God.

70.text:
Verse 70 brings the third question, and with it a small saving grace. They said, "Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow", adding by way of excuse, "for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow"**. The Israelites persisted in their obstinacy and asked Mūsā (Moses) to have Allah describe the cow still further, this time asking, as scholars understand it, whether it grazed freely or was used for labour, whether it ploughed the soil or not.

**"for all cows look the same to us"**. Their excuse was that cows answering the description so far were plentiful and they could not tell one from another, so they had not managed to find the one intended and needed more detail.

**"Then, Allah willing, we will be guided"**. If you describe it further, they said, we shall find it, or, on another reading, we shall be guided to the right description. One early commentary records the view that they meant being guided to the killer, naming the murdered man as ʿĀmīl. A hadith notes the importance of the proviso they added: had they not said in shāʾa Llāh, "if Allah wills", the matter would never have been made clear to them.

### The cost of hair-splitting

A modern commentator draws the lesson of these exchanges. One of the Israelites' recurring mistakes was to destroy the simplicity of divine religion by entangling themselves in complicated theological wrangling. They needed to learn to understand God's will in a straightforward way and obey it at once. The murder case became the occasion for teaching them that hair-splitting over the exact scope of a divine command only makes things difficult for everyone, and that piling on conditions complicates the carrying out of what began as a simple instruction.

### In short

- The third question asked whether the cow was a working animal, on the excuse that too many cows fitted the description.
- Their words "Allah willing" were, according to a hadith, the reason the matter was finally made clear to them.
- The passage teaches that religion is simple until people complicate it with needless questions.

71.text:
Verse 71 gives the final specification and the reluctant obedience that followed. Mūsā (Moses) relayed Allah's words: "It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish". They said, "Now you have come with the truth". And the verse closes with a telling remark: "Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly".

### Phrase by phrase

**"It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields"**. The Arabic describes a cow that is not dhalūl, not broken in or subdued for labour, neither for turning the earth in ploughing nor for drawing water to irrigate the tilled land. It was not a farm animal at all but an honoured and handsome creature, unyoked and unfettered. Grammatically, the clause about ploughing describes the word dhalūl and forms part of the negation.

**"wholesome"** translates musallamah. ʿAbd ar-Razzāq related from Maʿmar that Qatādah explained it as a cow free of any defect, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ and Mujāhid said the same. ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī specified that its legs and body were free of physical faults. One commentary adds that it bore none of the marks of toil.

**"and without blemish"**, lā shiyata fīhā, means that it carried no patch of any colour other than its own yellow, no spots or flecks of white.

**"They said, 'Now you have come with the truth'"** means now you have explained it clearly, now we know the cow's proper description. The words carry an unintended confession, since Mūsā had been bringing them the truth from the first word.

**"Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly"**. The Arabic says they slaughtered it "and they nearly did not do it". They searched for the cow and found it, according to one account, in the possession of a boy who was exceptionally dutiful to his mother, and they bought it for its weight in gold, or, in the other report, for its hide filled with gold. ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Wahb ibn Munabbih, Mujāhid and ʿUbaydah all said that the Jews bought it for a very large sum, though there is a difference of opinion about the details. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās explaining the final clause simply: they did not want to slaughter it. Even after all the questions and answers they were still reluctant, and the Qur'an criticises them for it, because their whole aim had been obstinacy. Some commentators attribute the hesitation to the enormous price, others to the arguing and stubbornness that had marked the affair from the start. A hadith sums the passage up: any cow they sacrificed would have been enough for them, but they were hard on themselves, and so Allah was hard on them.

### The cow that was never yoked

The devotional reading completes its account of the three attributes. Just as this cow was never broken in for work nor worn down in the pursuit of profit, and bore no colour inconsistent with the grandeur of its own, so the people of divine friendship (walāyah) exert themselves for no one and nothing other than God. They do not try to obtain things through secondary causes, do not rest their hearts on outward appearances and images, and do not trust their own choices and schemes. Desire cannot claim them as its prey, nor can the present world catch them in its claws. Carnal appetite does not rule them and no human authority controls them. They make no effort to grasp what they want and are not anxious to reach what they wish for. No mark of others is on them and no trace of reliance on causes, for they are upheld by God and annihilated from everything else, effaced, turned this way and that by God alone. God has conquered their hearts. Just as the one they worship (maʿbūd) is God, so their only aim (maqṣūd) is God. As their aim is God, so what they witness (mashhūd) is God and what they find (mawjūd) is God. Rather, they are effaced in God and God alone remains after them. Their spokesman put it in verse: if you want both of us to be pleased and want to hold our shared life's reins, then see the world with my eyes, hear with my ears and speak with my tongue.
