As for "they nearly did not do it", the Israelites looked for a way out for themselves, and only when their devices failed did they submit to the decree and find relief from the burden of the demands. Had they done what they were told at the outset, their misery would not have been doubled.

### In short

- The last specification: a cow never put to ploughing or watering, free of every defect and of any patch of a second colour.
- "Now you have come with the truth" was an admission that Mūsā had been truthful all along.
- They found the cow, paid a fortune for it, and still barely brought themselves to slaughter it, out of obstinacy and, some say, because of the price.
- The hadith's verdict: any cow would have sufficed, but they made it hard on themselves and Allah made it hard on them.
- Inwardly, the unyoked, unblemished cow pictures God's friends, who labour for nothing but Him.

72.text:
Verse 72 goes back to the beginning of the story of the cow. "This is when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed", it says. The sacrifice described in the previous verses was the means Allah chose to answer the question this verse poses: who committed the murder?

### Phrase by phrase

**"when a man was killed"**. Allah reminds the Israelites of the time when they killed one of their own. The murder is attributed to the whole people because it happened among them and they then hid it, and one early commentary gives the victim's name as ʿĀmīl. Grammatically, this clause is where the story actually begins, "and when you killed a soul", and the previous verses about the cow are an inserted scene that comes first in the telling. The verb for "you disputed" is iddāraʾtum, whose form shows a letter assimilated into the one next to it.

**"and you disputed who the killer was"**. Al-Bukhārī explained the word as "disputed", and this is also the explanation of Mujāhid, while ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said they quarrelled over the matter. Ibn Jurayj and ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam described the quarrel: some of them said, "you killed him", and the others said, "no, you killed him". Each party rejected the accusation and threw it at someone else, until they came to blows. The murderer had his own supporters who wanted to bury his crime, and so they went about accusing different people.

**"but Allah revealed what you concealed"**. Mujāhid explained the last word as "what you were hiding". Allah willed that the criminal be brought to account and so exposed what they had hidden about the killing of an innocent man, by the miraculous means the next verse describes. One commentary treats this clause as a parenthesis that gives the outcome in advance, before the story continues.

### Why the order is reversed

The murder and the mutual accusations came first in time, and the questions about the cow came afterwards, yet the Qur'an narrates the cow first and the murder second. Scholars find a purpose in the inversion. This long section of the sūrah is concerned with the transgressions of the Israelites, and the stories are told to bring those out rather than for their own sake. The present story exposes two misdeeds: committing a murder and then trying to conceal it, and raising uncalled-for objections to divine commands. Had the chronological order been kept, readers would have assumed that only the first was really intended and that the second was mentioned merely to round off the story. The arrangement as it stands makes clear that both misdeeds are being stressed equally.

### The secret that will not stay hidden

The devotional reading draws out the moral of "Allah revealed what you concealed". A disloyal person lives in fear, and out of fear that his secret will come to light he leans on concealment, deception, denial and evasion. But his fault (ʿawāruhu) is bound to be discovered, his secrets (asrāruhu) exposed and his coverings (astāruhu) pulled away, because of the shame of what he did. That is the force of Allah's words: He disclosed what they were hiding.

### In short

- A man was murdered among the Israelites, and the people fell to accusing one another while the killer's supporters tried to hide his guilt.
- Allah brought the hidden crime to light, and the sacrifice of the cow was the means.
- The story is told out of order so that both faults, concealing a murder and quibbling over a command, receive equal weight.
- No concealment can keep a guilty secret from Allah.

73.text:
Verse 73 completes the story and states its lesson. "So We instructed, 'Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow.' This is how easily Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand", it says. The cow, the murder and the questions all turn out to have been building toward a demonstration of resurrection.

### Phrase by phrase

**"So We instructed, 'Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow'"**. Allah commanded them to strike the murdered man with part of the cow they had been told to sacrifice, and told them that He would then bring him to life to say who had killed him. Any part of the cow would have produced the miracle, and the Qur'an does not say which part they used. Scholars observe that this detail would benefit us neither in religion nor in worldly life, or Allah would have made it clear, so since He left it unspecified we should leave it so. Some reports nonetheless name the part: an organ of the cow, and specifically its tongue or its tail. When the corpse was struck, the man returned to life, said who had murdered him, and died a second time. One account has him point out two of his cousins before dying, after which the two killers were denied the inheritance and were later put to death.

**"This is how easily Allah brings the dead to life"**. They struck him and he lived. The verse points to Allah's power to raise the dead, and Allah made the event a proof against the Jews that the Resurrection will take place, while at the same time ending their dispute and their stubbornness over the dead man. Just as He brought this man back to life, so He will bring the dead back to life on the Day of Judgement. The life to come is every bit as real as the life we know, and as this corpse was revived, so every soul will be raised and given new life in the Hereafter.

**"showing you His signs so that you may understand"**. His signs are the proofs of His power, here the raising of the dead. The purpose is that people should reflect and realise that the One who can revive a single soul can revive a multitude of souls, and so believe in resurrection after death and have true faith in Him. A precedent of this kind should move people to use their reason and see that what happened once in the past can as easily happen in the future.

### Five resurrections in one sūrah

Scholars note that Allah mentions His raising of the dead in five places in Sūrat al-Baqarah. The first was the raising of the Israelites after the thunderbolt, "then We brought you back to life after your death". The second is this story of the cow. The third is the story of the people who fled death in their land though they numbered thousands. The fourth is the story of the prophet who passed by a ruined town. The fifth is the story of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and the four birds, together with the earth that is brought back to life after it was dead. Every one of these alerts us to the fact that bodies will be made whole again after they have decayed. The same proof of the Resurrection is given in Sūrat Yā Sīn, where the dead earth that Allah brings to life, with its grain, its gardens of palms and vines and its gushing springs, is called a sign for them (36:33-35).

### Why this way?

One may ask why Allah made the dead man's revival depend on his being touched with a piece of flesh, when He had the power to revive him without any such means. One may also ask why the man needed to be brought back to life at all, when the murderer's name could have been revealed in some other way. The answer is that Allah is omnipotent and acts under no compulsion, and that all His acts proceed from His all-embracing wisdom. He alone knows, and can know, the reasons for what He does. We are not obliged by the Sharīʿah to discover the reason behind every divine act, and it is neither necessary nor possible that we should grasp it in every case. The right course is to accept what Allah and His Prophet ﷺ have said and keep silent about the rest.

### A legal note

In this case the statement of the murdered man was accepted as evidence to convict the murderer, because Allah had informed Mūsā (Moses) through revelation that the man would speak the truth when he returned to life. In the ordinary way no one can be convicted of murder without proper evidence, according to the rules the Sharīʿah lays down.

### The life of the heart

The devotional reading finds a second resurrection in the verse. God wished to bring the dead man to life so that his own testimony would expose his killer, and He made the slaughter of one of their animals the cause of his revival. The allusion is to anyone who longs for the life of his heart: he will attain it only by sacrificing his lower self, for the heart of whoever sacrifices his lower self through spiritual struggle (mujāhadāt) comes alive with the lights of witnessing (mushāhadāt). In the same way, when God wants a person's good name to live for ever, He lets his reputation in this world fade into obscurity first.

### In short

- Struck with a piece of the sacrificed cow, the murdered man revived, named his killer and died again. Which part of the cow was used is unspecified, and is best left so.
- The event is a proof of the Resurrection, one of five such proofs in this sūrah, and its stated purpose is to make people reflect and believe.
- Allah needed no means to revive him or to expose the killer. His acts flow from His wisdom, which we are not obliged to fathom.
- The dead man's testimony counted as evidence only because revelation vouched for it. Ordinary murder cases require the Sharīʿah's standards of proof.
- The heart lives only when the lower self is sacrificed.

74.text:
Verse 74 delivers the verdict on everything the Israelites have just been reminded of. After the covenant, the mountain, the Sabbath and the dead man raised to life, "your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder", the verse says, and then it turns the comparison against them: "for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah". It closes with a warning: "And Allah is never unaware of what you do".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Even then"** means after all that: after the murdered man was brought back to life and named his killer, and after the other signs that came before it. The Children of Israel witnessed tremendous signs, including the raising of the dead, and yet this is what followed. Al-ʿAwfī reported Ibn ʿAbbās describing the scene. When the dead man was struck with a piece of the cow, he stood up more alive than he had ever been. Asked who had killed him, he said that his nephews had, and then he died again. His nephews, once Allah had taken his life a second time, swore by Allah that they had not killed him, denying the truth while they knew it. Of that denial Allah said that their hearts became like stones, or harder.

**"your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder"**. Their hearts stiffened against accepting the truth and became like stones that never soften, dry and barren. A string of punishments and rescues should have taught the Israelites humility and obedience. Instead their hearts grew harder against divine guidance, and that insensibility led them into further misdeeds. With the passing of time their hearts became unlikely to accept any admonition, even after the miracles they had seen, and harder than stones, with no hope of softening. One commentary observes that they were harder than rock because rock changes and is transformed, as the rest of the verse describes, whereas they never changed. Because of this, Allah forbade the believers to imitate the Jews, asking whether the time had not come for believers' hearts to be humbled at the remembrance of Allah and the truth He revealed, and not to be like those given the Scripture before, who were left so long that their hearts grew hard (57:16). The people who had received the Torah and the Gospel are the warning example.

**"for some rocks gush rivers"**. Springs and rivers sometimes burst out of stone. One early commentary adds that Allah is not heedless of what they hide of their transgressions.

**"others split, spilling water"**. Some stones crack open and water comes from them even when there is no spring or river nearby. The verb yashshaqqaq has one letter assimilated into the next. The signs (āyāt) they had seen included the raising of the dead, and still the hearts did not yield.

**"while others are humbled in awe of Allah"**. Some stones come tumbling down from the mountain heights out of fear of Allah, while the hearts of these people are unmoved, unstirred and unhumbled. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq related Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation of the three kinds of stone along these same lines.

**"And Allah is never unaware of what you do"**. He will not leave your transgressions unpunished. He gives you respite until your appointed time comes. The verse warns the Israelites that Allah knows everything they have been doing and will hold them to account for it. A variant reading has "what they do", shifting the address to the third person.

### Do stones really fear Allah?

Some have claimed that the humbling of the stones is a metaphor. Ar-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī and other leading scholars said there is no need for such an explanation, because Allah creates this quality of humility in stones. The Qur'an speaks in this way often. Allah offered the trust (al-amānah) to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they declined to bear it out of fear (33:72). The seven heavens, the earth and all within them glorify Him, though we cannot comprehend their glorification (17:44). The stars and the trees bow down (55:6). The shadows of everything He has created incline to the right and the left in humble submission to Him (16:48). When He said to the heaven and the earth, "Submit, willingly or unwillingly", they both answered that they submit willingly (41:11). Had this Qur'an been sent down on a mountain, it would have been seen humbled and torn apart in awe of Allah (59:21). On the Day of Judgement the skins of the wicked will speak against them, because Allah makes all things speak (41:21). The Sunnah says the same. The Ṣaḥīḥ records the Prophet ﷺ saying of Mount Uḥud that it is a mountain that loves us and that we love. The yearning of the palm stump for the Prophet ﷺ, when he left it for the pulpit, is confirmed in authentic narrations. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records the Prophet ﷺ saying that he knows a stone in Makkah that used to greet him with salām before he was sent, and that he still recognises it. And he said of the Black Stone that on the Day of Resurrection it will testify for those who kissed it. There are several other texts to the same effect.

Scholars approach the same point from reason. The first two states of stone, giving much water and giving a little, are matters of everyday observation. The third, falling in fear of Allah, may raise a doubt, since the capacity to feel fear seems to require reason and sensibility, and stones are supposed to have neither. But reason is not a necessary condition of fear, for animals feel fear without possessing reason. Sensibility is required, yet no rational argument rules out sensibility in minerals. Sensibility depends on life, and minerals may well possess a subtle kind of life of which man is unaware. Scientists have in recent times found signs of life and sensibility in minerals too. In any case an explicit statement of the Qur'an carries an authority that no physical science or rational argument can overturn. Nor does the verse claim that the fear of Allah is the only reason a stone ever falls. It says this is so of some stones, so other falls may have purely physical causes while this is one cause among them.

### The force of "or even harder"

The scholars of Arabic agree that "or" here does not express doubt, but they differ on what it does express. Some say it means "and", so that the hearts are as hard as stone and harder, as when the Qur'an says not to obey "a sinner or a disbeliever" (76:24), or speaks of "ending excuses or giving warnings" (77:6). Others say it means "rather", so that the hearts are as hard as stone, or rather harder, as when a group feared people "as Allah should be feared, or even more" (4:77), or when Yūnus was sent to "a hundred thousand or more" (37:147), or when the distance was "two arms-lengths or even less" (53:9). A third group says that the hearts are of two kinds, some as hard as stone and some harder than stone, and Ibn Jarīr, while allowing the other readings, preferred this one: some of their hearts were like stone and some were harder. In support, this is like the two parables earlier in the sūrah, where the hypocrites are first compared to a man who lit a fire (2:17) and then "or like a rainstorm from the sky" (2:19), and like the parable in Sūrat an-Nūr, where the deeds of the disbelievers are compared to a mirage (24:39) and then "or like the darkness in a deep sea" (24:40). In each case the meaning is that some of them resemble the first example and others the second. Allah knows best.

### The order of the three stones

The three kinds of stone are placed in a deliberate order. In the highest degree stand the stones whose responsiveness is so strong that rivers gush from them, giving sustenance to beasts and men. Against these the hearts of the Jews are so hard that they cannot feel sympathy for fellow human beings even in suffering and pain, and so cannot wish them well. In the second degree come the stones that serve Allah's creatures, but less abundantly. Their hearts are harder even than these. In the lowest degree are the stones that benefit no one but can at least feel the fear of Allah. The Jews are said to lack even this minimum of sensitivity.

A modern commentator reads the same three stones as portraits of people. Streams run down the rocks of a mountainside and gather into rivers. That is the person in whose heart the fear of God sits like water in the bosom of a mountain, and flows from his eyes as tears. Some rocks look like dry boulders, but when they crack they reveal pools of water beneath, wells from which people drink. That is the person who seems far from his Lord until a calamity shakes his soul and he hurries back to God with his eyes streaming. And sometimes great slabs of rock come crashing down a mountainside. That is the person who has treated another unjustly, and who will not yield to any human being, but who submits at once, in all humility, the moment he is reminded of God's command, because his quarrel has become God's affair. Everything in nature carries a message, for God made the world as a source of admonition and remembrance to show man how to bring his life into line with the divine will. Throughout the universe that message is spoken in the language of silent examples. In the Qur'an it is set down in words. The same writer traces the hardening to its root. People who hunt for loopholes in God's commands grow steadily more insensitive. God is the name of the supreme Being, and a living faith in Him shakes the soul so deeply that talk gives way to stunned silence. When the heart hardens, however, people start to manipulate the divine scriptures as they are used to manipulating human writings, and this brazenness increases their insensitivity in turn, until their hearts are no longer moved before the might of their Lord and their souls no longer stir at the thought of God. They become as rigid as the most impervious rock.

### Two kinds of hardness

The devotional reading distinguishes the hardness of the ignorant from a very different hardness found in the recognisers of God. In the ignorant, hardness of heart means unkindness, a lack of mercy, and remoteness from the Real's path. In the recognisers, the purified and the limpid, hardness is strength of heart, stability, perfection of knowledge and clarity. Abū Bakr used to point to it in himself. When he saw someone weeping and writhing at the recitation of the Qur'an he would say that he had been like that too, until hearts became hard. This hardness is an allusion to the perfected state of the recognisers and the majesty of the rank of the sincerely truthful. At the beginning of the work, when desire is new, beginners shout, wail, cry and weep, because passion has not yet fully established its rule. When the work reaches perfection, the clarity of recognition grows strong and passion rules completely. Then the shouting and wailing are set aside and joy and revelry take their place. The tongue of their state says: when my passion for that beauty was new, my neighbours could not sleep at night for my weeping, and now I weep less because my passion has grown, for when the fire takes hold there is little smoke. The same reading notes that Allah ranked hard stones above cruel hearts. Water flows from stone, stone grows soft, and stone falls into the desert in fear of God, but the cruel heart of an estranged man neither groans in fear of God nor weeps in remorse, and neither mercy nor tenderness finds a way in. A story is told of one of God's prophets who, crossing a desert, saw a small stone from which flowed a quantity of water far beyond the stone's own measure, and the account breaks off there.

### In short

- After the raising of the dead man, and the nephews' denial of what they had seen, the Israelites' hearts hardened past the hardness of rock, the example the believers are warned against (57:16).
- Rocks give rivers, or crack and yield water, or fall in awe of Allah. Their hearts did none of these.
- The fear of stones is real, not a metaphor, as ar-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī held and as the Qur'an and hadith repeatedly show, from the trust refused by the mountains (33:72) to Uḥud's love and the greeting stone of Makkah.
- "Or even harder" has been read as "and harder", as "rather, harder", or as describing two kinds of hearts, which Ibn Jarīr preferred, on the pattern of 2:17 and 2:19, and 24:39 and 24:40.
- The three stones also picture three kinds of believer, while the hardness of the realised knower, as Abū Bakr described it, is strength rather than cruelty.

75.text:
Verse 75 turns from the Israelites of the past to the Jews living beside the Muslims in Madinah, and it speaks to the believers who were hoping to win them over. "Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you," it asks, "though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it". The long chain of stories was leading here: a people who tampered with revelation after hearing it is unlikely to accept a new one.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you ˹believers still˺ expect them to be true to you"**. The question is put to the believers, and in Arabic its opening particle expresses rejection rather than enquiry: do not be so eager, for they disbelieved long ago. The Muslims used to take great pains to bring the Jews into Islam. Having told so many stories of their waywardness, the Qur'an now tells the Muslims that no good sense can be expected from such people and that they need not trouble themselves over them. Now that their nature and stubbornness are known, the believers should not expect them to be truthful or to respond. Those meant are the deviant party of Jews whose fathers witnessed the clear signs and whose hearts hardened afterwards. One early gloss reads the question as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself: do you hope, Muḥammad, that the Jews will believe in you?

**"though a group of them would hear the word of Allah"**. Two identifications are offered. Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil said the verse was revealed about the seventy men whom Mūsā (Moses) chose to go with him to the meeting with Allah. They heard Allah's speech, commanding and forbidding Mūsā, and went back to their people. The honest ones among them reported exactly what they had heard, but a group of them claimed that they had heard Allah say at the end of His speech: if you can do these things, do them, and if you wish, leave them, and there is no harm on you. On this reading the "word of Allah" is what the seventy heard directly at Mount Ṭūr (Sinai). They had gone there seeking Allah's own confirmation of Mūsā's message, and the corruption is their announcement to their people that Allah had promised to forgive them if they failed to keep certain commandments. Most exegetes, however, hold that the verse was revealed about those who altered the verse of stoning for married adulterers and the description of Muḥammad ﷺ. On this reading the "word of Allah" is the Torah, which the Jews had "heard" from the prophets, and the group is a party of their rabbis and scholars, who heard it recited and knew what it said.

**"then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it"**. They changed its words and its meanings after they had grasped what it really meant, fully aware of the seriousness of the crime. The distortion touched the wording, the sense, or both. They understood well and still defied the truth, knowing their interpretations were false. Qatādah explained that these are Jews who heard Allah's words and altered them once they had understood and taken them in. Mujāhid said that those who altered it and hid its truths were their scholars. Ibn Wahb reported Ibn Zayd's description of how it worked. They altered the Torah that Allah had revealed to them so that it declared the lawful unlawful and the forbidden permitted, and the right false and the false right. When a man seeking justice came to them with a bribe they judged his case by the Book of Allah. When a man seeking to do wrong came with a bribe they brought out the other, distorted book, which declared him in the right. And when someone came who neither sought what was right nor offered a bribe, they commanded him to righteousness (al-birr). That is why Allah said to them: do you command righteousness and forget yourselves while you read the Scripture (2:44)? The verse resembles Allah's statement elsewhere that because they broke their covenant He cursed them and hardened their hearts, so that they distorted the words of the Scripture and neglected part of what they had been commanded (5:13).

### Why this mattered so much in Madinah

One reason the people of Madinah recognised the Prophet ﷺ so promptly was that their Jewish neighbours had often spoken to them of a final prophet who was to come, so they were expecting his arrival. In that sense the Jews were responsible for the Muslims' first fervour for Islam. It was natural, then, for the Muslims to hope that the Jews would accept his prophethood without hesitation, and they invited them to join in believing with high hopes and lofty feelings. The shock came when the Jews refused. Worse, the Prophet's opponents turned the refusal into an argument: how can you be so sure that Muḥammad is a prophet? If he truly were, the Jews, who know the scriptures far better than you, would have been the first to believe in him. But accepting a truth does not depend on knowledge alone. One must also be sincere. The Jews had already altered their own scriptures while knowing them to be the word of God. Wherever the scripture failed to match their wishes they hunted for a loophole, changing God's word at will and placing religion beneath their worldly interests. However true a thing may be, a person bent on denial and deliberate distortion will always find some justification for rejecting it, and that attitude ends in open misrepresentation of God's word. A person so irreverent toward the divine books can never feel the gravity of anything concerning God. He hears God's word and finds words to show that the command does not apply to him. He believes in God, yet his insensitivity leads him into flagrant rebellion that no one who really believed God was watching him and hearing him would ever dare.

### A people ruled by their desires

Men so enslaved to their desires and so shameless in pursuing evil cannot be expected to listen to anyone. The Jews who were the Prophet's contemporaries may not themselves have taken part in some of these crimes, but since they did not abhor what their forefathers had done, they are counted as their counterparts. The devotional reading makes the same point more sharply. Allah informs the believers of the standing of these people's faith and relates that after hearing God's address they set about altering it and tampering with it. So why should they believe you, when they have already heard by means of the message itself? How can people who did not remain in faith (īmān) after direct eyewitnessing (ʿiyān) come to believe through demonstrative proof (burhān)? What does not hold true toward the Real will not hold true toward you. How can those who felt no shame before the Real feel shame before you?

### In short

- The believers are told not to expect faith from a people whose forefathers heard Allah's word and knowingly corrupted it.
- The corrupters were either the seventy at Ṭūr, who invented a licence to ignore the commandments, or, as most say, the rabbis who altered the stoning verse and the Prophet's description.
- Ibn Zayd described a two-book system: Allah's Book for the honest, a forged book for the bribe-payer, and the words of 2:44 for everyone else.
- Those who did not keep faith after seeing with their own eyes will hardly be won by argument.

76.text:
Verse 76 exposes the double game played by some of the Jews of Madinah. "When they meet the believers they say, “We believe.”" In private, though, their leaders scold them: "Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?"

### Phrase by phrase

**"When they meet the believers they say, 'We believe'"**. The speakers are the hypocrites among the Jews, or, as some say, the lowly common folk among the People of the Book. Meeting Abū Bakr and his companions, they would say: we believe in your Prophet, and his description and his traits are mentioned in our Book. As Muslim power grew in Madinah and the surrounding area, some Jews pretended to have accepted Islam, and to prove their sincerity and win favour they would now and then let on that the Torah itself announced the coming of the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned the Qur'an. Another account of the occasion runs this way. They would tell the Muslims, "We believe that Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, but he was sent only to you Arabs." Among themselves they said: do not pass news of this Prophet to the Arabs, for you used to ask Allah for victory over them through him when he should come, and now he has been sent to them and not to you. Then Allah revealed this verse.

**"But in private they say ˹to each other˺"**. When these lowly people went back to their leaders, who had taken no part in the pretence, the leaders rebuked them. When they met other Jews who openly professed Judaism, they would confess that the whole thing was a ruse to deceive the Muslims and that their loyalty to their own faith was intact. They blamed one another for the admissions they had made.

**"Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you"**. That is, what He has made known to you in your Book of Muḥammad's description. Do you really talk to Muḥammad and his Companions about that?

**"so that they may use it against you before your Lord?"**. In the Hereafter the Muslims would hold the proof against them for not following him despite knowing he was sincere. The Arabic particle introducing the clause marks consequence, what the disclosure would lead to. The sense is: if you concede to them that he is a Prophet, when you know Allah bound you by covenant to follow him, they will realise that Muḥammad is the Prophet we were waiting for, whose coming we find foretold in our Book. So do not believe in him, deny him. The other group reprimanded the hypocrites because knowledge of the relevant verses of the Torah could help the Muslims defeat the Jews in debate, and the Muslims might use these admissions as proof that the Jews recognised the truth of his prophethood.

**"Do you not understand?"**. Have you no common sense? Do you not grasp that they will argue against you if you speak to them this way? So beware.

### The report of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī described the scene. When the Jews met the believers they would say, "We believe." When they met one another, some would say: do not speak to Muḥammad's companions about what Allah has foretold in your Book, so that this news does not turn into their proof against you before your Lord, and then the dispute will be yours. The verse records this instance of their inconsistency and deviousness: acknowledging that the Prophet ﷺ was genuine and his message correct, as the Torah itself testified, and then regretting the acknowledgment.

### A light that cannot be put out

The devotional reading draws the moral. They egged one another on to deny the Real and to keep the Muslims in the dark, unaware that God was telling His Messenger their secrets, and that no one's efforts can put out a light the Real has chosen to make manifest, for only He could do that. When the tongue agrees but the mind objects, the distance only grows.

### In short

- Some Jews professed belief to Abū Bakr and the Muslims, even volunteering that the Torah foretold the Prophet ﷺ.
- Their leaders rebuked them in private: such admissions would be used against them before their Lord.
- Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī reported the whispered instruction to keep the Torah's testimony from the Companions.
- Hiding what God has made manifest is futile, and a tongue that contradicts the mind only deepens separation.

77.text:
Verse 77 answers the whispering of the previous verse with a single question: "Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal". Whatever the Jewish leaders hid from the Muslims, nothing was hidden from Allah, who was informing His Messenger ﷺ of it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do they not know"**. The question is affirmative in force: surely they know. It is addressed to these leaders who told their followers to keep silent, and it reminds the Jews that Allah is all-knowing. He knows what they try to keep hidden as well as what they say or do openly.

**"that Allah is aware of what they conceal"**. What they kept hidden among themselves. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī explained that what they concealed was what passed between them when they were alone, away from the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ, forbidding one another to pass on to the Companions what Allah had revealed to them in their Book, for fear that the Companions would use it against them before their Lord. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said it means their secret denial and rejection of Muḥammad ﷺ, even though they find his coming recorded in their Book. Qatādah explained it the same way.

**"and what they reveal"**. What they proclaimed to Muḥammad ﷺ and his Companions, namely their words "We believe", as Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ and Qatādah said. Allah knows what they hide and what they show in this matter and in every other, so that they should desist. They behave in this pathetic way as though unaware that Allah knows what they conceal in word and deed and what they reveal, but He will bring it out and expose them.

### Why the concealment was pointless

It made no difference whether the hypocrites hid their unbelief from the Muslims or the other group withheld the verses of the Torah that spoke of the Prophet ﷺ, because Allah Himself, on various occasions, informed the Muslims in the Qur'an of the hypocrisy of certain Jews and of the Torah's testimony. This verse deals with the learned among the Jews. The verse that follows turns to the unlettered masses, and the one after that returns to the scholars who misled them.

### The Lord who knows the secret cores

The devotional reading hears in this question the speech of the Lord who is worshipped by those who voice His oneness (tawḥīd), who answers those who call on Him, who knows the states of His servants, who is aware of the apparent and the hidden, and who calls back those who have turned away. Some He calls with explicit words, presenting Himself as the Nurturer: "Turn to your Lord" (39:54). Others He calls with exalted allusions, turning the face of the heart from everything else to Himself, and presenting His lordship and kingship: do they not know that God is aware of their secret and their open speech? For the recognisers that allusion is enough. When the Lord of the Worlds declares His knowledge of the secret cores and His awareness of hidden things, they sweep the dust of others out of their innermost selves and allow no scatteredness into their hearts. When He declares His knowledge of the apparent, they bring truthfulness into their outward dealings with God's creatures. This is why the people of allusion have said that "what they keep secret" is a command to watchfulness between servant and Lord, and "what they announce" is a command to truthfulness in dealings and in settling accounts with creatures. In one of God's books it is written: if you are unaware that I see you, your faith is defective, and if you are aware that I see you, why have you made Me the least of those who look upon you?

Equivalent to this verse is the Exalted Lord's statement that He knows the sly glances of the eyes and what the hearts conceal (40:19). The treacheries of the eyes are many, because travellers on the path are many. The treachery of the worshippers' eyes is that in the dark of night, when the time for whispered prayer comes, they drop off to sleep and lose the intimacy of being alone with Him. Dāwūd (David) received the revelation: whoever claims to love Me is a liar if night falls and he goes to sleep on Me, for does not every lover love to be alone with his beloved? God praised Ibrāhīm (Abraham) for this quality when He said, "When the night grew dark upon him" (6:76).

### In short

- The leaders who silenced their followers surely knew that Allah sees both the secret denial and the public profession of belief.
- Al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ identify the concealed thing as the suppressed testimony of the Torah, and the revealed thing as the words "We believe".
- Allah had already told the Muslims in the Qur'an what the Jews were hiding, so concealment achieved nothing.
- For the seeker, "what they keep secret" calls for watchfulness before the Lord, and "what they announce" calls for honesty with people, down to the eyes that stay awake in the night (40:19).

78.text:
Verse 78 moves from the learned to the masses. "And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies, and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate". Having no direct knowledge of the Torah, the common people lived on hearsay and comfortable fables fed to them by their leaders.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And among them are the illiterate"**. Among the People of the Book, as Mujāhid said. Ummiyyūn is the plural of ummī, someone who cannot write, as Qatādah, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ and others explained. They could neither read the Torah nor write it. The rest of the phrase confirms the meaning: they do not know the Book, they are unaware of what is in it. Ummī was also one of the descriptions of the Prophet ﷺ, because he was unlettered: he could not read any writing before this revelation, nor write at all (29:48). He said, we are an ummī nation, we neither write nor calculate, and the month is like this, this and this, meaning thirty days or twenty-nine. This hadith shows that the timing of Muslim worship does not depend on books or calculations. And Allah describes Himself as the One who raised among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves (62:2).

**"who know nothing about the Scripture"**. These people had no knowledge of the Torah and were weak in understanding besides. Their scholars did not give them correct information about their religion, so their minds were stuffed with baseless superstitions that they found pleasant and flattering. They did not know what the Torah contained or what it said.

**"except lies"**. The word is amānī. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation that it means nothing more than false statements uttered with their tongues. Others said amānī means wishes and hopes. Mujāhid said that Allah described the ummiyyūn as not understanding any of the Book He sent down to Mūsā (Moses) and yet inventing lies and falsehood. So amānī here means lying and falsehood: the lies handed down to them by their leaders, which they relied upon and took to be the Torah that Allah revealed. All they had was the unfounded things they heard.

**"and ˹so˺ they ˹wishfully˺ speculate"**. Mujāhid said: they lie. Qatādah, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ said: they hold evil, false ideas about Allah. Everything they say is surmise, built on what their leaders told them. In rejecting the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ and in their fabrications about other matters they have mere conjecture and no firm knowledge.

### Tales of cheap salvation

According to Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Farrāʾ and Mujāhid, among the most reliable of the early commentators, amānī refers to the mythical tales invented by the Jewish scholars. The stories existed, above all, to prove that Paradise belonged to the Jews alone. Sayings in support of the "chosen people" theory were attributed to venerated saints of the past, and the religion was credited with magical properties, so that salvation was guaranteed by nothing more than going through the routine rites of Judaism. Recipes for cheap salvation of this kind are very attractive to the masses, because they confirm the wishful notion that there is no need for self-discipline or a responsible life, that charms and magical remedies will cure one's spiritual ills and get one into heaven. The scholars who taught these tales became highly regarded, since their theories were designed to win popular support, and the business of easing people's way to eternal salvation became a lucrative source of income. People flocked to them bearing offerings. The scholars pointed the way to a paradise nobody had to earn, and were paid with wealth nobody had to work for. In every age the People of the Book have shown this weakness. They wanted to live in a dream world, imagining that they had no obligations beyond the perfunctory performance of empty rituals and deluding themselves that God had granted them inalienable rights. Such people cannot accept the call of true religion, because truth tears down wishful thinking and forces them to confront life's hard realities.

### The three meanings of ẓann

The verse says that the illiterate Jews follow their ẓann, their conjecture. Some people ignore the context and conclude that it is never legitimate to accept or follow any view or ruling based on ẓann, which they always translate as "fanciful supposition". That is one of the word's lexical meanings, but only one. The Qur'an uses ẓann in three ways. It can mean perfect certainty, as of those who are certain that they will meet their Lord (2:46). It can mean the greatest likelihood, as when Yūsuf (Joseph) spoke to the prisoner he thought would be saved (12:42). And it can mean a mere fanciful supposition, as in the present verse. The ẓann the Qur'an forbids us to follow is the third kind, a fanciful opinion unsupported by any respectable argument or contrary to a valid one, and this is what the Jews are condemned for. The first two kinds, on the contrary, must be followed. When certain hadiths, or certain arguments and conclusions in the Sharīʿah, are described as resting on ẓann, the word is being used in the second sense. No sphere of life can do without this kind of ẓann, and the Sharīʿah requires us to accept and act on it. Some verses of the Qur'an do condemn those who follow their ẓann, but to stretch that condemnation to every possible case, and to use such verses to reject all the legitimate arguments and rulings of the Sharīʿah that rest on ẓann, is to betray ignorance of the Qur'an.

### The same word, two different meanings

The devotional reading notices that the word "unlettered" is used here as a censure of the estranged and a mark of their shortcoming, while in the verse about following the Messenger, the Prophet who is unlettered (7:157), it praises Muṣṭafā ﷺ and marks his perfection. This alludes to the fact that sharing a name does not mean being of the same kind. Names may agree while meanings do not. On this rule the Folk of the Sunnah built their position on affirming the Real's attributes. God has attributes and descriptions that befit divinity, and creatures are far from them. Created things have created attributes, and God is pure of those. "Exalted" (ʿazīz) is a name of God, and Yūsuf (Joseph) was also addressed as "exalted" (12:78), but God's exaltedness is worthy of Him and the creature's exaltedness is worthy of the creature. By the agreement of the Muslims and the admission of most unbelievers, God exists and the creatures exist, but the creatures exist because God gives them existence, while God exists by His own abidance, being and subsistence. The Muslims agree that God is alive, and many created things are alive, but the created thing lives through breath and timely nourishment, while God's life is His own life and subsistence, His firstness and His lastness, with no when, no how many and no how. Even those who oppose the Folk of the Sunnah say that God is a maker and the creature a maker, but the creature makes through artifice, instrument, striving and measure, and God makes by power and wisdom, whatever, however and whenever He wills. The Qur'an contains many such cases. The sum of it is that God knows how He is, and is exactly as He has said, while His howness lies beyond the servant's knowledge. What God said about Himself should be seized with the eyeteeth and assented to from the depths of the spirit. To fancy that sharing a meaning means being of the same kind is to take the road of the roadless, and it is sheer rebellion. To hope to grasp God through imagination and searching is absurd, and whatever is gained that way is faulty. Safety in religion lies in accepting the message, approving of the one who conveyed it, bowing the head and setting seeking aside. Whoever believes this walks the right path, and his end will be as the Exalted Lord describes, where the passage breaks off.

### In short

- The ummiyyūn are those who cannot read or write, as Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah, ar-Rabīʿ and Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī explained, and the word was also a title of the unlettered Prophet ﷺ (29:48, 62:2).
- Knowing nothing of the Torah, they lived on amānī: lies, wishful tales and the fables their scholars sold them as recipes for cheap salvation.
- Ẓann has three senses in the Qur'an, certainty (2:46), strong likelihood (12:42) and mere fancy, and only the third is condemned, so rulings of the Sharīʿah based on probable evidence stand.
- The same word can censure a people and praise the Prophet ﷺ (7:157): shared names do not mean shared meanings, which is the key to affirming Allah's attributes.

79.text:
Verse 79 pronounces a threefold woe on the men who manufactured those tales. "So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, “This is from Allah”", seeking a fleeting gain. "So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned".

### Phrase by phrase

**"So woe"**. Waylun, a familiar Arabic word, means destruction and perishing. It means a severe punishment, and some say it is the name of a valley in Hell. The verse describes a further category of Jews, those who called people to misguidance with lies about Allah and thrived on unjustly amassing their property. Since the dishonesty of the scholars was the real cause of the superstitions of the masses described in the previous verse, their crime was the greater, and so the verse turns on them.

**"those who distort the Scripture with their own hands"**. That is, making it up themselves. These are the Jews who altered the description of the Prophet ﷺ in the Torah, together with the verse of stoning and other details, and rewrote them differently from the way they had been revealed. Al-Kalbī related that they changed the description of Allah's Messenger ﷺ in their Scripture. They made him white and tall, whereas the Prophet ﷺ was of a brown complexion and medium height, and then said to their followers and companions: the description of the prophet to be sent at the end of time is before you, look at it, this man does not fit it. The rabbis and doctors of the law used to draw worldly benefits from the Jewish people and feared losing them if they ever showed the real description, and that is why they changed it. Greedy and self-seeking, eager to please people for the money and respect they received from them, they misrepresented divine injunctions, going as far as to change the words of the Torah or distort its sense, all the while pretending that this was exactly what Allah had said or meant.

**"then say, 'This is from Allah'"**. They claimed that it stood in the Book that had come down from Him.

**"seeking a fleeting gain"**. A small price of this world, whether money or leadership, means of subsistence and surplus property. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said that the "little amount" means this life and everything in it. They exchanged truth and guidance for it.

**"So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they have earned"**. Woe to them for the lies, falsehood and alterations they wrote with their own hands, and woe to them for the property they unjustly acquired: bribes (rishan, the plural of rishwah) and unlawful earnings. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās explaining that the torment is theirs because of the lies they wrote with their hands, and because of what they unjustly took from people, whether commoners or others. Two sins are punished here, distorting the word of Allah and earning money by doing so, and the tamperers lost both in the present and in the end.

### Ibn ʿAbbās's warning to the Muslims

Az-Zuhrī reported that ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿAbdullāh heard Ibn ʿAbbās say: O Muslims, how can you ask the People of the Book about anything, when the Book Allah sent down to His Prophet ﷺ is the newest of His Books and you read it still fresh and young? Allah has informed you that the People of the Book changed and altered His Book and wrote a book of their own with their hands, then said "this is from Allah" in order to acquire a small profit. Has the knowledge that came to you not forbidden you from asking them? By Allah, we have never seen one of them asking you about what was revealed to you. Al-Bukhārī also records this report.

### A trade in salvation

The tampering was a business. The scholars who attributed their tales to the saints of old became highly regarded, because their teaching was designed to win popular support, and the easing of people's path to Paradise became a lucrative source of worldly income. People flocked to them and showered them with offerings, buying a paradise that did not have to be earned from men who received wealth they had not laboured for.

### Blind following and insincere companionship

The devotional reading observes that these people differed in the degrees of their disbelief. One group was the most contemptible, while the majority relied on blind following (taqlīd) out of ignorance. It was not doubt that seized them but conjecture and speculation that misled them. Their only share in their scriptures was to recite them without knowing their meanings, and some of them cared mostly for what they desired for themselves. There was no helping them, and no sure way of finding the truth amid their conjectures. Then Allah related their bad end: woe for the writing of their hands and woe for their earnings. The verse alludes to those who lack sincerity (ikhlāṣ) in companionship (ṣuḥbah) on the path of the Real. They associate outwardly with the friends of God (awliyāʾ) but have no true spiritual desire (irādah), so they keep company with the heedless and see only a part of the path (ṭarīqah). Whenever the clamour of worldly fortune calls they rush to answer, but when the demands of the Real direct them to some effort they fare badly, for they lack sincerity. How bitter their remorse will be over what they hoarded away from God! There is no prospering for them.

### In short

- Woe, a word of destruction, falls on the scholars who rewrote the Torah with their own hands, including the Prophet's description, which al-Kalbī says they changed from brown and medium height to white and tall.
- Their motive was a paltry worldly gain, bribes and status, which al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī called this whole life and all it contains.
- The woe is doubled: for the lies they wrote and for the wealth they earned by them.
- Ibn ʿAbbās asked how Muslims could consult people who had rewritten their own book, a report al-Bukhārī records, and the verse also warns those who keep company with the friends of God without sincerity.

80.text:
Verse 80 quotes the comfortable belief that lay behind all this complacency. Some of the Jews claim, "The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days." The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask whether they hold a pledge from Allah, who never breaks His word, "or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?"

### Phrase by phrase

**"˹Some of˺ the Jews claim"**. When the Prophet ﷺ warned them of the Fire, this was their reply.

**"The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days"**. That is, it will afflict us only for a short time, after which it will cease. Al-ʿAwfī reported Ibn ʿAbbās saying that the Jews claimed the Fire would touch them for forty days only. Others added that these were the forty days during which their forefathers worshipped the calf. Ibn ʿAbbās also reported that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah he found the Jews saying that this world would last seven thousand years, and that for every thousand years of its days people would be punished in Hell for one day of the days of the Hereafter, so that the torment would last only seven days. Allah revealed the verse concerning this saying. Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās tells how the story ends. The People of the Book had learned that it takes a journey of forty years to cross Hell from one end to the other, so they said they would be punished only for the period laid down in the Torah. They will go on through their torment until they reach Saqar, where the tree of Zaqqūm grows, and until the number of days they spoke of has run out. Then the people of Hell will say to them: you claimed you would be punished only for a certain number of days. Those days have passed, and eternity remains.

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ 'Have you taken a pledge from Allah'"**. For what you are saying. Allah refutes the claim through this question. If you had a promise from Allah to this effect, then Allah would never break His promise. But no such promise ever existed.

**"or are you ˹just˺ saying about Allah what you do not know?"**. Things you know are not in your Book. You have no knowledge of what you say about Allah, so you are uttering a lie against Him.

### The argument behind the claim

Scholars have explained the Jews' claim that Hell would not hold them for their sins, or would hold them only a few days, in several ways. One explanation runs as follows. All the Sharīʿahs share the principle that a believer who commits sins may be punished in Hell for a time, according to the degree and kind of his sins, but because he possesses faith (īmān) he will not be consigned to Hell forever and will be released once his term is served. The Jews reasoned that the Sharīʿah of Mūsā (Moses) had, in their view, never been abrogated, so they remained true believers and had not become unbelievers by denying the prophethood of ʿĪsā (Jesus) and of Muḥammad ﷺ. Hence, they concluded, if they were sent to Hell for some sin they would be brought out again after a few days. This false assertion rests on another false assertion. Nowhere does the Torah declare that the Sharīʿah of Mūsā was meant to last forever, so the claim of perpetuity is baseless. Jews who made that claim and denied the prophethood of ʿĪsā and of Muḥammad ﷺ must, on account of that denial, be counted as unbelievers, and no Book of Allah promises unbelievers release from Hell after a while. The verse calls such a promise the "pledge" of Allah. Since Allah never gave it, the claim collapses.

### The poisoned sheep at Khaybar

Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr ibn Mardawayh reported from Abū Hurayrah that when Khaybar was conquered, a roasted sheep laced with poison was presented to the Prophet ﷺ as a gift. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered all the Jews there to be assembled before him and asked them, "Who is your father?" They named a man. He said, "You have lied. Your father is so-and-so." They said, "You have spoken the truth." He asked, "Will you tell me the truth if I ask you about something?" They said, "Yes, Abū al-Qāsim, and if we lie you will know it, as you knew about our fathers." He asked, "Who are the people of the Fire?" They said, "We shall be in it for a short period, and then you will replace us in it." The Prophet ﷺ said, "May you be cursed and humiliated in it! By Allah, we shall never replace you in it." He asked again whether they would answer truthfully, and they said yes. "Have you poisoned this sheep?" "Yes." "What made you do it?" "We wanted to know whether you were a liar, in which case we would be rid of you, and if you were a Prophet the poison would not harm you." Imām Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī and an-Nasāʾī record similar accounts. The Jews' own words at Khaybar repeat the claim of this verse, a short stay in the Fire and then release.

### The heart filled with false claims

The devotional reading sees in the verse an allusion to those whose hearts are filled with false claims. Conjecture has got the better of them, for in their utter foolishness they count themselves among the people of the story (ahl al-qiṣṣah), the chosen ones of whom the sacred accounts speak. Such a person makes his home among the murmurings of his lower desires. His judgement of the unseen rests on what he himself has neglected. The ugliness of his own deeds he forgets, and only the errors of his false thinking stay with him. He is a servant of his lower self, and his good opinion of himself has got the better of him, while in reality the results of his neglect and self-deception possess him. Allah said that the assumption they entertained about their Lord brought about their doom, so they became losers (41:23).

### In short

- The Jews claimed a stay of only a few days in the Fire, forty for the calf, or seven for the world's seven thousand years, after which, in one report, Hell's inhabitants will tell them that the days are over and eternity remains.
- Allah's answer is a question: do you hold His pledge, which He never breaks, or do you speak of Him without knowledge?
- The claim rested on the false premise that the law of Mūsā (Moses) could never be abrogated, so that denying ʿĪsā (Jesus) and Muḥammad ﷺ left them believers who would only be punished for a term.
- At Khaybar the Jews repeated the same boast to the Prophet ﷺ over a poisoned sheep, a report in Imām Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī and an-Nasāʾī, and the verse warns every heart that lives on self-flattering assumptions about Allah (41:23).

81.text:
Verse 81 states the real law in place of the Jews' wishful one. "But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever". Allah is saying that the matter is not as they hoped and wished.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But no!"**. Here Allah answers the Jews. It is not as they imagine. The Fire will touch them, and they will abide in it.

**"Those who commit evil"**. Whoever does an evil deed and persists in his error on purpose, arriving on the Day of Resurrection with no good deeds but only evil ones, will be among the people of the Fire. One early gloss reads "evil" here as ascribing partners to Allah.

**"and are engrossed in sin"**. Literally, whose sin has surrounded him. Abū Hurayrah, Abū Wāʾil, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥasan said this means that his shirk, his associating of partners with Allah, has surrounded him, so that he dies in that state. Al-Aʿmash reported from Abū Razīn that ar-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym explained it as whoever dies before repenting of his wrongs, and as-Suddī and Abū Razīn said much the same. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said it refers to the major sins. All these explanations come to similar meanings, and Allah knows best. The transgression overcomes such a person and encircles him completely, for he has died an idolater. The word for sin is read in the singular and also, in a variant, in the plural. Those who sink to the evil of disbelief, and whom disobedience rules, are repaid by Allah with the Fire.

**"will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever"**. Those with these attributes are the dwellers of Hell, there perpetually. They will neither die nor leave it. The word for "abiding" is plural because "whoever" carries a plural sense.

### How evil can take hold completely

Having refuted the Jews' claim, the Qur'an lays down the divine law on the matter. People who commit evil knowingly and deliberately, until evil takes hold of them so completely that no trace of goodness remains, will go to Hell and stay there forever, without respite or release. How can evil possess a person so completely? This happens only with unbelievers, never with Muslims, even sinful ones. Because of his unbelief, none of an unbeliever's good deeds is acceptable to Allah, and even the good he did before his apostasy and unbelief is lost and annulled, so on the Day of Judgement he has nothing to show but evil, and for that he lives in Hell forever. A person of faith, by contrast, begins with the greatest and highest of good deeds to his credit, faith (īmān) itself, and his lesser good deeds are recorded in his account as well. He can never be wholly without goodness, so evil cannot be said to have taken hold of him completely. In short, under this law the unbeliever must remain in Hell. Since Mūsā (Moses) was not the last prophet but was followed by ʿĪsā (Jesus) and Muḥammad ﷺ, the Jews became unbelievers by denying these two, and by this law they too will be consigned to Hell forever like other unbelievers, which shows their talk of release after a few days to be baseless. The Qur'an says the same elsewhere: it is not by your wishes nor the wishes of the People of the Book, for whoever does evil will be repaid for it, while whoever does good, male or female, and believes, will enter Paradise (4:123-124).

### Small sins that gather

Here belongs the hadith that Imām Aḥmad records from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: beware of the sins you belittle, for they gather upon a person until they destroy him. He then gave them an example. Some people camped on open ground, and their servants came, one bringing a piece of wood and another bringing a piece, until they had collected a great heap. Then they lit a fire and cooked whatever they put on it.

### A heart that has stopped calling for help

The devotional reading notes that in the language of the scholars the one encompassed by his transgression is the disbeliever, but that the allusion is to a person whose heart has ceased its constant calling for help. The possessors of realities are like grain in a frying pan in their moments of sobriety (ṣaḥw). Those among them who have become still are so because of His overwhelming majesty, not out of listlessness. Whoever leans on his obedience, seeks favour through it and imagines he can draw near by means of it should keep his distance from that idea. Whoever comes to know the truth of God's oneness knows that there is no way to Him except through Him.

### In short

- Allah rejects the Jews' hope: whoever earns evil and is encompassed by his sin dwells in the Fire forever.
- The encompassing sin is shirk, or dying unrepentant, or the major sins, according to Abū Hurayrah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, as-Suddī, Mujāhid, Qatādah and others, and the meanings converge.
- Only unbelief leaves a person with no good at all, since it annuls every deed, whereas a believer always has faith to his credit, as 4:123-124 confirms.
- Ibn Masʿūd's hadith in Imām Aḥmad warns that belittled sins pile up like sticks until they make a fire.

82.text:
Verse 82 completes the pair with the law's other side. "And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever". Faith and righteous deeds together, not membership of a chosen people, are what earn eternity in the Garden.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And those who believe"**. They believe in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, in Muḥammad and the Qur'an. Faith itself is the greatest good deed a person can bring, and no one who has it is wholly without goodness.

**"and do good"**. They perform the good deeds that conform to Islamic law, acts of obedience between them and their Lord. Since the Sharīʿah of the Prophet ﷺ has abrogated the earlier Sharīʿahs, good deeds now mean deeds done in conformity with it. Entry into the Garden is the reward of those who believe in Allah and His Prophet ﷺ and act well.

**"will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever"**. Perpetually, they will never die nor come out of it. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported Ibn ʿAbbās explaining the verse this way: whoever believes in what you Jews refused to believe in, and practises what you refrained from practising of Muḥammad's religion, will gain Paradise for eternity. Allah has stated that the recompense for good works and for evil works remains with its people forever. The same promise appears elsewhere: those who do good, whether male or female, and have faith will enter Paradise and will not be wronged even the speck on a date stone (4:123-124).

### Faith, deeds and Paradise as a single tree

It has been said that "those who believe" alludes to the tree of faith and its planting in the believer's heart, that "do good" alludes to the branches of that tree and their nurturing and growth, and that "the residents of Paradise" alludes to what the tree yields and to its fruit ripening. This is the tree the Lord of the Worlds speaks of in another place, the good word likened to a good tree whose root is firm and whose branches reach the sky, yielding its fruit in every season by the will of its Lord (14:24-25). Its fruit is unlike the fruit of other trees, which bear once a year, year after year. This tree puts out fresh fruit every hour, indeed every moment, each with another colour, another taste and another fragrance. The sweetness the worshippers taste is a fruit of this tree. The feast of the seekers' hearts is a fruit of this tree. The clarity of the recognisers' present moment is another of its fruits. Today, in the house of service and on obedience's carpet, they already possess the paradise of recognition, neither turned away from them nor veiled. Tomorrow, in the house of union and on friendship's carpet, the paradise of approval will be theirs, neither cut off nor withheld, with fruit never out of season nor forbidden, and raised couches (56:33-34).

### Why the two verses belong together

Read together with the verse before it, this verse closes the argument with the Jews. Their boast of a short stay in the Fire assumed that they were still believers under the law of Mūsā (Moses). But the law of reward is the same for everyone: the person whose sin swallows him, above all shirk against Allah's oneness, remains in the Fire, and the person who believes in Allah's final Messenger ﷺ, after Mūsā and ʿĪsā (Jesus), and does good remains in Paradise. Neither outcome has an end, and neither depends on lineage.

### In short

- Faith in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ together with good deeds under the Islamic law brings eternal Paradise.
- Ibn ʿAbbās read it as a direct answer to the Jews: whoever believes what you rejected gains what you claimed.
- Like 4:123-124, it ties reward to belief and deeds, not to a people's wishes.
- Faith is a tree in the heart, deeds its branches and Paradise its fruit (14:24-25), a fruit that ripens anew every moment and lasts without end (56:33-34).

83.text:
Verse 83 reads out the terms of the covenant itself. "And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel", it begins, and then lists what they had promised: to worship none but Allah, to be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, to speak kindly to people, to establish prayer and to pay alms-tax. The verdict follows: "But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away", except for a few, "and were indifferent".

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from the children of Israel"**. Allah reminds the Children of Israel of the commandments He gave them in the Torah, of the covenants He took from them to abide by those commands, and of how they knowingly and deliberately turned away from all of it. The promise was made between Allah and the Israelites, and they accepted its terms.

**"Worship none but Allah"**. Declare Him the only true God and ascribe no partner to Him. Allah commanded them to worship Him alone and associate nothing with Him, just as He has commanded all His creatures, for this is the purpose for which He created them. He never sent a messenger without revealing to him that there is no god but He, so worship Him (21:25), and He sent a messenger to every community saying, worship Allah and shun false gods (16:36). This is the highest and most important of all rights, Allah's right to be worshipped alone without partners. The Arabic is phrased as a statement, "you shall not worship any but Allah (lā taʿbudūna illā Llāha)", a form that carries the force of a prohibition. A variant reading has the third person, "they shall not worship", and another has the plain command, "worship not".

**"be kind to parents"**. After Allah's own right comes the right of His creatures, and first among them the right of the parents. Allah habitually mentions the parents' rights alongside His own. He says, be grateful to Me and to your parents (31:14), and He has decreed that you worship none but Him and honour your parents (17:23), continuing on to the command to give close relatives their due (17:26). Ibn Masʿūd asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ which deed is best, and he answered, prayer performed on time. Ibn Masʿūd asked what came next, and he said, kindness to one's parents. He asked again, and the answer was jihād in the cause of Allah. The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record this.

**"relatives"**. Keep contact with your kin. Kinship is joined to the parents here because the duty flows outward from them.

**"orphans"**. The young who have no fathers to fend for them. Be kind to them.

**"and the needy"**. Al-masākīn is the plural of miskīn, one who cannot find what he needs to spend on himself and his family. Be generous to them. These categories are treated more fully in Sūrat an-Nisāʾ, where this Ummah is given the same commands: worship Allah and associate none with Him, and be kind to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor and the rest (4:36).

**"speak kindly to people"**. Say good words to people and deal leniently with them. Commanding good and forbidding evil falls under this, and so does being truthful about the status of Muḥammad ﷺ, for one early gloss reads it as "speak the truth concerning Muḥammad". Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī explained that the good word means commanding good and forbidding evil, together with patience and forgiveness, and that the good speech Allah commands embraces every kind of behaviour that pleases Him. Imām Aḥmad narrated from Abū Dharr that the Prophet ﷺ taught: never belittle any act of righteousness, and if you find no good deed to do except meeting your brother with a smiling face, then do that. Muslim records this hadith in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and at-Tirmidhī, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ. A variant reading, ḥusnan for ḥasanan, uses the verbal noun as an intensified description, speak goodness itself. Allah commands His servants to speak well to people after commanding them to treat people well, so that two categories of manners are covered, good speech and good action. Tell people to do what is right and avoid what is wrong, but without harshness or severity.

**"establish prayer; and pay alms-tax"**. Allah then stresses His own worship and the doing of good by ordaining ṣalāh and zakāh: perfect the five daily prayers, and give from your wealth what is due to the poor, to those who have a right to it.

**"But you ˹Israelites˺ turned away—except for a few of you—and were indifferent"**. They accepted all this and then turned away, refusing to fulfil these obligations, knowingly and intentionally abandoning them. The address is in the second person, but the forefathers are meant, and the present generation rejects it as their forefathers did. The "few" were among those forefathers, and it is said that the phrase refers to ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions. "Indifferent" means denying the covenant and setting it aside. Of these very commands, this Ummah has practised what no nation before it practised, and all praise is due to Allah.

### Who were the few?

The few who kept the pledge were those who acted on the Sharīʿah of Mūsā (Moses) as long as it was in force, and who, once it was abrogated, followed the Sharīʿah of Muḥammad ﷺ. The verse also sets out the basic elements common to Islam and all the earlier Sharīʿahs: tawḥīd, the oneness of Allah, service to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, gentleness in speaking to every human being, and ṣalāh and zakāh.

### Speaking gently to everyone

The command to speak kindly asks for a gentle tone and an open-hearted manner towards others, good or evil, pious or impious, orthodox or wayward, followers of the Sunnah or people given to innovation. In religious matters, however, one must not hide the truth to please people or win their approval. When Allah sent Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron) to Pharaoh with His signs (20:42), He instructed them to use gentle and soft words, and no one who addresses another person today is superior to Mūsā, nor is anyone addressed viler than Pharaoh. Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUmar once told ʿAṭāʾ, the great master of exegesis and hadith, that he could see people of unorthodox beliefs around him, and that being short-tempered he dealt harshly with such people when they came to him. ʿAṭāʾ told him not to behave that way, recited this verse, and said that Allah has commanded us to speak politely to people. If Jews and Christians are all to be treated like this, he asked, would the command not apply to a Muslim, whatever kind of man he is? Al-Qurṭubī preserves the exchange.

### Kindness to the weak as a test

A modern reflection draws out the order of the duties. Man's first duty to God is to worship Him without ascribing partners to Him. His second is kindness to others, and kindness begins at home with parents and family, extends to neighbours and relatives, and finally reaches everyone one meets. The only proper way to deal with people is with justice and goodwill. The real test comes in how one treats the orphans and the needy, meaning society's weaker members. The strong are guaranteed respectful treatment by their very strength, but where the weak are concerned no such incentive exists, so one must take special care to behave well toward them. Those who are good to people without worldly power or resources do it for God's sake alone, since no other motive is available. There are many reasons why people feel little inclination to be kind to the weak. Benefactors often regard themselves as superior, and when they are not shown the deference they consider their due they treat the less fortunate with disdain. The thought of a permanent liability is often so irksome that they turn rude in order to shake off a burdensome obligation. Such an attitude leaves no room for the idea that the weak also have their self-respect. When the benefactor feels slighted, he writes the beneficiary off as unworthy and incompetent, and that thinking shows itself in many ways.

### In short

- The covenant's terms were worship of Allah alone, kindness to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, good speech, prayer and zakāh, the shared core of every Sharīʿah (compare 4:36).
- Allah's right comes first, then the parents' right, which the Qur'an pairs with His own (31:14, 17:23), and which the Prophet ﷺ ranked right after timely prayer.
- Good speech covers commanding good, forbidding evil, truthfulness about the Prophet ﷺ, and even a smiling face, as Abū Dharr's hadith teaches.
- The Israelites turned from the covenant, all but a few such as ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions, while this Ummah has kept these commands as no nation before it.

84.text:
Verse 84 adds the next articles of the covenant, the ones that governed how the Israelites were to treat each other. "And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other’s blood nor expel each other from their homes, you gave your pledge and bore witness".

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when We took your covenant"**. This covenant was made in the Book, the Torah. The verse supplements the one before it and sets out further terms of the pledge the Israelites took.

**"that you would neither shed each other’s blood"**. Do not kill one another. They had agreed not to slay each other in internecine war. One early reading applies the clause directly to the Jewish tribes of Madinah, Banū Qurayẓah and Banū an-Naḍīr. Allah speaks of "your own" blood here, just as He told the calf-worshippers to repent and "execute yourselves" (2:54), because the followers of one religion are like a single soul. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the believers in their mutual kindness, mercy and sympathy as one body: when one limb falls ill the whole body answers with fever and sleeplessness.

**"nor expel each other from their homes"**. No one of you may drive another from his house. The pledge also covered not forcing their own people into exile, that is, not harassing a man until he is driven to migrate. Nor were they to take part in fighting against their own.

**"you gave your pledge and bore witness"**. You agreed to this covenant and testified against your own souls that you knew of it and had witnessed it, fully aware of what you were doing. The agreement was willing. Sometimes a person does not state his willingness in so many words and only the manner of his speech suggests it, but the Israelites' consent was not of that kind. It was as clear and explicit as a witness's statement is.

### How the pledge was broken

The verse was aimed at the Jews living in Madinah in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They had long suffered from the armed conflicts between the two Arab tribes of the city, al-Aws and al-Khazraj, who before Islam worshipped idols and fought many battles.
