Three Jewish tribes lived around Madinah, Banū Qaynuqāʿ, Banū an-Naḍīr and Banū Qurayẓah. Although all three followed the law of Mūsā (Moses), ignorant prejudice split them into two camps enmeshed in the political manoeuvring of the pagans. One account places Qaynuqāʿ and an-Naḍīr with the Khazraj and Qurayẓah with the Aws, while Ibn ʿAbbās places Qaynuqāʿ with the Khazraj and both an-Naḍīr and Qurayẓah with the Aws. When war broke out between the Aws and the Khazraj their Jewish allies fought beside them, so that Jew killed Jew, drove Jew from his home and looted his goods, in defiance of clear texts in their own Books. The next verse takes the story up in detail and shows how this behaviour, practising part of the Torah while trampling the rest, became the occasion of these verses and the proof of their duplicity.

### In short

- The Israelites pledged in the Torah not to kill or expel one another, and testified to the pledge with full knowledge.
- "Your own blood" treats the whole community as one soul, as in 2:54, and as the Prophet's ﷺ image of the one body teaches.
- The Jews of Madinah, split between the Aws and the Khazraj, broke exactly these terms in the tribal wars.

85.text:
Verse 85 holds the Jews of Madinah to the covenant just described and shows how they kept one clause while breaking the others. "But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression", it says, and yet when the expelled come back as captives "you still ransom them". The verse then asks the question at the heart of the whole passage: "Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?"

### Phrase by phrase

**"But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes"**. After the pledge, after confirming it and bearing witness, they broke it. Allah had laid down three particular injunctions for the Israelites: not to kill one another in civil war, not to force their own people into exile, and, if they found one of their own a prisoner of war, to pay a ransom and secure his release. They disregarded the first two and acted on the third alone, which they supposed the easier to carry out.

**"aiding one another in sin and aggression"**. The Arabic verb for aiding has one letter assimilated into another, and a variant reading keeps the two letters separate. They conspired against their own people in disobedience and injustice, in contravention and offence, assisted by their enemies. The indictment of "sin and aggression" suggests that two kinds of right were infringed: Allah's right, through disobedience to Him, and the right of His creatures, through the pain and loss inflicted on them.

**"and when those ˹expelled˺ come to you as captives, you still ransom them"**. Captives of your own religion you free by paying ransom to the enemy, delivering them from captivity with money or the like. Variant readings exist for both "captives" and "ransom". This ransoming was itself one of the things to which they were pledged.

**"though expelling them was unlawful for you"**. Their expulsion and killing were unlawful in the first place. Grammatically this clause attaches to the earlier words about expelling, and what lies between is a parenthesis: expulsion was forbidden to you in the same way that failing to ransom was forbidden to you.

**"Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?"**. You believe in the part that requires you to free your captives from the enemy, and you disbelieve in the part that forbids fighting, expelling and assisting against one another. Another reading of the phrase: do you believe in the parts of the Scripture that suit your whim and disbelieve in the parts that do not? A further gloss has it that they ransomed their own captives but left the captives of their friends without ransom.

**"Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life"**. Degradation, disgrace and ignominy in this world, by being killed or taken captive as slaves.

**"and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment?"**. Returned to the most terrible of chastisements, as punishment for defying the Book of Allah that they possessed.

**"For Allah is never unaware of what you do"**. He is not reducing your punishment, because of the transgressions you commit, or, as some say, because of what you concealed. He will hold you to account. A variant reading has "what they do".

### The wars of the Aws and the Khazraj

Ibn ʿAbbās, through Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq ibn Yasār, explained the background. Allah mentioned what they were doing, and that in the Torah He had forbidden them to shed each other's blood and required them to free their prisoners. The Jews of Madinah were divided into two camps, Banū Qaynuqāʿ allied with the Khazraj, and an-Naḍīr and Qurayẓah allied with the Aws. When fighting erupted between the Aws and the Khazraj, Qaynuqāʿ fought beside the Khazraj and an-Naḍīr and Qurayẓah beside the Aws, each Jewish camp fighting its Jewish brethren in the other. They shed one another's blood although they had the Torah with them and knew their rights and duties, while the Aws and the Khazraj were idol-worshipping polytheists who knew nothing of Paradise, the Fire, the Resurrection, divine Books or the lawful (ḥalāl) and the forbidden (ḥarām). When a war ended the Jews ransomed their prisoners and applied the Torah: Qaynuqāʿ ransomed their men captured by the Aws, and an-Naḍīr and Qurayẓah ransomed theirs captured by the Khazraj. They also demanded blood money. During the wars they killed whomever they could, Jew or Arab, and helped the polytheists against their own brethren. So Allah reminded them: do you ransom them by the ruling of the Torah, and kill them though the Torah forbade you to kill them or expel them from their homes, and though it commanded you not to aid the polytheists against your brethren? All of this you do to gain the life of this world. Ibn ʿAbbās added that he had been informed that this conduct toward the Aws and the Khazraj was the reason these verses were revealed. In the victorious camp the Jews would release the prisoners of the defeated party, according to the Torah's rulings, having first killed, expelled and looted furniture and money in the fighting.

Another account describes the same hypocrisy from the Jews' own mouths. In these battles Jews lost their lives and homes as much as non-Jews, so the Jews of Qurayẓah shared in the slaughter and exile of the Jews of an-Naḍīr, and the reverse. Yet when Jews were taken prisoner, each Jewish group would persuade its own Arab friends to accept a ransom and release them. Asked why they showed such solicitude for the prisoners, they answered that ransoming was obligatory on them. Asked why, then, they fought them at all, they said it would be a real disgrace not to go to the aid of their allies, even non-Jewish ones, for fear their allies be humiliated. The verse exposes this duplicity and perversity, and the whole picture, as one modern writer puts it, shows the three tribes, united in Mosaic law, constantly at war with one another in two camps.

### Why they could not be trusted

These noble verses criticise the Jews for applying the Torah at one time and defying it at another, although they believed in the Torah and knew that what they did was wrong. For this reason they were not to be trusted to preserve or convey the Torah, nor to be believed about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: his description, his coming, his being driven from his land, his Hijrah, and everything else the earlier Prophets had told them of him, all of which they hid among themselves. Allah's verdict on such people is the disgrace of this world and the gravest torment of the next.

### Was their selective faith unbelief?

Scholars note that the Jews addressed here had already become unbelievers by refusing to accept the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ. The verse, however, does not point to that aspect of their unbelief (kufr). It rebukes them for having faith (īmān) in one part of the Torah and not in another. Read literally, the words mean that the Jews became unbelievers by not believing in some parts, that is, some injunctions, of the Torah. A divine Book has to be taken whole. Rejecting one part amounts to rejecting all of it, which is plainly unbelief. If instead the verse is taken as a rebuke for failing to act on certain commands, a question arises: how can breaking certain commandments be called kufr, when a believer is not counted an unbeliever so long as he accepts in principle the distinction between ḥalāl and ḥarām as the Sharīʿah lays it down? The answer is that the idiom of the Sharīʿah sometimes labels a very grave sin kufr to stress its gravity and its moral character. The hadith which says that whoever deliberately abandons the ṣalāh has become an unbeliever works in the same way. On this second reading, nothing softens the kufr of which the Jews were already guilty by denying the Prophet ﷺ.

### A punishment in this world and the next

The verse announces punishment not only in the Hereafter but in this world, in the form of humiliation and disgrace, and it came about as foretold. In the Prophet's ﷺ own lifetime the Jews of Banū Qurayẓah were slain or taken prisoner, and Banū an-Naḍīr were expelled for breaking the pact they had made with the Muslims, driven out to Syria, and the Jews were ordered to pay the jizyah.

A doctrinal question is raised about the "harshest punishment" promised to the Jews. Why should the direst punishment be reserved for them rather than for atheists, when the Jews at least believe in Allah? The famous commentator al-Ālūsī answers in his Rūḥ al-Maʿānī that every punishment given to unbelievers is "the direst" in the sense that it has no end or limit. The verse therefore does not mean that the Jews will be punished more severely than every other unbeliever, but that they will receive the kind of punishment that is endless and limitless, in other words a punishment more severe than that of Muslim sinners. If there turn out to be different degrees of punishment among different kinds of unbelievers, that does not conflict with the verse.

### Ritual without obedience

A modern reflection sees in this a permanent pattern. The basic teachings of Islamic law demand a complete renunciation of pagan ways, the suppression of selfish desire and the control of worldly wants, and that is exactly why its commands are ignored in politics. Obeying them would produce true piety, but people dislike such arduous practice. They prefer a pretence of piety made up of superficial rituals, which amounts to issuing a self-made edition of the divine religion, disregarding the Hereafter and prizing the worldly side of religion in the hope that zeal for acts bringing fame and honour will earn the reward that belongs to true piety. Such brazen distortion of religion earns only God's wrath and merits no reward from Him.

### Picking and choosing

The devotional reading puts the verse's logic simply. If you protect their rights by paying their ransom, you must equally hold your hands back from them and give up driving them out of their homelands. Having upheld part of what was made obligatory on you, what stops you from carrying out the rest of your commands? Whoever picks and chooses among his commands, believing some and disbelieving others, forfeits the reward of his deeds on account of what he left undone. They imagined that their actions would profit them. In the Hereafter they will discover that nothing they did was accepted, because it was mixed with harm and emptied of sincerity and devotion. Captives, moreover, come in different kinds. One captive is drowning in the sea of whim (hawā), and his rescue is to be turned toward guidance. Another is held by whisperings (wasāwis), and his ransom is to be shown the road to certainty by the glimmers of proofs.

### In short

- Of the three Torah commands, no killing, no expulsion, ransom your captives, the Jews of Madinah kept only the easiest, ransoming men whom they themselves had helped to kill and expel in the wars of the Aws and the Khazraj.
- Their own explanations exposed the double standard: ransom because we are commanded, fight lest our allies be shamed.
- Believing in part of the Book and rejecting part is treated as unbelief, either literally, since a divine Book is accepted whole, or as a grave sin labelled kufr for emphasis, like deliberately abandoning the ṣalāh.
- The promised disgrace arrived with the fate of Qurayẓah and an-Naḍīr, and the "harshest punishment" means, as al-Ālūsī explained, the endless punishment of unbelief.
- Religion that keeps the convenient rituals and drops the demanding commands is a self-made religion, and the believer must also ransom the captives of whim and whispering within.

86.text:
Verse 86 names the bargain behind all this. "These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced, nor will they be helped".

### Phrase by phrase

**"These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world"**. They have bought this world at the price of the next, preferring the temporary to the eternal, this lower world to the Hereafter, and disbelief to belief. This explains why the Jews must bear so severe a punishment. They disobeyed Allah to satisfy their desires and enjoy worldly pleasures, and for these things they sacrificed their salvation in the world to come.

**"So their punishment will not be reduced"**. It will not be lightened even for an hour. Some say it will never be lifted. Their sin is so great that Allah will neither reduce nor soften their punishment.

**"nor will they be helped"**. They will find no helper to save them from the eternal torment, and no one to grant them refuge from it or to shield them from Allah's chastisement. Allah will allow no one to intercede on their behalf.

### Losing both worlds

The devotional reading observes that whoever prefers anything to God has lost in this world and in the Hereafter alike. It quotes the saying: people turned from us for no cause or reason, and our need of them is even smaller than their need of us.

### In short

- The Jews of Madinah sold the Hereafter for worldly advantage, and that is why their punishment is unrelieved.
- No reduction, no respite and no helper await those who make this trade.
- Whoever prefers anything to Allah loses both worlds.

87.text:
Verse 87 sums up the long history of guidance offered to the Israelites and their response to it. "Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit." Then comes the charge: "Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, We gave Moses the Book"**. Allah gave Mūsā (Moses) the Torah, and the Jews changed and distorted it, defied its commands and altered its meanings. The verse reminds the Israelites how Allah in His mercy forgave their transgressions again and again and provided them with every means of guidance, beginning with a divine Book.

**"and sent after him successive messengers"**. After Mūsā, Allah sent messengers and prophets who followed his law. He revealed the Torah with guidance and light, and by it the prophets who submitted to Allah judged for the Jews (5:44). As-Suddī reported Abū Mālik's explanation that the verb qaffaynā means "We made succeed", while others said "We made follow". Both are possible, since Allah also says that He sent His messengers in succession (23:44). Among these prophets were Yūshaʿ (Joshua), Dāwūd (David), Zakariyyā (Zechariah) and Yaḥyā (John the Baptist), all of whom told the Jews that it was not enough to revere the Torah as a holy book, for its teachings had to be practised.

**"And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs"**. Last in the line of the prophets of the Children of Israel came ʿĪsā (Jesus), who was sent with some laws that differed from parts of the Torah. For that reason Allah supported him with miracles: bringing the dead to life, shaping birds from clay and breathing into them so that they became living birds by Allah's leave, healing the sick, the blind and the leper, and foretelling the unseen, as Ibn ʿAbbās described. His clear proofs also included commands, prohibitions, and the Gospel itself, irrefutable evidence of his prophethood. All these signs testified to his truthfulness and to the truth of what he was sent with.

**"and supported him with the holy spirit"**. Rūḥ al-Qudus is Jibrīl (Gabriel). This is Ibn Masʿūd's explanation of the verse, shared by Qatādah, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, Ibn ʿAbbās, as-Suddī, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Ismāʿīl ibn Khālid. Allah says of the Qur'an that the trustworthy spirit brought it down (26:193-194), and that the holy spirit brought it down from your Lord with the truth (16:102). The Arabic construction annexes the noun to its qualifying adjective, so that rūḥ al-qudus means "the sanctified spirit", and Jibrīl is so described because of the sanctity of ʿĪsā, whom he accompanied wherever he went. The poet and Companion Ḥassān ibn Thābit called him, in a couplet preserved in the hadith, "Jibrīl, the messenger of Allah, who comes to us, the holy spirit, the incomparable". Allah strengthened and helped ʿĪsā through Jibrīl in several ways: he was conceived through the breath of the angel, Jibrīl protected him from Satan's touch at his birth, the angel accompanied him constantly to defend him against the hostility of the Jews, and through him ʿĪsā was raised to the heavens.

**"Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you ˹Israelites˺ with something you do not like"**. Still you refuse to be upright. Whenever a messenger came with truth that your souls did not desire, that did not agree with your hearts and your religion, you reacted the same way. The question is a rebuke. The Children of Israel grew more defiant and envious of ʿĪsā and would not accept a difference from even one part of the Torah, although he told them that he confirmed the Torah and would make lawful some of what had been forbidden to them (3:50).

**"you become arrogant"**. You disdained to follow him, full of pride against the truth and looking down on the messengers of Allah. The Prophets commanded the Jews what differed from their desires and opinions, and they upheld the rulings of the Torah that the Jews had changed, which is why belief in them came so hard.

**"rejecting some and killing others"**. Some they called liars, such as ʿĪsā, and later Muḥammad ﷺ, and some they killed, such as Zakariyyā and Yaḥyā. The verbs are in the present tense, narrating past events as if they were happening now. Az-Zamakhsharī remarked that Allah avoided the past tense "killed" because attempts on the Prophet's ﷺ life, by poison and by magic, still lay ahead. During his final illness the Prophet ﷺ said that he still felt the effect of the food he had eaten at Khaybar, and that now his aorta was being cut. Al-Bukhārī and others record this hadith.

### Jibrīl as the holy spirit in the Sunnah

Al-Bukhārī records from ʿĀʾishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set up a minbar in the mosque from which Ḥassān ibn Thābit defended him in verse, and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed, "O Allah, aid Ḥassān with Rūḥ al-Qudus, for he has defended Your Prophet." Abū Dāwūd records it in his Sunan, and at-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Ibn Ḥibbān records in his Ṣaḥīḥ that Ibn Masʿūd heard the Prophet ﷺ say: Rūḥ al-Qudus has told me that no soul will die until it has used up its provision and its term, so have taqwā of Allah and seek your sustenance in the most fitting way.

### Why a people who revered the Torah killed its prophets

The Torah was God's Book revealed to the Jews, but gradually they stopped treating it as a source of guidance and came to regard it as a sacred relic of national heritage and a symbol of ethnic superiority, more a guarantee of salvation than a guide to earning it. The prophets who arose after Mūsā all insisted that believing in the sacredness of scripture is futile unless its message is lived out every day. The very people who held the Torah in such esteem could not tolerate these exhortations, because self-interest and worldly ambition ruled their lives while they passed themselves off as bearers of the true faith. As long as religion consolidated their worldly standing they welcomed it, but the pure message of truth looked to them like a threat to the hegemony they had built on religion. Their egoism blocked any true religiosity. They should have been the first to believe, and instead they rejected the message and the messenger, scorned and persecuted God's prophets, called them impostors and even killed them. Their stubbornness in the worship of their own desires meant that whenever the prophets brought injunctions that did not please them, they denied the prophets, even ʿĪsā, or killed them outright, as they did Zakariyyā and Yaḥyā.

The devotional reading finds the root of it in one word. Allah delivered His address to them and made messenger follow messenger, every one of them calling to the same thing, but they heard the callers with the ear of whim (hawā). Whatever their lower selves found pleasant they accepted, and whatever their whims found troublesome they rejected. They were marked by this self-serving desire and, worse, became its servants (ʿabadū). The attributes of the worshipper (ʿābid) became the thing worshipped (maʿbūd). What a terrible affliction lies upon them!

### In short

- Allah gave the Torah to Mūsā (Moses), sent a succession of prophets who judged by it (5:44, 23:44), and finally sent ʿĪsā (Jesus) with miracles and the Gospel.
- The holy spirit who supported ʿĪsā is Jibrīl (Gabriel), as Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and others held, and as 26:193-194 and 16:102 show, and the Prophet ﷺ asked that Ḥassān be aided by the same spirit.
- Whenever a messenger brought what they disliked, the Israelites responded with arrogance, calling some liars and killing others, among them Zakariyyā and Yaḥyā.
- The present tense "killing" points forward to their attempts on the Prophet's ﷺ life, as az-Zamakhsharī noted, and the whole pattern springs from listening to revelation with the ear of whim.

88.text:
Verse 88 records the Jews' own excuse and Allah's answer to it. "They say, “Our hearts are unreceptive!” In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief. They have but little faith".

### Phrase by phrase

**"They say, 'Our hearts are unreceptive!'"**. The Jews said this to the Prophet ﷺ mockingly. The word ghulf is the plural of aghlaf, something wrapped up in a cover, so the claim is that their hearts are encased and cannot take in what he says. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported Ibn ʿAbbās explaining it as "our hearts are screened". Mujāhid said "covered". ʿIkrimah said "there is a stamp on them". Abū al-ʿĀliyah said "they do not comprehend". Mujāhid and Qatādah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās read the word in a way that gives a different sense: our hearts are vessels already full of every kind of knowledge, and have no need of the knowledge you bring, Muḥammad. ʿAṭāʾ held this view too. In other words, our hearts can absorb any knowledge, yet they prove incapable of comprehending yours. The Israelites were arguing that their stubbornness was no fault of theirs, since nothing said to them could reach them or make sense to them. Scholars note the sarcasm in it. The Jews meant that Islam could never touch hearts as well guarded against it as theirs, and so they were congratulating themselves on the staunchness of their belief. The saying resembles the words of other deniers, that their hearts are veiled against what the Prophet calls them to, their ears are deaf, and a barrier stands between them and him (41:5).

**"In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief"**. The word "nay" introduces the rebuttal. It is not as they claim. Allah has cursed them, removing them far from His mercy, expelling them from it, depriving them of every kind of righteousness and degrading them for their unbelief, which is not the result of any defect in their hearts. He has sealed their hearts as a punishment for their disbelief, and it is this, not firmness of faith, that keeps Islam out. What they boast of is a damnation, for they deny Islam, which is now the true religion, and cling to a religion that has been abrogated. In Sūrat an-Nisāʾ Allah says the same: for their saying "our hearts are unreceptive", it is Allah who has sealed their hearts for their disbelief, so they believe only a little (4:155).

**"They have but little faith"**. The Arabic adds an extra particle to emphasise how little. Scholars differ on what this littleness means here and in the parallel verse. Qatādah understood it as "only a few of them believe". Others said that their faith is minute, because they do believe in the Resurrection and in the reward and punishment that Mūsā (Moses) foretold, yet this faith does not benefit them, since it is overshadowed by their rejection of what Muḥammad ﷺ brought. Others held that the Jews did not truly believe in anything, and that "little is what they believe" means they do not believe at all, like the Arabic idiom "hardly have I seen the like of this", meaning never. One early gloss offers both: they believe neither much nor little, or, as it is also said, they do not believe in what you say at all.

### Why a little faith does not count

The little faith the Jews possessed concerned doctrines common to Islam and Judaism, such as belief in Allah and in the Day of Judgement. But they did not accept Muḥammad ﷺ as a prophet or the Qur'an as the word of Allah, so their faith was incomplete, and because a little faith is unacceptable, they count as unbelievers. When the verse calls this little faith īmān, it does so only in the lexical sense, for īmān means total certitude, even if it attaches to some things and not others. From the standpoint of the Sharīʿah such partial faith cannot be called īmān at all. The Sharīʿah accepts as valid only the faith that affirms with certainty each and every thing it requires one to affirm.

### Pretension bares its fangs

The devotional reading adds that if anything in them had been free of pretension, finding meanings in God's signs and scripture would have become easy. But when the truth must be recognised, the fangs of pretenders are bared. As the saying goes, when tears run down the cheeks, the one who truly weeps is told apart from the one who only pretends.

### In short

- "Our hearts are unreceptive" was a mocking boast, read by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and Abū al-ʿĀliyah as covered, stamped or uncomprehending, or, in Ibn ʿAbbās's other reading, as already full of knowledge.
- Allah's answer is that the real cause is His curse and seal upon them for their disbelief, as 4:155 and 41:5 confirm.
- Their "little faith" is read as a few believers, as a faint belief in Allah and the Last Day that cannot save them, or as no faith at all.
- Partial faith is not faith in the Sharīʿah's sense, which requires certain affirmation of everything it demands.

89.text:
Verse 89 describes the bitterest irony of all. The Jews had been waiting for this very Prophet and praying for his arrival. "Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists, when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized, confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺, they rejected it. So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Although they used to pray for victory ˹by means of the Prophet˺ over the polytheists"**. Before this Messenger came, the Jews used to ask Allah to aid them through his arrival against their polytheist enemies in war, saying, "O Allah, give us help against them through the Prophet who is to be sent at the end of time." They would tell the polytheists that a Prophet was to be sent shortly before the end of the world, and that together with him they would wipe them out as the nations of ʿĀd and Iram were wiped out. One early gloss names the enemies as the tribes of Asad, Ghaṭafān, Muzaynah and Juhaynah. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the Jews of Khaybar were at war with Ghaṭafān and lost every encounter, so they devised this supplication: "O Allah, we beseech You by the truth of the unlettered Prophet whom You promised to send to us at the end of time, give us victory over them." Whenever they said it, Ghaṭafān was defeated. As-Suddī told it differently: the Arabs used to pass by the Jews and do them harm, and the Jews, who knew Muḥammad's description from the Torah, asked Allah to send him so that they could fight the Arabs alongside him.

**"when there came to them a Book from Allah"**. That is, the Qur'an, which Allah sent down to Muḥammad ﷺ.

**"which they recognized"**. They knew it to be the truth, and they knew the Prophet's traits and description from their own Book. The mission of the Prophet ﷺ was exactly what they had been told to expect.

**"confirming the Scripture they had ˹in their hands˺"**. The Qur'an agrees with the Torah and the Gospel in their universal true principles. To say that the Qur'an confirms the Torah means that the Qur'an is concrete evidence of the truth of the Torah's prophecies about the coming of the Prophet ﷺ and of the Qur'an itself. Whoever believes in the Torah cannot consistently deny the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ, because that denial would be a denial of the Torah too. The Torah had foretold his coming in several places, and the Jews had themselves told the Arabs to expect a new prophet and a new divine Book before long.

**"they rejected it"**. They denied that he was the one. They disbelieved out of envy and for fear of losing their leadership. Even after recognising its authenticity, the Jews denied the Qur'an out of sheer spite. The Arabic has two "when" clauses, and the answer to the first is supplied by the answer to the second.

**"So may Allah’s condemnation be upon the disbelievers"**. His wrath and torment are upon the Jews who disbelieved in Him and His Prophet.

### The occasion of revelation

Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq related from Ibn ʿAbbās that before the Prophet ﷺ was sent, the Jews would call on Allah to send him so that they might prevail over the Aws and the Khazraj. Once Allah had sent him, to the Arabs, they rejected him and went back on everything they had said about him. Muʿādh ibn Jabal and Bishr ibn al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr, of Banū Salamah, said to them: "O Jews, fear Allah and embrace Islam. You used to invoke Allah for the coming of Muḥammad when we were still disbelievers, and you used to tell us that he would come and describe him to us." Salām ibn Mishkam of Banū an-Naḍīr replied: "He has brought nothing we recognise. He is not the Prophet we told you about." Allah then revealed this verse about their statement. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said that the Jews' prayers for Muḥammad ﷺ to be sent were prayers for victory over the Arab disbelievers. They would say, "O Allah, send the Prophet we read about in the Torah, so that we can torment and kill the disbelievers alongside him." When Allah sent him and he turned out not to be one of them, they rejected him, envying the Arabs, although they knew that he was Allah's Messenger. As-Suddī adds their objection in their own words: all the messengers were descendants of Yaʿqūb (Jacob), so how can this one be a descendant of Ismāʿīl (Ishmael)?

### Knowledge is not faith

Why does the Qur'an call the Jews unbelievers when they recognised the truth as truth, which might seem to qualify them as believers? Because faith (īmān) does not mean merely knowing the truth. It means accepting the truth and affirming it in deed. Otherwise Satan would have to be called a believer, for he knows perfectly well what the truth is, and in his case that knowledge only intensifies the gravity of his unbelief (kufr). The next verse traces the Jews' unbelief to its source in malice.

### Empty words

A modern reading sees the Jews of Arabia repeating the old pattern. They had seen prophecies of a final prophet in their scriptures and eagerly awaited him. "When he comes," they used to say, "we will join him in a grand alliance against the pagans and idolaters." These proved to be empty words, a pretence aimed at consolidating their status as undisputed guardians of the divine faith. When the Prophet ﷺ came, their real position was exposed. They were steeped in bigotry, and a prophet from outside the Jewish race was more than they were willing to believe in. They could not dispute the authentic indications the Qur'an presented in support of his prophethood. All they could say was that it sounded very impressive, but their ancestral religion was good enough for them, their hearts were sealed, and they would accept nothing besides the faith inherited from their forefathers.

### The soldier who breaks at the muster

The devotional reading finds here an allusion to the person who resolves on purity and clarity (ṣafāʾ), promises complete loyalty (wafāʾ) and raises the banners of his zeal to march out to battle, but who, when the call comes to line up and advance boldly, collapses as the ranks are being rallied and slips away from the company for fear of dangerous attacks. Allah says of such people that when the matter was resolved upon, it would have been better for them had they been true to Allah (47:21).

### In short

- The Jews had prayed for victory through the coming Prophet, at Khaybar against Ghaṭafān, and in Madinah against the Aws and the Khazraj, and had described him to the Arabs.
- When the Qur'an came confirming their Scripture and they recognised the Prophet ﷺ, they rejected him, and Salām ibn Mishkam of Banū an-Naḍīr told the Muslims he was not the one.
- Their motives were envy, fear of losing leadership, and racial pride that a prophet should come from Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) rather than Yaʿqūb (Jacob).
- Recognising the truth is not īmān, which demands acceptance and action, and he who deserts when the call to advance comes has not kept his promise (47:21).

90.text:
Verse 90 passes judgement on the bargain the Jews made. "Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for", it says, which was "denying Allah’s revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants! They have earned wrath upon wrath. And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment".

### Phrase by phrase

**"Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for"**. Mujāhid said that the Jews traded truth away for falsehood and concealed the truth about Muḥammad ﷺ. As-Suddī said simply that the Jews sold themselves: what they chose for themselves, disbelief in what Allah revealed to Muḥammad ﷺ instead of believing in him, aiding him and supporting him, was an evil choice. What they gave away was their share of reward in the Hereafter, their portion of faith in Allah and His messengers. The Arabic construction singles out the very thing being condemned, the price.

**"denying Allah’s revelation"**. They disbelieved in the Qur'an that Allah sent down, in the Book and the Messenger together. This conduct was the fruit of their injustice, envy and hatred.

**"and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants"**. The word for resentment, baghyan, gives the reason for their disbelief: envy that Allah should send down of His bounty, that is, revelation, upon whomever He chooses to carry His message, meaning Muḥammad ﷺ. Out of His bounty Allah sent Jibrīl (Gabriel) to him with the Book and with prophethood, and they were resentfully envious of it. There is no envy worse than this. Prophethood cannot be earned by one's own effort or merit. It is a special grace that Allah bestows on whomever He likes, and the Jews, in denying the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an out of spite, were questioning the will of Allah Himself.

**"They have earned wrath upon wrath"**. They came back laden with Allah's anger. The indefinite form of the word stresses how awesome that anger is. Ibn ʿAbbās said that Allah was angry with them because they neglected part of the Torah, and angry again because they disbelieved in the Prophet He sent to them. Abū al-ʿĀliyah said that Allah was angry with them for their disbelief in the Injīl (Gospel) and in ʿĪsā (Jesus), and angry a second time for their disbelief in Muḥammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said the same. Another explanation is that the phrase means they deserved and acquired multiplied anger, or curse upon curse. The Jews earned divine wrath in two ways, for denying a true prophet, and for their envy and malice in doing so.

**"And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment"**. A disgraceful torment through which they will be humiliated, or, as some say, a severe punishment. Because their disbelief grew out of transgression and envy, which were themselves born of arrogance, they are punished with disgrace and humiliation in this world and the next. Allah says likewise that those too proud to worship Him will enter Hell humbled (40:60), meaning disgraced, degraded and humiliated. Imām Aḥmad narrated from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said that the arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection the size of ants but in the shape of men, with everything towering over them because of the humiliation laid upon them. They will be driven into a prison in Jahannam called Bawlas, where the fire will close over them from above and they will drink the pus of the people of the Fire.

### A punishment of disgrace, not of purification

The punishment announced here involves not only pain but disgrace and abasement. That added condition suggests that this kind of punishment belongs to unbelievers alone and is not meant for a true Muslim at all. A Muslim, however great his sins, is punished in order to be purified, not in order to be disgraced. For disbelieving in Muḥammad ﷺ and for distorting the Torah beforehand they deserved anger upon anger, and a humiliating torment on the Day of Judgement awaits those who denied his prophethood. The verse that follows reports what the Jews used to say about the Qur'an, and it shows their envy and malice as clearly as their unbelief (kufr).

### From nobility to ignominy

The devotional reading sums it up. Envy brought them down from nobility's abode to ignominy's lowland. Discontent with what the decree had brought reduced them to abasement, and they called down upon themselves what brings wrath upon wrath.

### In short

- The Jews sold their souls, their share in the Hereafter, for the wretched price of rejecting the Qur'an, as Mujāhid and as-Suddī explained.
- The motive was envy that Allah's grace of prophethood went to whomever He willed, meaning Muḥammad ﷺ, and no envy is worse than resenting Allah's own choice.
- "Wrath upon wrath" is the anger earned for neglecting the Torah and rejecting ʿĪsā (Jesus), compounded by the anger earned for rejecting Muḥammad ﷺ, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ʿIkrimah and Qatādah explained.
- Their punishment is humiliating as well as painful, the fate of the arrogant (40:60), who will be raised the size of ants, whereas a believer's punishment purifies rather than disgraces.

91.text:
Verse 91 records the Jews' standard reply to the call of Islam and turns it against them. "When it is said to them: “Believe in what Allah has revealed,” they reply, “We only believe in what was sent down to us,”" and so they deny what came afterwards, "though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures". The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask them a question that exposes the claim: "Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?"

### Phrase by phrase

**"When it is said to them: 'Believe in what Allah has revealed'"**. When the Jews and the People of the Book are told to believe in the Qur'an and the other Books, to believe in what Allah sent down to Muḥammad ﷺ and to follow him.

**"they reply, 'We only believe in what was sent down to us'"**. It is enough for us, they say, to believe in what was revealed to us in the Torah and the Injīl (Gospel), and this is the path we choose. They flatly refused to believe in any Book of Allah except the Torah, and they denied the Gospel and the Qur'an. That denial is itself clear proof of their unbelief (kufr). They added that they believed in the Torah because it had been sent down to them, which means that they rejected the other Books merely because those Books had not been sent down to them, an argument that betrays envy and malice. They also said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Our forefathers were believers."

**"and they deny what came afterwards"**. Whatever lies beyond the Torah, such as the Qur'an. The Arabic marks this clause as describing their state while they make their claim.

**"though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures"**. The Qur'an is the truth, affirming the oneness of Allah and agreeing with what they possess of the Book. The phrases "it is the truth" and "confirming" are two circumstantial qualifiers piled up for emphasis. Since the revelation given to Muḥammad ﷺ matches the revelation the People of the Book already hold, that very match is a proof against them. Allah says that those given the Scripture recognise this Prophet as they recognise their own children, yet a group of them knowingly hides the truth (2:146). Had they truly believed in what was revealed to them, they would have believed in the Qur'an.

**"Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, 'Why then did you kill Allah’s prophets before, if you are ˹truly˺ believers?'"**. If your claim to believe in what was revealed to you were true, why did you kill the Prophets who came to you upholding the law of the Torah, knowing them to be true Prophets? You killed them out of nothing but transgression, stubbornness and injustice toward Allah's Messengers, so you follow only your lusts, opinions and desires. The Torah you profess forbade killing them. The question concerns what their forefathers did, but it is addressed to the Jews of the Prophet's ﷺ time because they approved of what their forefathers had done. As-Suddī said that in this verse Allah chastised the People of the Book.

### Three answers to "we believe only in what was sent to us"

The Qur'an refutes the Jews' position in three ways. First, once the truth and authenticity of the other Books have been established by irrefutable arguments, what can a flat denial mean? Had they doubted those arguments they could have raised their doubts and satisfied themselves, but a plain refusal to believe is something else. Second, the other Books, the Qur'an among them, confirm the Torah, so to deny them is to deny the Torah itself. Third, killing a prophet counts as unbelief in every divine Book, and the prophets the Jews killed were themselves Israelites whose teaching rested on the injunctions of the Torah. The Jews not only killed these prophets but accepted the killers as their chiefs, a direct denial of the Torah that falsifies their claim to believe in it. Nothing the Jews say or do, in short, holds up from any point of view, and the verses that follow refute them on further counts.

### Group loyalty mistaken for love of truth

The Jews were not ready to accept the Qur'an because they considered themselves already rightly guided. They were sure that belonging to the largest body of followers of the truth, the Israelites, would be enough to earn them salvation. In reality it was ethnic superiority dressed up as love of truth. The communal values of their group had taken the place of pure truth, and so, when truth appeared in its original form, they could not accept it. Had their aim been to find pure truth, it would not have been hard, for predictions in their own sacred book, the Torah, had announced that the Book of truth to be followed was now the Qur'an and not the religion of their group.

The devotional reading sees the same selectivity on the inner path. When such people are told to recognise the truth of what has been shown them from the decree of divine harmony, by acknowledging the situation and the proof established, their lower selves admit whatever ambiguous part agrees with their self-serving desires, and then disbelieve in whatever lies beyond their worldly concerns. They remain far from the elite and are not counted among the masters with a special claim (arbāb al-ikhtiṣāṣ).

### In short

- Told to believe in the Qur'an, the Jews claimed to believe only in what was sent down to them, rejecting the Gospel and the Qur'an although both confirm the Torah (2:146).
- A Book is not denied because it was sent to someone else, and to deny the Books that confirm the Torah is to deny the Torah.
- The question "why did you kill Allah's prophets?" exposes the claim, since the murdered prophets were Israelites upholding the Torah and their killers were made chiefs.
- Behind the refusal lay ethnic pride mistaken for love of truth, and a faith that accepts only what suits the lower self.

92.text:
Verse 92 brings the second count against the claim of faith. "Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs, then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully". A people who turned to an idol while their own prophet was away can hardly claim that their forefathers were steadfast believers.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs"**. Mūsā (Moses) came with commands, prohibitions and miracles, clear signs proving that Allah had sent him and that no deity but Allah deserves worship. The signs named in this connection are the staff and the hand, the blood, the frogs, the lice, the locusts and the flood. His miracles also include the sea parting, the clouds shading the Israelites, the manna and quails, and the stone gushing water. Scholars note that these signs include ones that appeared even before the Torah was given, such as the staff that became a serpent, the shining hand and the sea split open as a road for the Israelites. Their purpose was to affirm Allah's oneness and omnipotence and to prove that Mūsā was a prophet.

**"then you worshipped the calf in his absence"**. You took the calf as a god instead of Allah, in Mūsā's own lifetime, after he had gone to Mount Ṭūr for his appointment with his Lord. In his absence his people made from their jewellery the idol of a calf that lowed, which could neither speak to them nor guide them, and took it as a god (7:148). The devotional reading hears in this the failure of tawḥīd: Mūsā had called them to declare God's unity and to separate the true object of worship (maʿbūd) from every other object and every limited thing (maḥdūd), but they inclined to worship only what attracted them, the calf they adopted and the idol they desired. The calf was taken away from them, yet its traces stayed in their hearts, and in the hearts of their descendants. That, on this view, is why most Jews believe in anthropomorphism (tashbīh).

**"acting wrongfully"**. You were unjust in worshipping the calf when you knew that there is no deity worthy of worship but Allah, and you were unbelievers in taking it as a god. Later they were filled with remorse, realised they had gone astray, and cried that unless their Lord had mercy on them and forgave them they would be lost (7:149). Worshipping others alongside Allah is wrongdoing, since He alone deserves worship.

### Why this answers the Jews of Madinah

The verse refutes the Jews by pointing out that for all their claim to faith (īmān) they had fallen into the sin of shirk, association, which involves denying not only Mūsā but Allah Himself. The Jews who were the Prophet's ﷺ contemporaries had not themselves worshipped the golden calf, but they respected the forefathers who had and took their side, so for all practical purposes they shared the guilt. The verse also hints that no one should be surprised if people whose forefathers denied Mūsā now deny the Prophet ﷺ.

### In short

- Mūsā (Moses) brought overwhelming proofs, the plagues, the staff, the hand, the sea and more, all pointing to Allah's oneness.
- While he was at Mount Ṭūr, his people worshipped the calf (7:148), an act of shirk that they later repented of (7:149).
- The Jews of Madinah inherited the guilt by approving their forefathers, and the calf's trace lingered in their hearts.

93.text:
Verse 93 returns to the covenant at the mountain and lets the Israelites condemn themselves in their own words. "And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey,” they answered, “We hear and disobey.”" The verse then explains why: "The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief." And it ends with a challenge: "How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!"

### Phrase by phrase

**"And when We took your covenant"**. When We took your consent, your binding promise to act according to what is in the Torah, to follow Mūsā (Moses) and to accept what he brought from Allah. Allah reminds the Jews of their errors, their breaking of His covenant, their transgression and their defiance.

**"and raised the mountain above you"**. He pulled it up, lifted it and fixed it over their heads, to drop it on them because they had refused to accept the covenant, and they were awestruck. Scholars trace the need for such a threat back to Egypt. When the Israelites had escaped from Egypt with Allah's help and crossed the sea, they came upon a people who worshipped idols, found the cult so attractive that they asked Mūsā to make them a visible, concrete god too, and repented when he reprimanded them. But repentance has many degrees, and theirs was not of a high order, so the darkness of that error never wholly left their hearts. It grew until it broke out in the worship of the golden calf. As penance, some of them had to be slain, while others, according to some reports, were forgiven and spared, and possibly their repentance too was of a low order. Those who had not joined in worshipping the calf did not hate the deed as much as they should have, so their hearts also carried a trace of shirk. Whether through feeble repentance or through a want of proper hatred for unbelief, their hearts grew indolent in religious matters, to the point that when Allah asked them to pledge to follow the Torah's injunctions steadfastly, Mount Ṭūr (Sinai) had to be suspended over their heads to threaten them. The story was told earlier in the sūrah in the first account of the raised mountain.

**"Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you and obey"**. Take forcefully, seriously and with effort what We have given you of the Book, be diligent and earnest with it, and listen to what you have been commanded, ready to accept it. Otherwise the mountain would fall on you.

**"they answered, 'We hear and disobey'"**. We hear your words and disobey your command. It is as if they said, were it not for the mountain we would have heard what you say and defied it. Out of sheer fright they said with their tongues that they had heard, that is, accepted, Allah's command, but their hearts gave no real consent, and their whole posture said that they would not, or could not, obey. They heard with their ears and rebelled in their actions, and they broke the covenant soon afterwards.

**"The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief"**. Literally, they were made to drink the calf in their hearts. ʿAbd ar-Razzāq related from Maʿmar that Qatādah explained it as absorbing its love until that love lodged in their hearts, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said the same. The love of the golden calf intoxicated their hearts the way wine does. Their love of worshipping it sank into their hearts as a punishment for their disbelief, their denial and ingratitude.

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ 'How evil is what your ˹so-called˺ belief prompts you to do, if you ˹actually˺ believe ˹in the Torah˺!'"**. Worse yet is the way you behaved in the past and behave even now, disbelieving in Allah's signs and defying the Prophets. If love of worshipping the calf weighs as much with you as love of your Creator, then evil indeed is what your belief commands, if you are truthful in claiming that your forefathers were believers. Faith does not command anyone to worship a calf, so the claim to faith is false. Their forefathers are meant, and the same logic applies to the present: you do not believe in the Torah either, because you have denied the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ, and faith in the Torah does not command you to reject him. Your disbelief in Muḥammad ﷺ is the worst of your deeds and the harshest of your sins, for you have disbelieved in the Final Messenger, the master of all Prophets and Messengers, the one sent to all mankind. How can you claim to believe while committing the evil of breaking Allah's covenant, disbelieving in His signs and worshipping the calf instead of Him?

### A faith judged by its fruits

Having set out these examples of perversity and rebellion, the Qur'an asks the Jews to look at themselves and at their claim to genuine faith. Could true faith ever inspire people to such deeds? If it is their brand of faith that leads them into such grave sins, it cannot be a true faith, and their claim to be true believers is plainly false. If they had any faith at all they would not disbelieve and turn away from what Allah instructs them to do. The devotional reading adds that the verse repeats the tale of their excessive love for the calf and their aversion to accepting the Real, and of their being warned of the punishment that would overtake them for their evil. No counsel helped them and no punishment made them give up their disobedience. They paid no attention to censure and did not act (ʿamilū) as the situation required.

### In short

- At the mountain the Israelites pledged to hold fast to the Torah and answered, in effect, "we hear and disobey", consent on the tongue with none in the heart.
- The calf's love had soaked into their hearts like wine, as Qatādah, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ explained, the residue of a shallow repentance that began with the request for a visible god after leaving Egypt.
- A faith that commands calf-worship, or the rejection of Allah's final Messenger ﷺ, is no faith, so the Jews' claim to believe in the Torah collapses.
- Neither counsel nor punishment moved them, a warning that belief is judged by what it prompts one to do.

94.text:
Verse 94 proposes a simple test of the Jews' claim that the next world belongs to them. "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!”" If Paradise is certainly yours, the verse reasons, you should be eager to reach it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺"**. Allah instructs His Prophet ﷺ to put this challenge to the Jews.

**"If the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you ˹Israelites˺ out of all humanity"**. If Paradise in Allah's keeping is purely and specifically yours, as you allege, and not for the believers in Muḥammad ﷺ and his Companions or for anyone else. The Jews claimed the blessings of the next world as their private reserve, meant for no other people. Other verses record the same claim from the Jews and from the Christians: that the Fire will touch them only for a number of days (2:80), that none will enter Paradise except a Jew or a Christian (2:111), and that they are the children of Allah and His beloved (5:18). What they meant was that since their faith was the true one, they were sure of salvation: the repentant and forgiven admitted to Paradise from the start, the sinners released from Hell after a few days' punishment, and the obedient welcomed like sons and beloved friends.

**"then wish for death"**. Ask for death. The Arabic ties both conditions to the verb "wish", so that the sense is: if you speak truly in claiming that it is yours, you will naturally incline to what is yours, and since the road to it is death, long for death. Wish for it and ask for it so that you may reach that place quickly and rest from the burdens and worries of this life. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq related from Ibn ʿAbbās that the meaning is "invoke Allah to bring death on the lying camp", whether the Muslims or the Jews. The Jews declined the Messenger's ﷺ offer. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise reported Ibn ʿAbbās explaining "wish for death" as "pray for death".

**"if what you say is true!"**. If you are truthful in your claim. This challenge was aimed not at the Jews of every age but specifically at the Prophet's ﷺ contemporaries, who denied him out of envy and malice despite recognising him as a genuine prophet.

### What would have happened had they wished

ʿAbd ar-Razzāq narrated from ʿIkrimah that Ibn ʿAbbās said: had the Jews invoked Allah for death, they would have perished. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded Saʿīd ibn Jubayr relating from Ibn ʿAbbās that had the Jews asked for death, every one of them would have choked on his own spittle. These statements have authentic chains back to Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn Jarīr wrote in his Tafsīr that a report reached them of the Prophet ﷺ saying that if the Jews had wished for death, they would have died and looked upon their seats in the Fire, and that anyone who called down such a curse against Allah's Messenger would have gone home to find neither family nor property. Had they made that wish on that day, not a Jew would have been left alive anywhere on earth.

### A test that needed only the tongue

Apart from improper expressions like "sons of Allah", claims of this kind are in themselves correct, provided they are made by people who follow a true and valid faith. The Jews, like the Christians, were still following a faith that had been abrogated and was no longer valid, and that nullified their claim. The Qur'an refutes it repeatedly in different ways, and this verse adopts a special method. The ordinary way of settling a dispute is a discussion in which both sides present their arguments, but the Jews knew they could not win and shied away from it. So the Qur'an proposes an unusual trial requiring no great knowledge or understanding, only a little strain on the tongue. If the Jews were so sure that the blessings of the next world were theirs, let them declare that they wished to die, and that declaration would establish them as sincere. If they refused the challenge, it would show them to be liars. The Qur'an also predicted that they would never have the courage to go through with it.

### The same challenge in Sūrat al-Jumuʿah and at Najrān

A similar passage in Sūrat al-Jumuʿah tells the Jews that if they claim to be Allah's chosen people out of all humanity they should wish for death, that they never will because of what their hands have done, and that the death they flee will overtake them and return them to the Knower of the seen and the unseen (62:6-8). Because they claimed to be Allah's sons and beloved ones, and said that only Jews or Christians would enter Paradise, they were called on to invoke Allah to destroy the lying party, themselves or the Muslims. When they declined, everyone was sure they were in the wrong, for people certain of their claims would have accepted, and their lies stood exposed. In the same way the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the delegation of the Christians of Najrān to a mutual curse after refuting them in a debate in which they had shown stubbornness and defiance. Allah told him to say to whoever disputed about ʿĪsā (Jesus) after knowledge had come: come and bring our children and yours, our women and yours, ourselves and yourselves, and then sincerely invoke Allah's curse on the liars (3:61). When the Christians heard the challenge, some said to each other, "By Allah, if you do this with this Prophet, not one of you will be left with an eye that blinks." So they made peace and paid the jizyah in humiliation, and the Prophet ﷺ accepted it and sent Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ back with them as a trustee. Allah also commanded His Prophet ﷺ to tell the polytheists that whoever is entrenched in misguidance, the Most Compassionate will give him plenty of rope (19:75), that is, whichever of us has deviated, may Allah increase and prolong his deviation. This mutual invocation (mubāhalah) is called a "wish" here, because every just person wishes that Allah would destroy the unjust opponent debating with him, especially when he holds clear proof of the truth he calls to. And the mubāhalah involves invoking death on the unjust party because, for disbelievers, life is the greatest prize, above all when they know the evil destination that awaits them after it.

### Longing for death as a sign of faith

The devotional reading notes that one sign of ardent longing (ishtiyāq) is to desire death while enjoying the best of health. Whoever is confident beyond all doubt that the Garden is his longs for it ardently. The Jews did not long for the Garden, and Allah said that they never would, and the fulfilment of this was a miracle for the Messenger ﷺ, for it turned out as He had said. In this there is good news for believers who long for death: forgiveness is theirs, for Allah bestows that longing only so that it may be realised when they reach the Garden. As was said of old, for the negligent, shame will be enough on the Day of Meeting.

### In short

- If Paradise were exclusively the Jews', they should have longed for the death that leads to it, and they were invited to pray for death on whichever party was lying.
- Ibn ʿAbbās and the early authorities say that had they done so, they would have died on the spot, and Ibn Jarīr relates the Prophet's ﷺ word that they would have seen their seats in the Fire.
- The test required only words, yet the Jews, who knew the truth of Islam in their hearts, dared not take it, which is itself evidence for Islam.
- The same mubāhalah logic appears in 62:6-8, in the challenge to the Christians of Najrān (3:61), who chose the jizyah instead, and in 19:75.

95.text:
Verse 95 announces the outcome before the test is even taken. "But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers".

### Phrase by phrase

**"But they will never wish for that"**. They will never ask for death. Given their hostility to the Prophet ﷺ, one might have expected them to seize on so simple a challenge, but in their heart of hearts they knew that the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims stood for the truth and that they themselves were champions of falsehood, in fact unbelievers. They refused the trial because they were struck with awe, afraid that the moment they voiced the wish, death would come and they would be sent to Hell. Their refusal is itself evidence of the truth of Islam.

**"because of what their hands have done"**. Because of what they themselves had done in the religion of Judaism: disbelieving in Allah, rejecting His prophets, distorting His scriptures, and rejecting the Prophet ﷺ, the consequence of their mendacity. They knew that they recognised him and disbelieved in him anyway.

**"And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers"**. He knows the evildoers, the disbelievers among them and among others, and He will requite them. Each person will be given what he has earned.

### Could they have wished in secret?

No one should suppose that the Jews perhaps accepted the challenge and wished for death silently in their hearts. First, the Qur'an itself predicts that they would never wish for it. Second, had they been able to wish it in their hearts, they would certainly have declared it aloud, since their victory lay in exactly such a declaration, and it offered the easiest possible way of refuting the Prophet ﷺ, yet they did not take the opportunity. Nor can one suppose that they did make a declaration that simply went unreported. The opponents of Islam have always outnumbered its adherents, and had any such thing happened they would have trumpeted it to the world to show that the Jews had passed the test the Qur'an itself proposed.

### In short

- The Jews never wished for death, exactly as the verse foretold, because their own deeds told them what awaited them.
- Their refusal to take so easy a test is an argument for Islam, and no secret or unreported acceptance is conceivable.
- Allah knows the wrongdoers and will repay each according to what he has earned.

96.text:
Verse 96 explains the refusal. "You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists. Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years. But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment. And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do".

### Phrase by phrase

**"You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people"**. The sentence opens with an oath-particle in Arabic: you will certainly find the Jews the most covetous of mankind for life, eager to remain in this world even if that life is miserable and lowly. They are greedy for a longer life because they know their evil end and that their only reward with Allah is total loss. This world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever, so the People of the Book want to put off the Hereafter as long as they can. They will nevertheless meet what they are trying to escape.

**"even more than polytheists"**. Even greedier than the Arab idolaters, who reject the Resurrection and the reckoning. The Jews know that their journey ends in the Fire, while the idolaters do not believe even in that. The polytheists, who have no divine book, would naturally love a long life, since for them physical life was the be-all and end-all. The Jews acknowledged the next world, and even imagined that they alone deserved its joys, yet no one wished to stay in this world as long as they did. That very desire shows how hollow their pretension was, and that they themselves knew the fires of Hell awaited them, so that physical life, for as long as it lasted, was a kind of protection against their final fate. The Jews know what humiliation awaits them in the Hereafter for ignoring a truth they recognised. This is the basic weakness that kept them from accepting the challenge of the preceding verses.

**"Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years"**. Any one of them would love to be granted a life of a thousand years. The Arabic particle law, "if only", together with its clause spells out the object of the verb "would love".

**"But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment"**. The granting of such a life would not budge him from the chastisement of the Fire. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq related Ibn ʿAbbās explaining that a long life will not save them from torment. ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said that the Jews are the most eager for this life and wish they could live a thousand years, but living a thousand years will not save them from torment any more than Iblīs's long life benefited him, since he was a disbeliever. No length of life, however great, would put any distance between them and Allah's punishment.

**"And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do"**. Allah knows what His servants do, good or evil, and will repay each accordingly. He sees their contraventions and rebellion, and what they hide about the description and traits of Muḥammad ﷺ. Nothing is hidden from Him. A variant reading has "what you do".

### What their history proves

That the Israelites were never really concerned with truth is proved by their own history. They had killed their own prophets, such as Zakariyyā (Zechariah) and Yaḥyā (John the Baptist), for no other reason than that these prophets criticised their way of life and tried to bring them back to the divine path, a fact recorded in their own scripture in the book of Nehemiah. They had watched Mūsā (Moses) perform undeniable miracles, but as soon as he left them for forty days on Mount Sinai they began worshipping the golden calf, since only his personal authority had kept them in check. When the Mount was raised threateningly over their heads they agreed for a time, as the book of Exodus records, to do all that the Lord had spoken, but afterwards most of them went back to their disobedient ways. Had they truly been seeking God, their attention would have been fixed entirely on the life after death, whereas in fact they, more than anyone, were obsessed with love of the present world.

### Love of life as heedlessness

The devotional reading explains that love of this worldly life is the result of heedlessness (ghaflah) of God, and the worst heedlessness is their excessive love of remaining in this world. The believer's state is the opposite. The heedless and the insolent are eager for life only because they know how they have failed in obedience, just as a runaway slave has no wish to be brought back to his master. For believers, the passage of death to the One from whom only good is expected is better than remaining among those from whose evil they are never safe. Prolonging life in the face of certain death holds no value for them, since death comes unannounced and life is cut short. What is coming is near, and when a life span is complete nothing can fend off the assault of the appointed time from the shoulders of hope.

### The occasion that follows

The verse leads into the next passage. ʿAbdullāh ibn Ṣūryā asked the Prophet ﷺ, or, in another report, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, which angel brings down the revelation. Told that it was Jibrīl (Gabriel), he said: "He is our enemy, because he brings chastisement. Had it been Mīkāʾīl (Michael) we would have believed, for he brings fertility and security." The verses that follow were revealed in answer to this.

### In short

- The Jews cling to life more than anyone, even more than idolaters who deny the Resurrection, because they know what awaits them.
- A thousand years of life would not move them an inch away from the punishment, as Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd ibn Aslam explained, no more than Iblīs's long life helped him.
- Ibn Ṣūryā's objection to Jibrīl, which the verse leads into, caps the picture. Their own history, prophets killed, the calf, the broken pledge at Sinai, shows a people more attached to this world than to truth.
- Love of this life is heedlessness of Allah. The believer, expecting only good from Him, does not fear the journey to Him.

97.text:
Verse 97 answers the Jews' newest excuse, that the angel who brought the Qur'an was their enemy. "Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart by Allah’s Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers.”" The angel is only a messenger, and the message he carries is exactly what a divine Book should be.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ 'Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel'"**. Imām Abū Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī recorded that the scholars of Tafsīr agree this verse and the next were revealed in response to the Jews, who claimed that Jibrīl (Gabriel) was their enemy and Mīkāʾīl (Michael) their friend. The saying is traced to ʿAbdullāh ibn Ṣūriyā in particular. Let whoever is an enemy to Jibrīl die in his exasperation, for an enemy of Jibrīl is automatically an enemy of Allah, and he is misguided. ʿIkrimah explained that the elements Jibr, Mīk and Isrāf all mean "servant", while īl means "Allah". Others say that īl means "servant" and the word attached to it is a name of Allah, since īl is the constant element in such compounds, just as ʿabd is the constant element in ʿAbdullāh, ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān, ʿAbd al-Malik, ʿAbd al-Quddūs, ʿAbd as-Salām, ʿAbd al-Kāfī and ʿAbd al-Jalīl while the remainder varies, and so too with Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, ʿAzrāʾīl and Isrāfīl. Allah knows best.

**"should know that he revealed this ˹Quran˺ to your heart"**. Whoever is Jibrīl's enemy should know that he is Rūḥ al-Qudus, who brought down the glorious Reminder (dhikr), the Qur'an, to your heart from Allah. He is therefore a messenger from Allah, and whoever takes one messenger as an enemy has taken all the messengers as enemies. Jibrīl did not choose his missions himself but acted on his Lord's command. The angels say that they descend only by the command of your Lord (19:64), and the Qur'an is a revelation from the Lord of all worlds, brought down by the trustworthy spirit upon the Prophet's heart (26:192-194).

**"by Allah’s Will"**. By Allah's leave and command. Allah sent Jibrīl to the Prophet ﷺ with the Qur'an.

**"confirming what came before it"**. Affirming the earlier Scriptures, the Torah and the Injīl (Gospel), and affirming the oneness of Allah that they taught.

**"a guide and good news for the believers"**. Guidance for their hearts away from error, and the good news of Paradise, which belongs exclusively to the believers, the bliss Allah has prepared for them. Allah says of the Qur'an that it is guidance and healing for those who believe (41:44), and that He sends it down as a healing and mercy for the believers, though it only increases the wrongdoers in loss (17:82).

### ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and the three questions

Al-Bukhārī records from Anas ibn Mālik that ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām was out working his land when news reached him that the Prophet ﷺ had arrived in al-Madinah. He came to him and said: "I am going to ask you about three things that no one but a Prophet knows. What is the first portent of the Hour? What is the first meal the people of Paradise will eat? Why does a child resemble its father, and why its maternal uncle?" Allah's Messenger ﷺ replied, "Jibrīl has just told me the answers." ʿAbdullāh said, "He, of all the angels, is the enemy of the Jews." The Messenger ﷺ recited this verse, then said that the first portent of the Hour would be a fire gathering people from the east to the west, that the first meal of the people of Paradise would be the extra lobe of the liver of a fish, and that if the man's discharge comes first the child resembles the father, while if the woman's comes first it resembles her side of the family. ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām declared, "I testify that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah." He then said: "Messenger of Allah, the Jews are liars. If they learn of my conversion before you ask them about me, they will slander me." When the Jews came, ʿAbdullāh went inside the house. The Messenger ﷺ asked them, "What kind of man is ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām?" They answered, "The best of us and the son of the best of us, our master and the son of our master." He asked, "What would you say if he embraced Islam?" They said, "May Allah save him from that." ʿAbdullāh then came out before them, bearing witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muḥammad is Allah's Messenger. At once they said, "He is the worst of us and the son of the worst of us," and went on abusing him. Ibn Salām said, "This is what I feared, Messenger of Allah." Only al-Bukhārī records this hadith with this chain, and al-Bukhārī and Muslim both record it from Anas through another chain.

### Why the Jews hated Jibrīl

The Jews' perversity was fertile in excuses for denying the Prophet ﷺ. When they learned that the angel Jibrīl had brought the Qur'an, they said that he was their enemy, since he had always been the bearer of the harsh commandments and the catastrophic punishments sent down on them, and so they would not accept a Book that came by his hand. They added that they could have accepted it had Mīkāʾīl brought it down, for he is associated with rain and divine mercy. The background is that in ancient times the Israelites, through their own rebelliousness, brought severe punishments upon themselves, and it was God's way to warn them in advance through the prophets, who acted on the words of Jibrīl. The lesson was that people must follow God's commandments or face His wrath. Instead of heeding the warnings, the Israelites came to see Jibrīl as their enemy because he was always the one who gave notice of impending doom. So when the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ proclaimed that he received his revelation through Jibrīl, they said: so it is our old enemy, who always brings commands from heaven against us, and no wonder the Scriptures, which are the Israelites' birthright, are now being delivered to a man of another tribe. But angels, rarefied creatures that they are, hold no grudges against mortals. They descend only by divine command to carry out the tasks their Creator assigns, in this case revealing the Scripture to the prophet God Himself chose. Given the clear proofs that the Arab Prophet had received the same revelation as Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Mūsā (Moses) and ʿĪsā (Jesus), and that it tallied with the earlier scriptures, the Israelites had no grounds for rejecting it. Their reaction sprang from insincere, unrestrained lives ruled by self-interest, empty convention and racial prejudice, with religion kept up only superficially to maintain the pretence that they were faithfully treading God's path.

The Qur'an's refutation is simple. Jibrīl is only a messenger who, acting as a messenger, brought the Qur'an down to the Prophet ﷺ under divine command. Why be so particular about the messenger and never look at the Book itself? The Book confirms the earlier Books of Allah, guides people and gives good news to the believers, and since that is what divine Books are for, the Qur'an is evidently a divine Book and must be obeyed. To reject it out of hostility to Jibrīl is sheer stupidity or outright perversity. The devotional reading puts the same point as a question: whoever thinks Jibrīl brought no good, what good is greater than the Qur'an that came down through him?

### "To your heart": words as well as meanings

Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī warned in his Bayān al-Qurʾān against a grave error that could be drawn from the phrase "revealed to your heart", namely the conclusion that Allah revealed only the meanings of the Qur'an and not its words. The supposition is baseless, because many verses of the Qur'an name Arabic as the vehicle of revelation for this particular Book, which should leave no room for doubt. Moreover, the heart perceives words as much as meanings. The heart is the perceiving agent, and the ears and other organs are only its instruments. In the state of revelation especially, the outer senses go dormant, and the words themselves reach the heart directly, bypassing the ears. Although the nature of revelation cannot be properly understood, a mundane analogy helps: in dreams we hear words and remember them afterwards even though our external hearing was suspended while we dreamt. So revelation of meanings to the heart in no way excludes revelation of the words. In any case, relying on one's own conjecture against a clear and definite statement of the Qur'an is a sin and an intellectual dishonesty.

### How the revelation came down

The devotional reading dwells on the phrase in another way. Magnanimous and beautiful is the Qur'an that Jibrīl brought down from the All-Merciful: the repose of the spirit of the friends of God, the healing of sick hearts, a mercy to the faithful, and that is why Allah says he sent it down "upon your heart", as elsewhere He says that the trustworthy spirit brought it down upon the Prophet's heart (26:193-194).
